MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay.
SEN. MARK KELLY: Got us into another war with- without- without a plan and without explaining- explaining to the American people what are we going to get out of this.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Senator, I'm sorry to cut you off, but I'm out of time, I have to leave it there. Thank you. We'll be right back.

title: Transcript: Energy Secretary Chris Wright on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Oct. 4, 2026
summary: The following is the transcript of the interview with Energy Secretary Chris Wright that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Oct. 4, 2026.
story: The following is the transcript of the interview with Energy Secretary Chris Wright that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Oct. 4, 2026.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Good morning, and welcome to Face the Nation. We begin with one of the Trump administration officials tasked with working to lower those high gas and oil prices, Energy Secretary Chris Wright. Good morning to you.
SECRETARY OF ENERGY CHRIS WRIGHT: Good morning, Margaret.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So, it's good to have you here. You said this past week that Americans can expect lower gasoline prices and diesel prices by election day. The Wall Street Journal editorial board has a piece outlining that the campaign to squeeze around financially is working, but they can still knock out significant Gulf energy infrastructure. They could be planning an October surprise before the U.S. midterms. We are still seeing Iranian attacks on ships now. I mean, how can you be so confident prices are headed down?

SEC. WRIGHT: Well, because we've got increasing supplies coming out of the Strait of Hormuz and they've continued to rise over the last months, over the last recent weeks. We've got U.S. gasoline production today at record high. We have demand for gasoline, as we come out of the summer driving scene, starting to go down. Similar stories with diesel. Diesel's mostly been infected by the Russia-Ukraine war and also by China's decision not to export diesel or gasoline into the marketplace. And of course, we're living with two refineries that were recently closed, large refineries in California that Gavin Newsom forced the closure of. And frankly, 15 years of Democrat policies that have been energy subtraction, trying to close coal plants, close refineries, and shrink our capacity. Which means when you get in crisis, we're just less resilient than we should be.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But you still think that in the next four weeks prices are going to go down?
SEC. WRIGHT: Absolutely. Diesel prices have been going down. Gasoline prices have been going down. I expect that to continue.

MARGARET BRENNAN: I want to talk about diesel in a minute, but I- I was reading that the U.S. was sending more defensive equipment to the Gulf countries to protect their oil infrastructure. I see there was a gathering of national security advisers at Camp David on Friday to talk about Iran and the conflict in Yemen. Can you share any outcome from that? I mean, is- is the U.S. about to escalate? We did just see a third carrier strike group get sent to the region.

SEC. WRIGHT: Look, the president has- has taken a strong stand that Iran, the world's greatest terrorist regime- regime, cannot and will not have nuclear weapons. So, of course, we're looking at every avenue to achieve that goal economically, to be prepared for what comes militarily. But we cannot pass to the next administration an Iran armed with nuclear weapons. Not only is that a threat to peace and stability--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Right.
SEC. WRIGHT: --that's a massive long-term threat to energy prices.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Right, but he's also said that they're not seeking a nuclear weapon. He said that just the other day that they might have actually already stopped. But in the immediate sense of threats to our neighbors who have refinery and production capacity, how do you guarantee that there is no October surprise that sends those prices going the opposite direction?

SEC. WRIGHT: Hey, well, there's no guarantees. There's no guarantees in conflict. There's no guarantees in life. But everything we're doing is to grow the supply of diesel, to grow the supply of gasoline, and frankly, again, to reverse years of policies that have been directed exactly the opposite, to shrink our ability to produce, refine, and deliver hydrocarbons.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Can you say whether the president has decided he will escalate post-election day? That's when that third carrier strike group will be arriving, mid-November.
SEC. WRIGHT: Oh, I'm definitely not going to get in front of presidents' plans or policies. But remember--
MARGARET BRENNAN: He'd thrown that out there himself.

SEC. WRIGHT: He's- he's always planning for contingencies and he's always negotiating. How you communicate, what you- what you lean in on, it sends a message to the other side. He's been a master, a master at doing that.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So he's got both tracks still going, diplomatic and military pressure?
SEC. WRIGHT: Of course, of course. At all times.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay, you talked about diesel. The world's wealthiest countries, the G7, this past week agreed to release 100 million barrels of fuel over four months. They're going to front load it with a lot of diesel in the next 20 days. I know you asked our friends and allies to consider doing this. How significant a price impact and for how long?

SEC. WRIGHT: It's a big deal. It's a big deal. Europe has very large diesel stores. They, you know, they don't refine enough diesel to supply their own economies, so naturally they store a lot of diesel. They're very keen to see American diesel continue to flow to Europe. They've got a lot of diesel in stores. Why not release some of that? This is what you store diesel for. When all the Russian exports of diesel are shut down, when the Chinese have said we're not going to deliver any more diesel, and you still have a reduction of diesel flows coming out of the Gulf, but we're restoring those, but that takes time. This is just common sense. This lowers diesel prices, not just in the United States, but it lowers them in Europe and around the world. But it will drive diesel prices down as those releases come. It'll drive diesel down through the winter in the United States and around the world. And- and by then we'll be in another place. We'll have more refining capacity online. I- I suspect we'll continue to see diesel decline as we go into next spring as well.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So below six bucks? Which is where it is.
SEC. WRIGHT: Yes.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah. By post-midterms?
[CROSSTALK]
SEC. WRIGHT: It's- it's down a little over 20 cents so far.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.
SEC. WRIGHT: I think you'll see it continue to go down. Yeah, you should see it below $6 before too long. But exactly when, I certainly don't know that.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So the allies did this after President Trump said he was considering a diesel export ban. You had so many quotes where you were telling people, "This was not a good idea." "Let's not do a diesel export ban." But the president kept saying it was a consideration. Has he completely ruled out an export ban at this point?
SEC. WRIGHT: Look, every day he's throwing out ideas. He's engaging with discussions with me, others in the administration--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Even when you're saying it's not a good idea?
SEC. WRIGHT: Absolutely. No, he- he- he's--
MARGARET BRENNAN: But you're the expert.

SEC. WRIGHT: --he says well- well, but there's different ways to slice this cat. There's different ways to look at it. He's always looking, "How do I lower energy prices? How do I lower heating prices, electricity prices, gasoline prices, diesel prices?" In fact, I would say his constant communication of that may have been quite helpful in achieving- in achieving the deal we just struck.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Because people thought he might actually not listen to you and go ahead and do it?
SEC. WRIGHT: I--
MARGARET BRENNAN: That was the- the ploy, essentially?
SEC. WRIGHT: It wasn't a ploy. It's just a constant dialog about the many levers we have. How can we drive down diesel prices and drive down gasoline and other prices along with it?

MARGARET BRENNAN: So we checked, and it looks like because of this Lindsey Graham bill that gives the president more, sort of, powers to punish the buyers of Russian fuel, he has to make a decision by October the 18th as to whether he's going to put tariffs on the biggest buyers. That would be China, and that would be India. Is he going to do that?

SEC. WRIGHT: Look, he- he leaves every decision till the end. He'll evaluate the trade-offs. He has worked ceaselessly to try to end this war. Not only would end- would ending this war end the killing of- of tens and of thousands of people every month, it would dramatically lower energy prices. He's wanted to end that conflict, yes, since before he was president. So, and- and there is constant, constant dialogs with both sides in that to try to bring that war to an end.

MARGARET BRENNAN: But at this point, like, what's the direction here? You just had this big state visit. Are we actually in a position where the U.S. might put tariffs on China for buying Russian oil? Are we actually going to see that, and what impact would that have?
SEC. WRIGHT: Again, I won't get in front of the president on that. We're trying to have the best relations we can--
MARGARET BRENNAN: I'm sure you've looked at the projections on what it would do for pricing.

SEC. WRIGHT: Of course, we're trying to have great relations with China and move that ball forward. I think things are going reasonably well there. But then the flip side is you've got to look at every leverage you've got to bring a murderous conflict to an end.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So he may and you would encourage him to?
SEC. WRIGHT: I'm not going to say- I'm not going to say on--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay.
SEC. WRIGHT: --either one of those. He's- he's looking to how to end that conflict and how to lower prices for Americans every day.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah. Well, the date just stood out, you know, weeks before the midterms, doing something that could arguably push prices back up. And so, if it's a national security decision versus a political one. Be interested to know your point of view.
[CROSSTALK]

SEC. WRIGHT: If his decisions were political he would have just kicked the can down the road and delivered a nuclear-armed Iran to the next president. You've got to respect that. That's an incredible move to lean in and say I'm not going to let them become nuclear-armed. He knew it was going to elevate energy prices in the short run. He said, "I'm going to take a hit there, but I got to do the right thing."
MARGARET BRENNAN: You did tell him that? That there would be a huge energy price spike when he made the decision.

SEC. WRIGHT: He- he was well aware of- of the risk to energy flows that were coming out of the Persian Gulf region. He said, "I simply cannot. The world cannot sustain a nuclear-armed Iran, and I'm not going to do it."
MARGARET BRENNAN: Secretary Wright, thank you for your time today.
SEC. WRIGHT: Thank you, Margaret.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Face Nation will be back in a minute. Stay with us.

title: Energy Secretary: Trump was "aware of the risks to energy flows" before Iran war
summary: Energy Secretary Chris Wright said that President Trump was "well aware of the risks to energy flows" before launching the war in Iran earlier this year, but argued "the world cannot sustain a nuclear-armed Iran."
story: Washington — Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Sunday that President Trump was "well aware of the risks to energy flows" before launching the war in Iran earlier this year, but argued "the world cannot sustain a nuclear-armed Iran."
"He knew it was going to elevate energy prices in the short run, he said, 'I'm going to take a hit there, but I got to do the right thing,'" Wright said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."

Americans have been feeling the financial squeeze of soaring gas and diesel prices in recent months. But the Trump administration has pointed to the potential threat a nuclear-armed Iran could pose, and how it could represent a long-term threat to energy prices. Wright defended the president on Sunday, arguing that Mr. Trump has taken a "strong stand that Iran, the world's greatest terrorist regime, cannot and will not have nuclear weapons."

Wright expressed confidence that prices will fall, pointing to increasing supplies coming out of the Strait of Hormuz, U.S. gasoline production, the summer driving season slowing, among other factors. Asked whether he expects prices to go down over the next four weeks — as Republicans eye a tough environment in the lead up to the midterm elections — Wright said, "absolutely."
"Diesel prices have been going down, gasoline prices have been going down," Wright said. "I expect that to continue."

Diesel prices soared of above $6.50 a gallon in recent weeks, squeezing farmers, who rely on diesel to run agricultural machinery, along with industries from construction firms to food banks, which rely on diesel to fuel their vehicles and delivery trucks. Wright noted that diesel prices are down a little over 20 cents so far in recent days, adding that he expects the prices to continue to go down.
"You should see it below $6 before too long," he said. "But exactly when, I certainly don't know that."

Wright said "everything we're doing is to grow the supply of diesel, to grow the supply of gasoline, and frankly, again, to reverse years of policies that have been directed exactly the opposite-to shrink our ability to produce, refine, and deliver hydrocarbons."

Wright wouldn't weigh in on the president's plans and whether things would escalate militarily after the midterm elections. But he said Mr. Trump is "always planning for contingencies and he's always negotiating," and both diplomatic and military tracks remain open.

The energy secretary said securing the agreement from the Group of Seven countries last week to release 100 million barrels of fuel over four months is a "big deal." He called it "common sense" and said it will drive diesel prices down in the U.S. and around the world through the winter.

"Europe has very large diesel stores. They don't refine enough diesel to supply their own economies, so naturally they store a lot of diesel. They're very keen to see American diesel continue to flow to Europe. They've got a lot of diesel in stores. Why not release some of that?" Wright said. "This is what you store diesel for when all the Russian exports of diesel are shut down, when the Chinese have said we're not going to deliver any more diesel, and you still have a reduction of diesel flows coming out of the Gulf. But we're restoring those, but that takes time."

Asked whether the president has ruled out an export ban on diesel, which Wright has opposed, Wright said "every day" Mr. Trump has been "throwing out ideas," and the president remains engaged in discussions.

"There's different ways to look at it. He's always looking, 'How do I lower energy prices? How do I lower heating prices, electricity prices, gasoline prices, diesel prices?' In fact, I would say his constant communication of that may have been quite helpful in achieving the deal we just got," he said.
Wright added, "It's just a constant dialogue about the many levers we have, how can we drive down diesel prices and drive down gasoline and other prices along with it?"

title: Key Biden aide recalls "draconian measures" being considered against Israel
summary: In a CBS News interview, Biden-era Middle East adviser Brett McGurk recounted the administration's response to the Oct. 7 attack, its handling of the Israel-Hamas war, the role of Iran and the long-sought push to normalize relations between Israel and Saudi Arabia.
story: President Joe Biden was on the verge of taking "draconian measures" after an Israeli military drone strike killed seven World Central Kitchen aid workers in the Gaza Strip in April 2024, but U.S. intelligence that Iran was about to launch an "unprecedented" aerial attack on Israel prevented Biden from moving forward, according to Brett McGurk, a top Middle East adviser to four presidents.
In an interview with "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" taped Thursday, McGurk described Biden as "fed up" with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's handling of the war in Gaza.

"At that moment, if not for that impending missile attack, which we then had to deploy military forces … I think we would have taken some pretty draconian measures against Israel," he said, adding that cutting off U.S. weapons to Israel "was very much on the table."

The U.S. and its Arab and European partners helped protect Israel from the Iranian attack, which McGurk said included 120 ballistic missiles, 170 drones and 30 cruise missiles that were "all launched to land at the same time."

In his new memoir titled "Brink," which is set to be published Tuesday, McGurk recalled a tense conversation between Biden and Netanyahu around that time in which the U.S. leader warned the prime minister he could end the weapons supply. At the time, the Israeli government said it believed there were more than 130 hostages in Gaza and around 34,000 Gazan deaths, according to the Hamas-run Gaza Ministry of Health.
"You think I'm Santa Claus? No Santa in Israel, pal," McGurk quotes Biden as saying.

In McGurk's interview with CBS News, the longtime foreign policy aide recounted the Biden administration's initial reaction to Hamas' Oct. 7 terror attack on Israel, its handling of Israel's war against Hamas in Gaza, the efforts to secure an Israel-Hamas ceasefire and hostage release deal, the role of Iran and — starting years earlier — a long-sought push to normalize relations between Israel and Saudi Arabia.
McGurk is no longer working with the Bidens and is currently a CNN contributor.
McGurk: "If you just stop American support for Israel, that is not going to end the crisis"

Biden's handling of the Israel-Hamas war has drawn years of scrutiny — including from within his own party. During the 2024 presidential campaign, the administration faced intense pressure to stop military aid to Israel amid the humanitarian crisis in Gaza.

The U.S. is the largest weapons supplier to Israel, and provides billions in aid. A 2023 State Department review of Israel's conduct found that it was "reasonable to assess" that Israeli security forces have used U.S.-made weapons in ways "inconsistent with" international humanitarian law obligations. Casualties in Gaza, "including high levels of civilian casualties," raised "substantial questions as to whether the IDF is using" U.S.-made weapons "effectively in all cases," the report said.

Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen told "Face the Nation" in November 2024 that Biden didn't use U.S. leverage effectively, arguing he sent Israel "more bombs and more money" after Netaynahu disregarded his requests, and pointed to U.S. laws blocking arms shipments to military units that violated human rights.

Since then, debates over the future of U.S.-Israel relations have continued to rage. Some of the criticism that the Biden administration was not strong enough in its response to Israeli actions in Gaza has been directed at McGurk, who was the White House National Security Council's coordinator for the Middle East and North Africa and one of his most influential advisers.

McGurk noted that the Biden administration did pause some weapons transfers to Israel, including 2,000-pound bombs but never instituted a weapons halt. He believes some of the calls to go further may not have been effective.

"Israel also has one of the largest arms industries in the world, so the idea that had Biden gone further on a step on that course, it would have stopped the war, I just think the record does not support that," McGurk said.
McGurk also argued that exerting too much public pressure on Israel could have hardened Hamas' stance, ultimately setting back the negotiations to end the war in Gaza and release the hostages.

"I come back to the question: How do you end this crisis?" he said. "And I think the record shows: If you just stop American support for Israel, that is not going to end the crisis, it's going to make it worse."

At the same time as the Israel-Hamas war, attacks on U.S. forces by Iranian-backed proxy groups surged. McGurk pushed Biden to punish Iran in an effort to deter the attacks, and expressed some frustration with Biden administration colleagues who were wary of striking Iranian officials in response.
What would've happened if Iran "made a dash" toward weapons-grade uranium
McGurk said part of Biden's goal was to prevent the outbreak of a broader regional war. Meanwhile, periodic aerial attacks between Iran and Israel continued.
In December 2024, McGurk traveled to Israel with national security adviser Jake Sullivan as they worked toward a deal with Hamas to release the remaining Israeli hostages.

During the visit, according to McGurk, Netanyahu talked about taking out nuclear sites in Iran, including at Fordow, a facility built inside a mountain that processed and stored highly enriched uranium. Fordow was one of the three Iranian nuclear sites that President Trump ordered to be bombed  in June 2025, eight months before the Trump administration and Israeli forces launched a wider war against Iran.

McGurk said the Biden administration was concerned in late 2024 that Iran "might make a dash" toward making weapons-grade uranium, and officials were open to carrying out strikes if there were evidence obtained that showed Iran was making a bomb. Netanyahu urged the US not to wait for that step. Iran had been building up a stockpile of 60%-enriched uranium, which is a short step from the material required to build a bomb.

"We actually had a principals committee meeting — that's everybody around the table — what would we do if we see that?" McGurk said. "And as I recall, unanimity on: We would do the strike in Fordow. We didn't see that. We sent a message to Iran, don't even think about it. But yet Netanyahu was clearly contemplating that."

Hamas and Israel struck a ceasefire deal that led to the release of some hostages a month after that, just days before President Trump was inaugurated and the Biden national security team left the White House. McGurk said he and Mr. Trump's Middle East envoy Steve Witkoff "agreed we're going to work in lockstep." He described how the Biden and Trump teams put pressure on both Hamas and Israel.
Hamas released the last living hostages in October 2025, as part of another ceasefire agreement.
U.S. saw no "warning or indicator" of Oct. 7 attack

The circumstances leading up to the Oct. 7 attack have drawn renewed attention in recent weeks, as The New York Times, The Atlantic and the Israeli newspaper Haaretz report on warnings that officials in Egypt and the United Arab Emirates allegedly delivered to Israel that Hamas was planning a major attack. Netanyahu has strongly denied that there were any warnings, but his opponents in Israel's election later this month have expressed outrage.

CBS has confirmed via a former US official and a diplomatic source that Emirati Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed al Nahyan, President of the UAE, did share a warning with Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu in the weeks leading up to the attack. The UAE had learned that Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar was preparing a major attack but did not have specific intelligence such as a date, time or location.
McGurk told CBS News the U.S. had no intelligence that could have warned about Hamas' Oct. 7 attack.
"We did not have anything in our system that would have been a warning and indicator," he said. "No U.S. intelligence of a warning or indicator."
But he said Israel should launch an official inquiry that probes its own security establishment and political leadership, much like the U.S. did after the 9/11 attacks.

"I think they had an assumption that was deeply ingrained that Hamas was deterred, assuaged, and was not about to do something massive on any scale like this," McGurk said. "I think that was a false assumption in their system, a failure of imagination, and it was tragic."
McGurk on the Biden-MBS fist bump: "I encouraged the president to just shake his hand"

Hours before the Oct. 7 2023 attack, McGurk said he met with the Saudi Arabian Ambassador to the U.S., Princess Reema Bandar,  to discuss a different issue — a potential pathway for Israel and Saudi Arabia to normalize relations.

MB SUGGESTIONED INSERT: Just weeks prior, Prime Minister Netanyahu had stood at the UN General Assembly in New York and predicted a new Middle East to include normalization between the Jewish State and the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, birthplace of Islam.
"I believe that we are at the cusp of an even more dramatic breakthrough: an historic peace with Saudi Arabia," Netanyahu said.

The idea of Saudi Arabia establishing formal diplomatic ties with Israel had been floated to McGurk by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman nearly two years earlier, in January 2021, shortly after Biden took office, McGurk said, a deal that would have included a pathway to a Palestinian peace agreement. McGurk said he reported that extraordinary offer back to the President, but the U.S. did not act on it.

Biden was skeptical of Saudi Arabia, vowing in the 2020 Democratic primaries to treat the kingdom as a "pariah" due to U.S. intelligence indicating that Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman was linked to the murder of Washington Post columnist Jamal Khashoggi.

McGurk also explained that Biden did not want to focus on the Middle East, and only reached out to the Gulf States after the chaotic August 2021 U.S. exit from Afghanistan caused the emergency need for the U.S. to ask those governments to take in Afghan allies fleeing the Taliban. The U.S. needed another favor in 2022 when Russia invaded Ukraine, and turned again to the Gulf states, specifically Saudi Arabia, asking them to pump more oil to alleviate a spike in prices.

Rebuilding frayed relations because a necessity for U.S. national security. McGurk said it was a "mistake" that administration officials did not engage with Saudi Arabia more frequently early in Biden's term. He convinced him to visit in 2022.

McGurk offered rare criticism of Biden over his 2022 visit to Saudi Arabia, which came during a global spike in energy prices. He recounts that for 18 minutes Air Force One sat on the tarmac in the Kingdom as Biden argued with aides over how he would greet the Crown Price at his palace.
Rather than shaking bin Salman's hand, Biden famously gave him a fist bump.

"He was concerned about the optics and the imagery," McGurk told CBS News, and "I encouraged the president to just shake his hand." He later said: "We were asking some very hard things to the Saudis that we needed for our core interests, and so I think the fist bump set us back."

By 2023, the U.S., Israel and Saudi Arabia were working toward a normalization agreement, a complicated deal that likely would have involved the U.S. offering Saudi Arabia a civil nuclear program and Israel agreeing to concessions around the Palestinian territories. The Oct. 7 attack derailed those talks — and President Biden often openly theorized that Hamas may have sought to prevent normalization.
McGurk said he "never saw anything to tie a direct connection," but didn't rule out that idea.

"Hamas, of course, does not recognize Israel, wants to destroy Israel, and I would not be surprised if one of the motivations on October 7th was to knock this agenda off the table," McGurk said, calling the prospect of Saudi-Israeli normalization "one of the biggest deals since the Cold War."

President Trump has revived the terms of that U.S.-Saudi arrangement, including the pledge to develop a civil nuclear program. However, the current Israel government has refused to discuss a Palestinian state in the wake of Oct 7 attacks, and the civilian death toll in Gaza from the war makes normalization more politically difficult for Saudi leaders.

title: Transcript: Brett McGurk on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Oct. 4, 2026
summary: The following is the full transcript of the interview with Brett McGurk, who served as a top Middle East adviser to former Preident Joe Biden, a portion of which aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Oct. 4, 2026.
story: The following is the full transcript of the interview with Brett McGurk, who served as a top Middle East adviser to former Preident Joe Biden, a portion of which aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Oct. 4, 2026.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So, October 6th, 2023, Saudi Princess Reema Bandar shakes hands with you on a deal meant to normalize relations, or start normalizing relations between Israel and Saudi Arabia, create a pathway for the Palestinians, give Saudi the civilian nuclear deal, and within hours this incredible attack happens in Israel. Why, in the book, do you argue that those two things are connected?

BRETT MCGURK: Well, first, Margaret, it's great to be here. And I try to just tell this history. It's chronological, but I really try to bring the reader into the room. And the book starts about three days into the Biden administration, President Biden asked me to go see the Crown Prince of Saudi Arabia about some significant changes we were going to make in Saudi policy, including cutting off various weapons systems and a number of steps. And the Crown Prince in that meeting kind of put on the table the possibility of recognizing Israel, a kind of big, you know, breakthrough possible deal. And we didn't really pick that up until about a year and a half into the administration, and I describe, I think, that was lost time and unfortunate. But once we did pick it up, we made some real progress on it, and we had a package of agreements, including the Palestinian Authority was working with us on this deal. And on October 6, you're right, I had a Saudi delegation in my office with Princess Reema. Tony Blinken was about to go to the Middle East. And we had mapped out- I still can't say if not for what happened a few hours later, we definitely would have gotten the deal. But it was definitely- it was moving in that direction, and we were quite confident. And Reema and I shook hands on by the end of the year, really, to have this in place, and then talk about the- the rollout of it in the first quarter of 2024. What happened just a few hours later obviously knocked that issue off- off the agenda and everything else. I think it's- it's tragic because I think that deal, when you step back, if you look at what was happening just a few weeks before the events of October 7th, we're now the third anniversary, you had things happening that had not happened in 55 years. You had a senior Saudi official visiting Ramallah in the West Bank to see the Palestinian Authority, first time since 1967. You had Israeli officials in Israel- or Israeli officials in Saudi Arabia, and- and I think a package that would have set the foundation for what is now in a UN Security Council resolution, Margaret, a credible pathway to Palestinian state determination and statehood. That's what we were talking about. Hamas, of course, does not recognize Israel, wants to destroy Israel, and I would not be surprised if one of the motivations on October 7th was to knock this agenda off the table.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Do you believe that Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar knew that there were these plans for a Palestinian pathway and normalization between Israel and Saudi Arabia, and that factored into his thinking?
BRETT MCGURK: We never saw anything to tie a direct connection.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay.

BRETT MCGURK: I never saw anything to tie a direct connection, but certainly it was known that this deal was moving in that direction. Mohammed bin Salman said it in September. It's like a- one of the biggest deals that- could be one of the biggest deals since the Cold War--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --Transform the Middle East if it had happened.

BRETT MCGURK: Yeah, so it was very much in the- But I think October 7th had been planned, from what we later learned, for a period of years, and this was not something that just suddenly put together. But I learned about the attack that night around midnight from Mike Herzog, the Israeli ambassador. I got a call from the Situation Room, also. It was rocket attacks and then cross-border attacks, and, you know, events kind of unfold- I describe it in the book of, as a crisis unfolds, you- you learn and you- you see jagged pieces. And it still wasn't clear even by daybreak, when I was at the White House, and eventually saw President Biden later that morning, just the scope of the scale of- of what was underway.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, you wrote that the U.S. "had no clear warnings; nor did the Israelis, from what they told us." But you leave open the idea that there were missed signals. Was this a total intelligence failure?
BRETT MCGURK: I think, Margaret- So we have really looked, we did not have any- anything in our system that would have been a warning and indicator.
MARGARET BRENNAN: No U.S. intelligence.

BRETT MCGURK: No U.S. intelligence of a warning or indicator. I can't speak to whether the Israelis- the Israelis still have to this day not had a commission of inquiry. We had a 9/11 commission that I think made a number of reforms that have helped keep our country safe since 9/11. The Israelis still have not done that. I think they have to, they should do that. But from what I, in dealing with all these guys in Israel, security echelon, political echelon, I think they had an assumption that was deeply ingrained that Hamas was deterred, assuaged, and was not about to do something massive on any- any scale like this. I think that was a false assumption in their system, a failure of imagination, and it was tragic. I can't speak to whether or not there was a specific warning. We did not, we did not know of any.

MARGARET BRENNAN: The U.S. didn't know, and the U.S. didn't warn. But there has been recent reporting in the New York Times, in the Israeli paper Ha'aretz, in the Atlantic, about multiple sort of heads up from other regional leaders. Emirati leader Sheikh Mohammed apparently reported to Israel's Prime Minister Hamas was planning a major attack. The Atlantic said Egypt's intel chief also came to Israel in late September and warned Hamas was mobilizing for an attack. He didn't have a date, he didn't have the specifics, but he had a warning. Why wasn't that taken more seriously?

BRETT MCGURK: So again, I- I know Sheikh Mohammed quite well. When something on- is on his mind, he'll call. He called me at the White House once. Great respect for him. But we- we did not- we were not aware of- of a phone call. And Abbas Kamal, the Egyptian intel chief, is a main character in the book, we're with him all the time. Again, I also I just never- I had not- I did not hear–and I've checked with a number of my- my colleagues on this–of a pre-warning of October 7 from those two individuals. So I can't- Again, this is why I think Israel should have a clear investigation of what was known, what was missed at the very top, and also, you know, what intelligence analysts might have been seeing things that others weren't, why that information wasn't passed up. That's what has to happen in a situation like this. Again, we went through it, and I think Israel should do the same.

MARGARET BRENNAN: But just days after the attack, on Capitol Hill, you know, the head of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Mike McCaul, said Egypt did give a heads up. Diplomatic sources said that there were messages conveyed in late summer and September, including a warning from Yahya Sinwar that he was going to do something. But you say it's just a failure of imagination, that as to what that something was.

BRETT MCGURK: I think, I suspect when you look back, you will find similar to the types of warnings that were in our intelligence system before 9/11. Nothing of a, kind of, an actionable nature. And remember, Hamas and Israel before October 7th, they were in a negotiation, this kind of ties into the theme of the book, Margaret, a hostage negotiation, because Hamas had been holding two Israeli hostages: [Avera] Mengistu and Hisham al-Sayed. Two- one Arab Israeli, one Ethiopian Israeli, who were mentally ill, found their way in Gaza, and Hamas have been holding them for 10 years, and the remains of some Israeli soldiers from- from an earlier war. That negotiation had been going on. Again, this just gets to Hamas. They hold hostages for- to exceed maximum leverage and concessions. And I think in the course of putting a new demand on the table, Hamas saying it's either this or else, given the assumptions that were in the Israeli system, it probably would have been a warning would have been read in that--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --In that context.

BRETT MCGURK: --this is Hamas trying to play for that negotiation. But again, I have to say, I don't- I don't know what was in the Israeli system and what was known in the Israeli side. I think that's why they have to, you know, they're going to have an election soon, and everything before an election, particularly in Israel, can get a little crazy. But once there's a new government, I think having a serious commission of inquiry for what happened and making any reforms to ensure nothing like this can ever happen again is very important.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Because you believe there should be accountability from the top down?
BRETT MCGURK: Yeah, I believe that- what was--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Or there is culpability?
BRETT MCGURK: --what was missed. Clearly, what- what was missed. I think it's very important for any country to go through something like that after a horrific incident like this.

MARGARET BRENNAN: In talking about Hamas, you write extensively about the country of Qatar and their centrality to the deal-making with Hamas because you weren't talking directly to the terror group, you were speaking through this country as an intermediary in order to get the hostages out. And you reveal that the Emir of Qatar told you Hamas was a burden to them, one he'd shed if only the U.S. asked. Do you mean to say Hamas is still only in Qatar because America wants them there? That we want that way to get in touch with the terror group?

BRETT MCGURK: Well, Qatar- and I go through this in- in the book. When you're- we're in this awful, horrific, awful crisis in every dimension and how do you- you can't just say stop the war release the hostages, you have to actually make that happen using diplomacy, leverage. And Qatar is the key mediator with Hamas leadership, and that is something that we inherited in our administration. It's been that way, they've been in Doha since the outbreak of the Syrian Civil War when they moved from Damascus to Doha, again, with the basically tacit agreement of Israel and also the agreement of, then, the Obama administration. So what the Qataris will say is, look, they're- they're here, they have their offices here partially for your benefit. So do you want us to get rid of them? Sometimes they would say that to us, and sometimes I said in peak of frustration, yes.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Kick them out?

BRETT MCGURK: Yeah, the question is then: where are they going to be, and how do you actually get something done? I mean, this is what was so tragic, Margaret. I mean, here- here we have the worst day in Israel since the Holocaust. We have about 1,200 people dead. We have the largest mass hostage attack in- or hostage crisis in modern history, and Hamas knew that by taking hostages on this scale, they will be treated as, basically, statesmen in a negotiation. I mean, that's kind of how it- how it plays out, and the asymmetry there is incredibly frustrating, obviously, to the Israelis, it's frustrating to me throughout the process, but Qatar plays a critical role. And Sheikh Mohammed, who's a character in the book, the Prime Minister and Foreign Minister of Qatar also, was a key intermediary. I don't think we could have gotten this done without him.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, it's a point in the context of the Israeli elections that's interesting because you know some of the candidates who are running to replace Netanyahu are saying Qatar's an enemy state. They're funding terrorism, and they need to go after them.

BRETT MCGURK: I have a chapter in the book where I lay out the the kind of enigma in dealing with Qatar, and, you know, the Gulf states are very often very divided because- you mentioned Sheikh Mohammed and UAE, and this gets into relations with- the relation between the state and political Islam with the Muslim Brotherhood, and countries like Egypt, Jordan, Saudi Arabia, UAE completely banned, for example, the Muslim Brotherhood. Whereas Qatar has a very different philosophy. Their philosophy is we have to deal with everybody. Of course, we have one of our largest military bases in Qatar. Qatar also has Al Jazeera. I was in the Bush administration, I remember President Bush railing on the Qataris about what was being played on Al Jazeera. So it is a chronic issue and something I think we raise with Qatar very strongly. But when it comes to these deals, Qatar plays a central role. It's just- it's just a fact of it, and I talk about this in the book. When you're in the middle of the crisis, we're trying to get hostages home, we're trying to manage what could be a broader regional war. We're constantly- one reason it's titled "Brink," we are constantly on the brink of a broader regional war, and without Qatar, we would not have had some very critical channels to try to keep things under- under control.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Let me ask you about the Israeli Prime Minister. You dealt with him quite directly. Throughout the book you document that. And in February 2024, you talk about a meeting you had with him. You were very focused on these hostages and trying to get them out. You said "for more than thirty minutes he never mentioned the hostages…Netanyahu was animated in discussing the military campaign and far less so when discussing the hostages–when he chose to discuss them at all."
BRETT MCGURK: Yeah.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Why? Why do you think that is?

BRETT MCGURK: Well, first of all, I describe Netanyahu, I spent a lot of time with him, he's kind of– As a negotiator, there's a term of art in the book called a ZOPA, Zone of Possible Agreement. And if you- if you just kind of line this up, where was the- you have Hamas saying, their core demand is they have to stay in power, go back to October 6th status quo, they stay in power, they will reconstitute, they'll be on Israel's border, they want all Palestinian prisoners released, and then we can release the hostages. Israel's core demand after October 7th is that Hamas can no longer be in power in Gaza, ever. Completely irreconcilable. And the hostages are such a central piece of this because you're never going to actually stop the war without- without the hostages. And there's a continuum in a hostage negotiation, and I've done them before, even outside this context, with Iran in particular, in which the hostage negotiator sets a price. And Maimonides, who was a 12th-century Jewish legal theorist, and he has a, kind of a commandment, and I have it in the book. There's no higher commandment for a state, for a government, than the redemption, he says, of hostages, of captives. But he also says there's a- the price cannot be so high to basically put the rest of society in jeopardy. And this is the- this is the tension, the- the demand to- to bring the hostages home, and ensuring that the price is one that doesn't encourage further hostage taking or set the conditions for the next war. Okay. So, and this- this is a debate, Margaret, that goes through Israeli society and went through the highest echelons of the Israeli government. It plays throughout this book. It went into this- Keith and Aviva Siegel, who were taken hostage on October 7th, in their home, they have a sticker–and they're very cooperative for this book–it says, "Gilad is alive." That was Gilad Shalit, an Amer- an Israeli soldier, held by Hamas for five years, released after five years for 1,000 Palestinian prisoners, hardcore Hamas operatives, including Yahya Sinwar, and like many Israelis, they supported that deal. And on October 7th, on Yahya Sinwar's orders, the elite units of Hamas are approaching Kfar Aza, their kibbutz, and eventually entering their home, taking them hostage. So where do you draw this line? And Netanyahu was- was focused far more on the military campaign and ensuring Hamas can never retain power in Gaza, believing the military campaign and the pressure on Hamas would lead to a deal that released all the hostages, whereas we were trying to focus on a phased deal. At least let's get some of the hostages out first. And Netanyahu always believed that more military pressure will actually deliver a better deal, whereas Sinwar believed more time would put more pressure on the U.S. and others to deliver him a better deal. So it makes this almost an impossible situation to deal with.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But it also reveals your frustration in that, that you felt the U.S. was putting more value on those lives than the Israeli government did?

BRETT MCGURK: I feel- I think the- the U.S. role in this, in all dimensions, we're trying to stop a war and- and get the hostages home, and the two were- the two are completely linked, and to reduce human suffering as much as possible in Gaza. You know Netanyahu, I describe him as obviously very confident in his assumptions–and he has a brother who was killed in the Entebbe raid–very confident in terms of his belief in how to deal with these groups, and yet I believe a lot of times there were miscalculations. This is also very very difficult. Yeah, but I describe my meetings with him- again, I bring readers inside the room. You're sitting there with Bibi Netanyahu. You're with intelligence chief of Egypt when Hamas is on another floor. You're- you kind of get a sense of what this is like in the day- in the day-to-day.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, it's an interesting dynamic because now, since the end of the Biden administration, there continues to be, sort of, debate about this strategy. And National Security Advisor Jake Sullivan has publicly suggested that the U.S. focus was so much on the hostages that it was almost a "trap," as he put it, "in thinking that we can get to a ceasefire and a hostage deal," and other things were sublimated to that objective. I mean, in hindsight, do you share that feeling?

BRETT MCGURK: I do not, and no- no one's been able to point to me to a moment in which we could have ended this war without the hostages. The war would not have stopped without the hostages. I don't- I don't believe that. And I think it's important to kind of really go through the history, as the book does. And if I could just pause on- on when we did have a hostage deal. About a month into the war, we had- we had a deal with Hamas–not easy, I described what it was like to get it–for all women and children. It's very clear, all women and children hostages are going to come out, and- in exchange for a number of Palestinian prisoners. And we had a ceasefire for eight days, and about 100 hostages came out. I'm talking about this with you here, Margaret, because three of those women that did not come out, because on the eighth day, Hamas said, "we're not going to release the younger women, actually. We'll release the young toddlers like Abigail, the young American girl. We'll release the 80-year-old grandmothers. We're going to hold on to the younger women." They said "We can't find them," which was completely untrue.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Wasn't part of the excuse that they were of military age too?

BRETT MCGURK: No, they said some- they claimed that, but they said let's- let's keep the ceasefire and talk about the older men. And in the book, I go through this night, midnight here in Washington, December 1st, and it's a moral quandary, and this is what a hostage-taker does. Hamas is good at this- Iran is- this is- they're masters at this. They put the moral onus on the other side. Do you skip the younger women, start talking about older men, keep the ceasefire, or say no, you broke the deal. Three of those women, Romi, Doron, and Emily, Margaret, came out on January 19th. I was actually on your program and I broke the news--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --I remember.

BRETT MCGURK: --I learned that- I learned about it–because I'd been up all night, they came out–in the green room here. One was taken from Nova Festival. Two were taken from their home in Kafr Aza. Late 20's, one is 31 years old. They should have come out in that November deal. Carmel and- and Eden, two other women, were later killed in a tunnel under Rafah together with six hostages, including the American, Hersh Goldberg, which I still- So, and I'm very clear in the book–when that deal broke down in November, because Hamas would not release those younger women, I thought we would be able to get to another deal sooner. One reason we didn't is that we came under massive attack, and I go through that in the book. In the next two months, we're consumed with that, and I go see the Iranians in Oman. But no, I do not think that there was a way to stop this war without the hostages. It had to be a hostage deal, and it took a lot to get there. I go through it in the- in the book.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Just on that point of those women. Some of them, after they were released, talked about the sexual assaults--
BRETT MCGURK: Yeah.
MARGARET BRENNAN: --that they experienced in captivity. Is that why the women, those young women, were held for so long?

BRETT MCGURK: Well, this got- that- that moment, and if you read the book, you're there. And I let readers make judgments. What would you do in this moment? We have a ceasefire. Eight days, the guns are silent. You have humanitarian aid flowing throughout Gaza. We have a deal for all women and children. Hamas says we're going to hold on to the younger women, and let's talk about the older men. Some of the older men were in their 80's. Do you say, okay, okay, let's- let's skip over the younger women and move to the men? Israel was unanimous that they cannot do that because it'll- it'll be the death sentence for the women, and given how some of the younger women were believed to have been treated, as you just referred to. Why did they want to hold on to the younger women? I think Hamas thought they were their- they were their, as Hamas would put it sometimes in the negotiation, their most precious cards, and--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Why?

BRETT MCGURK: I don't want to think about how they were being treated. I mean, there are many many testimonials now. Hamas wanted to hold on to them, and they thought they could get the highest price for some of them. I mean, ultimately, for women soldiers, it was 50- the keys, the nomenclature is: this is the keys, an exchange ratio for women soldiers [was] 50 life sentence Hamas, life sentence Palestinian prisoners, often who have killed many Israelis. They got the most- they got the most keys for the women.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Just to clarify that, there were literally, like, mathematical equations there of what one Israeli was worth in terms of Palestinians who could be released from detention, not necessarily from prisons, but from detention.
BRETT MCGURK: Both.
MARGARET BRENNAN: That's the key. From both places.
BRETT MCGURK: Yeah, this negotiation was- I mean, I- I don't think it has been--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --It was a ratio.

BRETT MCGURK: --so tedious and negotiated down to the individual names, and a ratio for how many prisoners for an older man, how many prisoners for a female soldier, and Hamas played with this all the time, all the way down to the very end of the negotiation, where they threw in a wrench at the end for even civilian, sick and wounded hostages. They put a new demand on the table for 300 life sentence prisoners, which had never been- those are all- life sentence prisoners were- was the key for soldiers, and Hamas changed that at the end. But I bring this- I bring it back to this because I think some of these facts have been lost in the horrific nature of this crisis, which is so polarizing and so difficult. But Romi, Emily, and Doron should have come out in November. The deal was unequivocal. And they didn't. Carmel and Eden should have come out, and they were later killed by Hamas in a tunnel under Rafah. And I go back to that November deal a lot, and- and could we have done something differently to keep that on track? And it's very tragic. But to your question, I- no, I do not think there was a way to end this crisis without- without the hostages. And- and I've told some of the hostages that have come out, Keith and others, I think Hamas intended to hold on to hostages for- for many years.
MARGARET BRENNAN: In order to stay in power.
BRETT MCGURK: Yeah, definitely.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Which ultimately they still are, just Yahya Sinwar and his family are not. But let's- let's talk about- you mentioned how polarizing this issue is. You have worked for both Republicans and Democrats. You are a national security official here, but all of what you were trying to do was happening at the same time as the American political cycle here–a presidential election. And there appeared to be unquestioning U.S. support for Israel and providing military support to Israel, and this became a political issue, particularly among Democrats. Then, the Republican candidates, including now-President Donald Trump, were criticizing that you weren't strong enough in support of Israel. How aware were you of the politics of the moment as you're making decisions like this?

BRETT MCGURK: Well, as you said, Margaret, I- I'm very independent. I've worked with Republican presidents, Democratic presidents. I was a law clerk for two judges appointed by Republicans, one by a Democrat. And- but let me bring you into the Oval Office in kind of, in a scene in which I think encapsulates this very issue. April 4th, 2024. President Biden, it's his reelect- he's- he's on the campaign trail, obviously frustrated about the situation, unable to articulate because the hostage talks have now collapsed. They had recently collapsed for a number of reasons I go through in the book. He's frustrated by being unable to point to how are we actually going to try to bring this to a close. We had a horrific airstrike from the Israelis that killed nine aid workers with World Central Kitchen, Jose Andres--
MARGARET BRENNAN: An Israeli drone--
BRETT MCGURK: --and which was so trag--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --hit the clearly-marked convoy.

BRETT MCGURK: --so horrific. And, so we have a call between Biden and Netanyahu, and Biden is just, like, completely fed up. And at the same time, however, Iran is planning to launch- we have intelligence that Iran is about to launch a massive ballistic missile drone attack directly against Israel, which is totally unprecedented, and- which if those missiles get through, you're talking about thousands of casualties. So this is how, kind of, everything converges. And I think at that moment, if not for that impending missile attack, which we then had to deploy military forces, we built an unprecedented coalition with Arab partners, European partners, and of course the U.S. military and General Kurilla, who was kind of putting this together. If not for that, I think on that- that moment, I think we would have taken some pretty draconian measures against Israel.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Really?
BRETT MCGURK: Yeah, I do not--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Draconian how? What do you mean?

BRETT MCGURK: Well, I think we would have-- you just mentioned cutting off weapons and other things. That was very much on the table. But also at that time in April, Congress, bipart- a massive bipartisan majority approved a $26 billion aid package for- for Israel, right in April, right in that moment. So to put this- I try to bring readers here into the immediacy of the actual moment and what was happening. But the the focus very quickly shifts to how do we defend Israel from this- from this missile attack, It ended up being 120 ballistic missiles, 170 drones, 30 cruise missiles, all- all launched to land at the same time. I described that in the Situation Room, that moment, and just what that was like.

MARGARET BRENNAN: And ultimately, the United States and all of these regional partners and allies protect Israel from that incoming attack, and it was a pretty extraordinary effort. But on the World Central Kitchen event, cause that- people remember that. There was outrage around that. You wrote that President Biden told Bibi Netanyahu, the Prime Minister, that he could, in theory, "cut Israel from military aid at a finger snap," leaving Israel on its own. "You think I'm Santa Claus? No Santa in Israel, pal."
BRETT MCGURK: Yeah.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But he didn't. He didn't cut.
BRETT MCGURK: Well, I mean, we--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Did he actually mean that as a threat?

BRETT MCGURK: We selectively- we talked about it in that- in the Oval Office around that time. We selectively, after that call, the president stopped all sales and deliveries of heavy payload munitions, 2000-pound bombs. We- we stopped--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, he delayed them, ultimately.

BRETT MCGURK: Well, we- we didn't- we didn't deliver them and we didn't approve any other sales. President Trump reversed that immediately after coming into office. We selectively paused weapon systems that could have been used in the West Bank by Itamar Ben-Gvir--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Some extremist members of--
BRETT MCGURK: --given issues in the West Bank--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --the Israeli government.

BRETT MCGURK: So it was a selective- it was a selective use. But I think- and I- I know this is- this is obviously a debate now, and I think the question you have to ask, and what I always asked, and- and the theme runs out throughout the book. Would a certain step, whatever it is, help reduce human suffering in Gaza and help facilitate an end of the war? And that is the key question, the key test. And when we did a UN Security Council resolution calling for a ceasefire without the hostages, it actually set the process of- set the talks back. Hamas leaders went to Tehran right after that and basically hardened down. When we increased public pressure on Israel, you could see Sinwar kind of backing off. So this is the difference between private pressure, which the president was doing there on that call, and- and much more public measures. Because the public statements are read by all the other actors in this crisis, Margaret. And the actors are not just Biden and Netanyahu, it is Khamenei and Nasrallah and Sinwar and everybody else.
MARGARET BRENNAN: The Iranian leaders, the Hezbollah leaders--
BRETT MCGURK: Right.
MARGARET BRENNAN: --all the players are parsing every word.

BRETT MCGURK: Right, and remember, Israel also has one of the largest arms industries in the world, so the- the idea that had Biden gone further on a step on that course, it would have stopped the war- I just think the record does not support that.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, and of course, Republicans criticized even the idea of the delay--
BRETT MCGURK: Well, the House- the House voted with- the House voted to reverse it.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.
BRETT MCGURK: Actually, yeah. So I think put- put all this together- I say in the book, if there was an easier path for the president to take to end this crisis, he would have taken it.

MARGARET BRENNAN: But- but I bring this up because it continues to be a live issue now, particularly on the left, and it was an- an issue that became so politically heated in 2024, and it drew in members of the national security team. I mean, it was February 2024, the administration sent out to the very key state of Michigan, where there's a very large Arab-American and Jewish population, the Deputy National Security Advisor Jon Finer, who told members of the Arab community he was aware of missteps, including "a very damaging impression based on what has been a wholly inadequate public accounting for how much the president, the administration, and the country values the lives of Palestinians." He said that began "pretty early in the conflict." Do- do you agree that that was a mistake?
BRETT MCGURK: I--
MARGARET BRENNAN: That Biden didn't show empathy, is what he's saying, for civilians, particularly Palestinians who were caught in the midst of this horrific war between Hamas and Israel.

BRETT MCGURK: I just know- what I think Jon would have been talking about there is that this is something that- I describe it like a tear in your soul working on this and trying to bring it to a resolution. But I think the time sequencing is important, and I hope whatever side of the issue you might be on, if you read this book, and I don't- I- the reader can make its own judgments of what was happening at the- at particular times. In February, that's the time frame you just mentioned, we just had three Americans killed in a- in an Iranian drone attack fire by Kata'ib Hezbollah, their- their marquee militia group in Iraq, directly targeting our living quarters. It wounded dozens of Americans and killed three soldiers on January 28, and that came after a series of escalating attacks against our people, trying to kill Americans. I went to see the Iranians in January, in Oman, all about this. The attacks continued to escalate, and President Biden, in early February, ordered the largest airstrikes, Margaret, since early in the Iraq War and also ordered airstrikes against an Iranian commander in Iraq. I was- so I document all this and explain it, and I say that just because the- the crisis in its multiple dimensions was so regional in scope, and what the president had on his mind constantly was trying to prevent an all-out regional war.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

BRETT MCGURK: I mean there was, you know, headlines "We're on the verge of all-out regional war," and one reason the book is called Brink, as I mentioned, is because we were oftentimes on the brink of an all-out war, and I go through those moments. But anyway, I- I can't speak to exactly what Jon was talking about there. Yeah.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But that must have- I mean, he's the Deputy National Security Advisor. You must have had these debates.
BRETT MCGURK: Well, Jon's a- Jon's a close colleague of mine.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

BRETT MCGURK: He ran the- he ran the Deputies Committee meeting. I mean, everybody in the U.S. government had their- had their views expressed in the Deputies Committee meeting. The question always was, how do we bring this to a close? Period. How do you- again, you can't just say end the war. You can't just say contain it and don't have a regional--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

BRETT MCGURK: --conflict, bring the hostages home. How do you actually do it? And the- and the- Sinwar is holding the hostages. He will not release the hostages until, what? How do you get him to a yes on- on terms that can be accepted also by the Israelis.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Right, but the president made a very big point–and you were talking about the public versus private message. The president made this very big point of going and giving a bear hug to Prime Minister Netanyahu to say: the U.S. and Israel, there's no daylight here, we are with you, there is American support for you defending yourself. And it seems like there is an acknowledgement that there was not the public asterisk: but by the way, this civilian casualty count is far too high. At least it didn't come from the president himself. Do you agree with that?

BRETT MCGURK: I don't. I think the president- the horror of this war, the horror of October 7th, and the horror in Gaza, truly hell on earth, and nothing diminishes the lives lost. But you- you're talking there about the president's trip to- to Israel in particular, and let me give an anecdote because it's important. I describe this as, I've never seen a worse backdrop to a military- was going to be a military battle, ever. Hamas spent 20 years building military infrastructure under Gaza. You've known me a long time, Margaret. I was in the counter ISIS campaign. I was in Mosul. I saw it up close. Nothing like this. And we immediately said- the president said, "Where are the civilians going to go?" And--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Because this is 25 miles, Gaza's small.
BRETT MCGURK: Very small. It's extremely tiny. I think Americans who haven't been to Israel or been there, they don't understand how small everything is.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So you drop a 2,000-pound bomb, and that's going to have a blast radius that kills civilians.
BRETT MCGURK: We want to get civilians out of harm's way. In Mosul, we got a million civilians out. There were still many left there--
MARGARET BRENNAN: You're talking about in Iraq, with the ISIS fight--

BRETT MCGURK: --and- and in Syria, 6 million Syrians left the civil war. This is- in Gaza, there was nowhere for people to go. I- I called Abbas Kamel, the intel chief of Egypt, said, "Look, we got to find a way to allow Gazans at least to come temporarily into- into Sinai." Answer is absolutely not. The president on that trip--
[CROSSTALK]
MARGARET BRENNAN: Egypt refused--
BRETT MCGURK: --this is why this is important--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --to take them. Mmhmm.
[END CROSSTALK]

BRETT MCGURK: The President on that trip was going to Amman- to Amman first. About eight days into the war, president wants to go to Israel. I explain why he wanted to go to Israel at a critical moment. We're going to stop in Amman to see King Abdullah, to see Mahmoud Abbas, the head of the Palestinian Authority, and President Sisi to have this discussion. And unfortunately, that trip was pulled down because the day we were leaving, there was an air- looked like an airstrike at a hospital, Al-Ahli Hospital, and there were headlines that an Israeli airstrike killed 500 Palestinians–turned out not to be true. But because of that, King Abdullah said, "please don't come." We understood why, and we only went to Israel, and we did not have that- that engagement. I think the- this is- the fact that in Gaza civilians had nowhere to really take shelter, the underground facilities were only for Hamas, they made that very clear. And even when the Israelis said, let's- once they gave us a map, you know, "let's- we will declare this area a safe zone."
MARGARET BRENNAN: Right.
BRETT MCGURK: It's Mawasi, and--
MARGARET BRENNAN: You write about this.

BRETT MCGURK: --and the UN refused to work with them on that, as did we, because we said, "No, no, you can't, you- you can't kind of force people into a certain area." But then it was like, where are people going to go? So the whole backdrop to this is so horrific, and- and it took a massive toll on civilian life, and it took a massive toll on- on Israeli soldiers as well, as I talk about. It was a real war.

MARGARET BRENNAN: I mean, you nod to some regret in that incident. You said [about] that declaration of a safe zone, you regret that the U.S. wasn't "more creative," as you put it, "in working with Israel on an imperfect solution" to humanitarian corridors.
BRETT MCGURK: Yeah.
MARGARET BRENNAN: I mean, are you saying it was a delusion to think there was a perfect solution, or do you think there really was more that could have been done?

BRETT MCGURK: I- I think, very imperfect mechanisms to get civilians out of harm's way, that the UN and others could have supported. Often, everybody is kind of on the- on the sidelines, saying the war should stop somehow. But without like- let's think, how can we actually get civilians out of harm's way? Now the Israelis did tell people to move, and they did it kind of on their own. But they did- they got no help from that, from the UN, or others. They would just not even be a part of encouraging people to move or to setting up safe areas--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Claiming it would appear to be forced displacement.

BRETT MCGURK: Yeah, and- and working with the Israelis and all the history here, which I go in in the books. I- but the- it comes back to the core question of, given Hamas has this underground military infrastructure, how- the- the campaign is going to be so destructive. That's what concerned me from the start. I saw not Mosul and Raqqa, which you did not have this underground infrastructure or, you know, decade or so to prepare. It's absolutely awful.

MARGARET BRENNAN: It was Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen who kind of forced the hand of the administration in publicly reporting some of the U.S. assessments of how Israel was using the U.S.-provided weapons, because under U.S. law, they have to be compliant with American standards. And Secretary Blinken came on Face the Nation shortly after the report was released, and we had Senator Van Hollen on after him. Van Hollen said the administration ducked the hard questions. They didn't provide an "unvarnished account of facts and the law," and has set, as a standard, a "very, very low bar, a very low standard for what is acceptable." He said it will come back to haunt the United States. In hindsight, do you think he has a point there? That not being more fact-driven and making this information public, or concern about how U.S. munitions were used, that it could hurt, in the longer term, U.S. credibility?

BRETT MCGURK: I think I- I- that effort from Senator Van Hollen and the State Department report that came out- I describe it- I mean, I'm mostly, at that time, I'm overseas trying to get this- this hostage deal going on. But I start the book with a meeting in the- in the Situation Room, about two weeks left in the Biden administration, about this question, about to take more measures against Israel or not. And again, my- came down to, in my view, and I have to say, the, you know, the lawyers who set the- set the table would describe the legal parameters, and it was always a policy call. And in that particular scene, again, we're close to a deal. If you want to stop the war, you have to get a deal. And is the measure on the table going to move you closer to getting a deal or not? I mean, that was a very- to me, the only way to stop this war was a deal. So I don't- I- I can't take- I haven't seen that exact quote of what Senator Van Hollen was talking about in that time frame. I remember that debate, but I come back to, how do you actually end this war? And it was ultimately a ceasefire deal.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, it was such a public debate at the time about America's role in the world, the standards America is held to, and whether America is complicit in how our weapons are used. And under the Leahy Law, as you know, you know, countries that receive U.S. weapons have to avoid committing human rights violations or risk losing the weapons supply. Blinken said "it was reasonable to assess, in certain instances, Israel has not acted in a manner that's consistent with international humanitarian law," and that Israeli civilian harm mitigation efforts were "inconsistent, ineffective, and inadequate." Do you agree with that State Department memo?

BRETT MCGURK: I think the Leahy Law applies to individual units, and broadly speaking, that's why it's not- no aid to any country is unconditional, including- including to Israel, and- but security assistance is a- is a complex, multi-institutional, multi-branch endeavor. And again, these- most of these appropriations were appropriated by massive bipartisan majorities in Congress at the time. But- and the State Department has a role, and the Pentagon has an important role.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Right. He was saying hit the brakes on deliveries. Or re-examine--

BRETT MCGURK: Again, we- we hit the brakes on some- on some deliveries selectively. But to have a broad-based stoppage of- of support–again, for Israel at a time- I don't know what the time frame was for that statement, but I can--
MARGARET BRENNAN: That was in May--
BRETT MCGURK: So in May--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --2024.

BRETT MCGURK: Yeah. So in May we just had the largest ballistic missile and drone attack ever in history. We- but let me lay this out. So May. That's why the time frame and chronology is so important. Having lived through this, I remember it quite well. Largest ballistic missile attack in history. We help the Israelis defeat it. We say to Netanyahu- Biden's quote in that meeting is "I just saved your ass." We're getting back to the hostage deal, okay? We spend the month of May putting together a detailed four-page, three-phase agreement, single spaced, every detail there. We go to the Israelis and to Netanyahu and say, "we need you to sign up." And it went very far in the direction of Hamas. Frankly, it was a better deal for Hamas than what they have right now. And Netanyahu on May 27th signed on to that deal. On May 31st- because what were we doing in May? On May 31st, President Biden laid out that deal to the world in a speech, and he said, "Israel has accepted this deal. Hamas, say yes. Let's end this war." U.N. Security Council endorses that deal. It's May 31st. What happens? In early June, after this is on the table–we can stop the war right now if Hamas says yes–Khamenei, Supreme Leader of Iran, gives a defiant speech praising October- October 7th, and basically Iran is telling Hamas to not- to not compromise in any of the terms. Hezbollah launches its largest attack of the war, 250 rockets into northern Israel. This is when we have a ceasefire deal on the table. We don't get an answer from Hamas until July 2nd, almost five weeks later, and they put all sorts of things in it that set the talks back. So, I- I say this because we were working to end this crisis and end this war, and- in May, June, and we had the deal on the table to do it. My approach would have- is, this deal is on the table to stop the war. All pressure, everything, public, everything else has to come down on Hamas and their enablers to say yes to end this deal, or to end this war. But Hamas did not say yes, and they kept stringing us out, and they would put an issue on the table, then Israel would take a hard position. But that's what was happening in May, and if you go to that, you know, Biden goes to the world, says this is the deal. He had a phone call with, I think, 18 heads of state because these hostages are from countries all around the world. They all said- they called on Hamas to take the deal, and Hamas did not take the deal. And we were working at that time to end the war through a deal, and I think, again, all vectors of pressure should have been on Sinwar to say yes.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But you're not saying--
BRETT MCGURK: And the war would have stopped.
MARGARET BRENNAN: You're not saying that the Democratic Party pressure and calling out compliance with U.S. law was enabling Hamas. That's not what you're saying?
BRETT MCGURK: No, no, no. And I'm also not--
MARGARET BRENNAN: But you're saying it's almost, like, naive?

BRETT MCGURK: And I'm also not getting into internal party debates, I've never been a part of that. I'll let- I'll let political parties have their- have their debates. Not my role at all. I come back to the question: How do you end this crisis? And I think the record shows if you just stop American support for Israel. That is not going to end the crisis. It's going to make it worse.
MARGARET BRENNAN: And you think even just a statement that was more definitive on that would have been damaging?
BRETT MCGURK: No, we made- I mean, I- we made a lot of statements. We did U.N. Security Council resolutions, we did a number of things, which I think there's a- there's a real--

MARGARET BRENNAN: But this- this whole political argument at that time with the National Security Memorandum that was made public. It was, like, five out of eight State Department groups said, you know, basically they were not compliant with U.S. law. But you read it, and it's sort of, it looks like American diplomats are going out of their way not to say it directly, in order to avoid taking action that would result in the cutting off of aid.
BRETT MCGURK: I don't know. I- I--
MARGARET BRENNAN: It looks like the politics were influencing the policy, and I guess that's what I'm asking you to reply to.

BRETT MCGURK: I can't- the- the State- that State Department memo that was- that was done, again, at the request of Senator Van Hollen, and the Senate has its own dynamics for asking us to do certain things to keep votes off the floor that Senator Van Hollen might have wanted to take. But no, I thought that was, from what I understand, that was a very rigorous exercise. But had that memo said something differently, would that have ended the war? Would that have eased the humanitarian suffering in Gaza? Would it have gotten hostages home? No. I mean, that is where- like, that memo is so divorced, in my view, from the gritty, awful reality of how do you actually return hostages and end a war? I mean, and I- this is not a book about meetings in Washington. I've read a lot of books like that. I said this in this meeting. No- some of that. This is a book about being in the middle of it, overseas, where you're in the room with just the two or three people that can actually get something done, and- and trying to achieve the objective that everybody in Washington wants, and trying to actually accomplish that objective is exceedingly hard. And whatever that memo might have said, or whatever something might have been said in Congress, is that going to achieve the objective we're trying to achieve? I think the answer is no. So I- I come back to just what it takes to actually stop something like this.

MARGARET BRENNAN: And- and we had some of those hostage families and advocates on Face the Nation throughout the crisis who were appealing to the American president to stay focused on the hostages because they were frustrated that the Israeli government was not, and that Hamas was not interested. So I hear you on that. Let me just put a fine point on the issue here because I want you to be able to respond to this. There's another new book out about the Biden administration's handling of Israel's war in Gaza. It's written by Akbar Shahid Ahmed. He makes some very specific claims about things that you said and did. One administration official told him you seemed to be acting as Israel's lawyer when you were discussing IDF actions in October 2024. That you saw pictures of famine in early 2024, and you said people in Gaza did not look skinny. There are other claims in here, that your name was turned into a verb. Humanitarian officials were used to what one USAID staffer referred to as "getting McGurk'd," which meant overruling aid experts on Gaza. That sounds like a lot of internal disagreement. Were you aware of this?

BRETT MCGURK: I haven't read that book. That's categorically false. I've never- I've never said something like that. And in fact, and I think those who were actually- whether it was David Satterfield or others in charge of the humanitarian response, always knew if you need something done, you know, give me a call. I talked to David multiple times a day when he was the humanitarian coordinator. That is categorically false and just complete fiction.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Because this issue lives on now in our politics, particularly among progressive Democrats. I mean, Gaza, cutting off U.S. aid to Israel or reducing it, and on the right, we're hearing more about that as well.
