Has it surprised you that, like, the politics of this moment continue to be so infused with what happened then?

BRETT MCGURK: Well, I think on- you know, again, on the- on the aid question, there's one thing getting aid into- into Gaza, which we're very focused on, and pushing the Israelis on, and then actually distributing it throughout Gaza, which is- which is role for the U.N., and there was like almost been a breakdown there. It was incredibly frustrating, but no, I- my- my job was to try to bring this war to a close. And the way to bring it to a close was to get an agreement that included the release of the hostages. It's all- it's intertwined. You're not going to reduce human suffering, and you're not going to have aid flowing throughout Gaza like you need without a ceasefire, and you're not going to have a ceasefire without the hostages. This was just the- the awful, gritty reality of the- of the situation.

MARGARET BRENNAN: You wrote about- you nod fairly diplomatically to any disagreements within the administration at the time, but you write during this period of time- you're referring to January 2024 or so. You write: "During this period, I felt out of sorts with some of my colleagues, who seemed to take a two-dimensional view of the crisis, focused solely on Gaza and not the regional threat that Iran had unleashed, and which every day risked American lives." Who were you thinking of there? Why- why did you write that?
BRETT MCGURK: That was January, and the time frame is important. That was January 2024.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Mm-hmm.

BRETT MCGURK: We come under attack after- between October 7 and end of the year, attacks against us increase almost sevenfold. Almost every day we have attacks against us. It's very clear the attacks are intended to kill Americans. On Christmas Day, we have three wounded Americans in northern Iraq, one with Iranian shrapnel through his brain. Attack- Houthi attacks start against American ships, including against U.S. naval ships. These are anti-ship ballistic missiles going Mach 4, first time they've ever been used in combat. What I'm hearing from our military people is, "What are we doing about this?" Every single day. And what's keeping me up in this time is I'm going to wake up, and we're going to have two dozen dead American sailors in the Red Sea, or we're going to have two dozen dead American soldiers in Iraq and Syria. And the attacks kept coming, and we had a call with President Biden on New Year's Day, talking about how to respond. And we had the Iranian commander, I call him Mohsen in the book, we knew who he was, we kind of- we were close to his location, and I thought we should target him, to stop and deter these attacks.
MARGARET BRENNAN: A drone strike?

BRETT MCGURK: Yeah. President Biden in that meeting asked me, "Can you go see the Iranians? Knock this off." And I did, I went- and I had met with the Iranians many times over the years. I went to Oman on January 10th. I had a meeting with the Iranians. I describe it in detail in the book with the Omanis [intermediating]. And I describe what's happening in the region. We are under attack in Iraq. We're under attack in Syria,. We're under attack in the Red Sea. It's only by the skill of our military personnel, our defenses, that we have not had dozens of American dead and wounded, and this has to stop, or we're heading for direct confrontation.
MARGARET BRENNAN: And you can't get the president to act--
BRETT MCGURK: Well, he wanted--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --You were frustrated.

BRETT MCGURK: --to try to take this diplomatic path, and the Iranians in that meeting were complete- were- I describe it in detail, completely rejected having anything to do with this, which was total- a total lie.
MARGARET BRENNAN: They wouldn't sit across from you even. You're passing notes.

BRETT MCGURK: You're doing intermedia-, similar to now, what is still happening. So that- those talks failed. We started strikes against the Houthis, actually, the next day after that meeting failed. But then in January, the time frame, we come und- every single day, and I document this. And on January 28th, we have the three Americans and dozens of wounded from an Iranian drone. Yeah, my focus in that month was deterring these attacks and- and deterring what Iran had unleashed, including against us. That was my over- because I- what was keeping me up was, "We're going to have dead Americans," and then we did have dead Americans, and President Biden ordered a strike on Mohsen and other militia leaders that night, and the attacks stopped.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But the president was so concerned about avoiding a regional war.

BRETT MCGURK: The president, in his use of military power, Margaret, was very deliberate. We're- we're in this regional crisis. And he used to say–and this relates to the current moment–he used to say the American people understand the use of force to protect our people, and kind of a real core, vital American interest. They will not- they will not understand if we're being sucked into a broader Middle East war or reacting on behalf of Israel. It was a line he drew in his pulse of the American people and his role as Commander in Chief. It was an important line to draw. And he ordered, I mean, a decisive use of force in that incident in February, but he was- and, and defending Israel twice against direct ballistic missile attacks. But he was very deliberate, and he said it in a number of these meetings, which I talk about in the book, about- about drawing that line very carefully.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But you talk about "feeling out of sorts with some of my colleagues."
BRETT MCGURK: Yeah.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Are you going to tell us what was happening when you were having those disagreements? Who was arguing against defending these Americans?

BRETT MCGURK: There was an argument that if we target an Iranian officer–which is a big step, I recognize it–that could unleash a broader escalation. I just didn't agree with that. I thought we were- we were under attack constantly. We had to actually act to deter it. And one of the themes in the book is, Margaret, is that diplomacy, if not backed by power, is completely feckless.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But your--

BRETT MCGURK: And this was- this was- this was playing in, also, to the hostage talks. I mean, Hamas was just not even willing to engage because they thought everything was kind of going their way. You got Hezbollah barrages coming every day in the north. You have the Houthis attacking commercial and U.S. and U.K. naval vessels in the Red Sea. You have Americans under attack almost every day in Iraq. And until we contained that and stopped it, it was very hard to see a way forward on the- on the Gaza talks. It was all- all interrelated. So my consuming focus–I fully admit it in the book–in this period, was stopping those attacks, and I thought to stop those attacks we had to use military force.

MARGARET BRENNAN: But around that same time, in January 2024, Israel bombs Syria, killing an Iranian military advisor. In April, strikes Iranian diplomatic mission in Syria. In July, strikes Tehran and kills the top Hamas leader. Then that stunning operation to take out Hezbollah leaders with the exploding pagers. And killing Hezbollah's leader Hassan Nasrallah. On that particular strike, the U.S. didn't get a heads up.
BRETT MCGURK: Let's talk about some of those.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah, but that seems to be a building- the Israeli government doing the thing President Biden was saying don't do, which is risk a regional war.

BRETT MCGURK: Let's talk about some- some of those. Mohammad Reza Zahedi, he was the Quds Force officer, Margaret, that was killed in that strike in Damascus, April 1, 2024, same day as the World Central Kitchen attack. Who is Mohammad Reza Zahedi? He is the head of the Quds Force unit that enables and supplies Hezbollah. Hezbollah is firing into Israel every single day--
MARGARET BRENNAN: From Lebanon.

BRETT MCGURK: --From Lebanon. A strike against Mohammad Reza Zahedi, in our view, was a very legitimate self-defense strike. The Iranians said he was in a compound of the- of their embassy in Damascus. That's actually never been demonstrated. But in any event, the Iranians attacked our embassy. I was at our embassy in Baghdad multiple times, where they launched- their militias launched rockets at our embassy. We did not respond by firing 200 ballistic missiles into- into Iran. That's how Iran responded to that- to that attack. The Lebanon operation that the Israelis conducted beginning in September came after the complete breakdown of the- of the hostage talks. And because dates matter, we- we had a- we had an offer on the table, Margaret, on August 16th, endorsed by, you mentioned the Emir of Qatar, Tamim, fully endorsed 100% by Sisi. It went even further in the direction of Hamas. On April 16th, we never got an answer, and on- at the end of the month, we had six dead hostages in- in a tunnel underneath Rafah. And that's when that whole process just completely collapsed, and Israel went north into Lebanon. And when I look at this history now, and you kind of piece- it was after Yahya Sinwar was killed on October 16. It was after we defeated a second Iranian missile attack in October. It was after Hezbollah cut a ceasefire deal that there was an opening for the ceasefire to end the war in Gaza. It was the regional balance of power changing that opened the path to finally getting this- getting this deal.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But I bring up those series of events because the lack of heads up to the United States signals some growing distrust between the United States and Israel at that point in time.
BRETT MCGURK: Sure.
MARGARET BRENNAN: I mean Israel gave a heads up as the operation to kill Hassan Nasrallah was underway. Were you upset that there wasn't more advance notice?

BRETT MCGURK: Well, the Zahedi strike, I describe in the- in the book, did get an advance- I got a notice from- from the Israelis just before walking into a situation room meeting. I describe that in some detail. I think you're right, the Nasrallah strike the Israelis took, they didn't give us a heads up on that. That doesn't particularly surprise me, honestly. The Haniyeh intelligence operation in Tehran, which I also talk about in the book, we did not have a heads up on, but it was an intelligence operation in Tehran. This is not something that, like, Bibi Netanyahu can just say, "Hey, let's go after Haniyeh in Tehran." This is something that takes months of preparation, and- and it's a kind of a you- the stars align, and you- you take the action or you don't. But in many ways, those steps actually helped us open the path to ending the war in Gaza.

MARGARET BRENNAN: But the- well, it changed the dynamic in the Middle East, put Iran on the back foot in many ways, but I- I bring it up too because there is this perception- you know, at one point, I think it was the New Yorker**, quoted General Austin, then-Secretary of Defense, as saying that the Netanyahu government felt that it was playing with house money, that they knew America would be there no matter what, so they could up the level of risk even if President Biden wasn't happy with it. Did you feel like you were stuck in the middle of that dynamic where it was- the assumption was America was going to support it no matter what, and that they weren't necessarily going to listen to U.S. counsel?
BRETT MCGURK: Well, Netanyahu thought and believed, and has said publicly, he thought we cut off their weapons. So--
[CROSSTALK]
MARGARET BRENNAN: Back when we were talking about the--
BRETT MCGURK: Yeah. And he since has said that Biden had a--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --the Santa Clause reference that you write about.
BRETT MCGURK: --that Biden put an arms embargo on us. And he still believes that--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Which was not true.
[END CROSSTALK]

BRETT MCGURK: No, it's not true. But in terms of these particular operations in this broader war, that I mean, why, why was there this Hezbollah confrontation after October 7th? Because Hezbollah, on October 8th, started a war into northern Israel. Iran turned this whole thing up. It was a tragic mistake they made after the October 7th attacks. And I describe this in detail. We did not have information that Iran knew about the Hamas attack, but after that attack, they sensed a vulnerability against Israel, and they turned on all their proxies, and it continued to kind of escalate up the ladder, and then Israel is responding to- to that.

MARGARET BRENNAN: And I think what I'm hearing you say is you think President Biden's not given credit for stopping these things exploding into a regional war at once. He's not getting credit for the thing he prevented.
BRETT MCGURK: Yeah, it's not about credit--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --Is that right?

BRETT MCGURK: --What I try to do here, I don't say in the book- credit or not. You're there in the Situation Room with President Biden after we defeat one of the largest missile attacks at that point in history. You can hear everything he says. You are there, actually, in the Oval Office, I was overseas and dialed in shortly after the president learned about that intelligence operation in Tehran against Haniyeh, and he calls up Bibi Netanyahu. So a reader will hear exactly what happened in- in those moments. And no, I don't think it was simply, you know, Netanyahu took- took things for granted. It was a very difficult regional military equation, intelligence equation, diplomatic equation, humanitarian equation, all of which is playing out in real time.

MARGARET BRENNAN: You know, it's an incredibly complex set of challenges all at once. I want to get to Saudi Arabia in a moment, but just to button up on Iran. On the nuclear program. Biden's national security adviser Jake Sullivan explained to Netanyahu when he pitched going and bombing the nuclear sites. He said it was, you know, of questionable legality and risky. But the administration was unanimous that if Iran was about to make a bomb, that the Biden administration would have gone and bombed. At that point, were you thinking that, essentially, the war we're in now was inevitable?

BRETT MCGURK: So, it's in the book. I go to Israel in December, this is after the election, with Jake. We see Bibi Netanyahu. And we got him to sign on to a key term for the hostage deal, which is the focus here. And he said, "I think we should take out Fordow and the- and the nuclear sites." And we were concerned after the election, just given some things we were seeing, that Iran might- they were already enriching to 60 percent, and- and 90 percent is weapons-grade enrichment, and it's not- that's very easy to do. That they might make a dash, and once you do a dash, they have a canister of weapons-grade uranium, and you're really in a much worse situation. We actually had a principals committee meeting, that's everybody around the table, what would we do if we see that?
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

BRETT MCGURK: And as I recall, unanimity on we would do the strike in Fordow. We didn't see that. We sent a message to Iran, don't even think about it. But yet Netanyahu was clearly contemplating that, and--
MARGARET BRENNAN: In the middle of the hostage crisis.
BRETT MCGURK: Yeah, in December of 2024.
MARGARET BRENNAN: He was thinking about bombing Iran.

BRETT MCGURK: And we said there would be no- unless we see the Iranians moving in that direction, and there are questions of legality and everything else, that's always been around this issue. This- this strike against Fordow has been a, again, war game multiple times. But yeah, you will- that conversation is- is in the book in December of 2024 with- with Netanyahu.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Because you diplomatically point out that he was more focused on bombing Iran than the hostages. He pitched you, "why wait" until they race for a bomb? Why not act now? You made the point that he spoke with far greater intensity about Iran than he spoke about the hostages. You sound--
BRETT MCGURK: True.
MARGARET BRENNAN: --pretty annoyed by that.

BRETT MCGURK: It's true, and yet in that same meeting, in that same meeting where all that's going on, we get Netanyahu to agree- this is early December 2024. If I have the list of hostages, if Hamas produces the list–there are 33 names that Israel had. If Hamas agrees to the list of 33 hostages, meaning we have to know the hostages who are coming out in the deal, I accept the deal. We got that from Netanyahu in that meeting. And then all we needed- this gets back to this theme we've talked about here, Margaret, in the last hour or so. All we needed at that moment to stop the war was an agreement on the list of hostages. And I describe in the book Hamas would not agree on the list of hostages, and then they said, of the 33, only 12 will be alive. And so again, everybody wants this war to end. You've mentioned people with very strong views on the issue. So you're there, mid-December 2024. You have a full hostage deal. Hamas says, "But we'll only release 12 hostages alive." And I'm sitting there with Sheikh Mohammed. I have the list of hostages, Keith Siegel's on the list--
MARGARET BRENNAN: The American.

BRETT MCGURK: --We can get out these 12 hostages, and the war will stop. But what about all the other hostages that Hamas is not putting on the list, including Sagui Dekel-Chen, an American wounded twice on October 7th, Hamas is saying we don't consider him wounded. What do you do in that moment? Do you take the 12 in hand, or do you put down a harder line and say no, no, we need the full list, which was ultimately 25 living hostages? Eventually, it was after New Year's, heading into 2025, Hamas produced the full list, but then they put more issues on the table. I bring this up to say, this is how close you are to ending the war. It's there. And in that meeting on, on Fordow, where yeah, Netanyahu was very adamant on the nuclear threat, he signed on to this deal, so long as we have the list of the hostages. And then once again, it's on Hamas to- you want to end the war? All we need is the hostage list from Hamas.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Ultimately, you talk about January 19, 2025, on Face the Nation when you finally were able to announce that those three women, in particular, were going to be released by Hamas. But you write in the book a lot about Steve Witkoff and what he is like as a negotiator. You teamed up, actually, in those final days. And he said to you at some point he was actually surprised you weren't talking directly to Hamas. He said, if I sell- "If a guy's selling me a building…I look in his eyes, face-to-face…only way to do a deal."
BRETT MCGURK: Yeah.
MARGARET BRENNAN: What did you say when he asked you, "Why aren't you talking to Hamas?"

BRETT MCGURK: First, the story with Steve I think is unique because when President Trump won the election, if left to its own devices here, Margaret, in Washington these days, it would be, the Biden people would say good luck Trump folks, and the Trump people would say we're not going to do anything that the Biden people said. Right after the election, I called Jared Kushner, and I said, "look, you don't want to come into office with this Gaza thing still going on, and we got a chance to get the hostages out," because at that point Nasrallah is dead. We have- we're moving towards a ceasefire in Lebanon, the whole regional picture is changing. Yahya Sinwar is out of the way, We just defeated another missile attack. And we agreed to work together. And when Biden and Trump met in the Oval Office of all the other issues, they agreed to work together on this. I then- Jake and I went to see Mike Waltz, his incoming successor, and I met Steve Witkoff, and we agreed we're going to work in lockstep. Talk about no daylight, we're going to have no daylight, and, and we did that. And by the time Steve came out to- to Doha, we kind of had two issues. Finally got the hostage list [as] I mentioned. Hamas had raised two entirely new issues. We had to bridge those, and it was only by working together that we were able- to able to do that. On the dynamics of the negotiation, the- the cards on the table are Palestinian prisoners being held by Israel, and a ceasefire and various redeployments of Israeli forces, and so- and other- some many other things. Israel had a direct channel with- with Hamas when they needed it, and we had the mediators, often, with Hamas right downstairs. We thought if we were to go face-to-face with Hamas, it could actually, Hamas could use that to play one side off another, and so we trusted the Egyptians and the Qataris and we had good information of everything going on. And that's the way- the way- we, we handled it. I think- I don't think a more direct channel would have produced a faster result.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But you've got some colorful anecdotes in there about him, kind of closing with Netanyahu, saying, you gotta do this, you have to agree to this.

BRETT MCGURK: So again, we have- we have a full deal. Hamas accepts the list, and then Hamas comes in with a totally new demand: for the nine sick and wounded hostages, they need 300 life- Palestinian prisoners serving life sentences, mostly Hamas, very hardcore Hamas terrorists, many of them who've killed Israelis and killed Americans, they insist on coming out--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --huge political risk at home--

BRETT MCGURK: --for- for the civilians. There's a totally unprecedented demand over a year of talks. We whittled that down to 110 life-sentence prisoners for those nine sick and wounded civilians, and the buffer zone that Israel would be in in this first phase of the deal. Israel wanted 1,200 meters. Hamas wanted 500. We cut it to 700. But you mentioned this kind of extraordinary moment. I mean, we're all in Doha and kind of agree to divide labor because we had Hamas and Israel in the same building. And Steve went to see Netanyahu. It was a week before the inauguration, and I called into the meeting in the Israeli cabinet room. I went to see the Israelis in Doha, I'm with their team, called into the meeting with Netanyahu and their cabinet, and Steve Witkoff is there, saying, "this is the deal. It's going to be 110 life-sentenced prisoners," which was very difficult, and we- we kind of cut the- split the middle on the buffer zone, and- and the Israeli reaction was extremely negative, but ultimately we had the envoy of one president on the line, and we had the envoy of the incoming president say, this is what we got to do. It was the last final issue, and the Israelis accepted that deal, and that's how we got- again, Romy, Doron and Emily came home on the 19th, I announced it on your- on your program, but they should have come out in that November deal.

MARGARET BRENNAN: As we wind down, I just want to make sure I ask you about Saudi Arabia because you mentioned it right at the top. This is now January of 2021. You're at the beginning of the Biden administration. You fly to Saudi Arabia to meet Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, MbS as he's known, he's persona non grata because of the murder of Washington Post columnist Jamal Khashoggi. That's the moment we are in. You go there to explain what President Biden is going to do, and MbS shocks you because he makes you an offer you never expected. He says 'I want to normalize relations with Israel.' Did you go back and tell President Biden that? Because he didn't, as you write, act on it for a year or more.

BRETT MCGURK: Yeah, MbS in that meeting- I've known him for a long time, but I was very clear on, we are going to cut off offensive weapons for Saudi Arabia. We're going to issue new sanctions across the board of many of your security services related to Khashoggi. We're going to release the intelligence report on- on Khashoggi and a number of other things. But Biden was very clear before I went. He also wanted to make sure we're not- we're not totally breaching our relations with Saudi Arabia, a very important country. And we had a very pointed conversation that is in the book in AlUla, in a tent, this was during COVID, and I said to him, finally, I said, "look, where do you want to be in three years?" And he was kind of in, like, peacemaking mode. He said, look, I- we're going to have a back channel with the Iranians through Baghdad. I do think we can bring the Yemen war to a close. But for that to happen, the U.S. and Saudi Arabia have to be seen as working together. And then he said, I'm- I'm prepared to work towards recognizing Israel, diplomatic relations with Israel, and that had to include a number of components, and we talked through it, including a pathway on the Palestinian piece. That was hard to envision. But yes, certainly, that was the key to my report back when I saw the president, that that might be something in the [unintel]--
[CROSSTALK]
MARGARET BRENNAN: But you said--
BRETT MCGURK: --but at the time--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --President Biden didn't want to have anything to do--
BRETT MCGURK: --at the time--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --with the Middle East.
[END CROSSTALK]

BRETT MCGURK: --and I'd be fair to myself. I mean, I- I didn't seize on it either. I just- and I look back on that, I think we should have moved right away. And it wasn't until- you know, this is the thing about the Middle East, Margaret. You can- you can back out of it. The world intervenes. Okay, the world intervenes. So that first year, we had almost no engagement with, particularly, the Gulf States. I mean, I was out there a lot as the Middle East White House envoy. We significantly withdrew our military presence, air, naval, air defense. Then we have Afghanistan evacuation, and--
MARGARET BRENNAN: That changed everything--

BRETT MCGURK: --that's when a call came to me. Can you call all the leaders in the Gulf to open up their air bases and say we're going to be landing thousands of Afghans, I don't know how long they'll be there. And every country said yes.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Which is an amazing thing--
BRETT MCGURK: Including Saudi Arabia and UAE and Qatar and Kuwait, Bahrain, everybody.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Without knowing who these people are--
BRETT MCGURK: Right.
MARGARET BRENNAN: --But trusting America that they're sending people who aren't a risk.

BRETT MCGURK: And without that phone call and without those platforms, we would have been in an even worse situation at that time. I was not working Afghanistan; I worked on that aspect of it. Then the war, Russia's invasion of Ukraine, and then suddenly--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --America needs the Middle East--

BRETT MCGURK: --The old issues of energy supplies, and the only swing producer is really Saudi Arabia, and you need- we need Saudi Arabia, and to do that, the decision maker is the Crown Prince of Saudi Arabia. I describe this in the book, that's- we eventually worked our way back towards decent relations with Saudi Arabia and started to work towards the normalization deal. But that was not- that deal, Margaret, was not, it's not like we, you know, we were pushing it. The Saudis asked us to work with them on it, the Israelis asked us to work with them on it, and we put these stepping stones. You know, there's this news just this weekend- or this week about this airplane over Saudi Arabia, we actually negotiated an agreement between Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and Israel about getting American forces off an island in the Red Sea. They've been there since the Camp David Accords, and in exchange for that, Saudi Arabia opened its skies to all civilian planes, regardless of destination. President Biden announced that on the trip. That was kind of one, one public point of where this process was going, and yeah, I wish we had started sooner.
MARGARET BRENNAN: This was, 2022 Russian invades Ukraine--
BRETT MCGURK: --2022.

MARGARET BRENNAN: --as you say, there's a global energy crisis, suddenly. But you also say, other than you, no senior official had met with the Crown Prince. That means the secretary of defense, the secretary of state, the national security adviser. None of them could be bothered to go to one of our closest partners in the Middle East? I understand there's disagreement, but that's a huge oversight.
BRETT MCGURK: In that first year, yeah, yeah--
MARGARET BRENNAN: And a huge missed opportunity--

BRETT MCGURK: I think Secretary Austin made a trip out, but I think Saudi was the last on the- on the agenda, and that trip, that stop eventually got pulled down for reasons. So yeah, it was a mistake.
MARGARET BRENNAN: And you--

BRETT MCGURK: --Because these- these countries in the Gulf- I have an epigraph in, in the- in the book, Margaret, by- by John F. Kennedy. It's one of my favorite speeches of his. A speech he gave in Utah just two months before his death, and he says the purpose of foreign policy is not to provide an outlet for our own hope or indignation, it is to get real things done in the real world. And in the executive branch, if you're in a White House to get real things done in the real world, you have to have relations with countries that might not share all of your values.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So all of what you just laid out leads to this moment in July 2022 when President Biden goes to Saudi Arabia, and we had the fist bump heard around the world, as you refer to it. You said it was "absurd." It was a "self-made scandal."
BRETT MCGURK: Yeah.
MARGARET BRENNAN: That's about as critical as you get when it comes to President Biden, you were very deferential to him. But you were ticked.
BRETT MCGURK: I--
MARGARET BRENNAN: He was refusing to go and shake the hand of the crown prince at the entrance to his own palace.

BRETT MCGURK: We didn't know what was going to happen in that moment, and I was of the view, got to shake his hand, and- and we had set up this trip–you think about where we were, we had– I mentioned that deal we had. We had the Israel process moving, we had in Israel, President Biden met with Prime Minister Lapid at the time and encouraged Lapid to announce his support for- for two states, which Lapid believed before, but he hadn't said as Prime Minister–I have that scene in the book. A lot of things had kind of come together, and the Saudi stop was- was so important--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --You were trying to rebuild–
BRETT MCGURK: --Well, you mentioned how politics can intrude into a lot of things. I think the- I have a scene with Jake and I, Jake is one of my closest counterparts--
MARGARET BRENNAN: The national security adviser--
BRETT MCGURK: --the national security adviser, and he's hearing from the White House about how things are playing out. And so, um--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --and President Biden said, you recount that, "I'm going to get killed for this." And he's talking about politically.

BRETT MCGURK: Yeah, we landed in Saudi Arabia, and I went to the pool notes from the media pool, and there was an 18-minute from when he landed until when he got out. So I say in the book, let me tell you what happened in those 18 minutes, and I tell you what happened. He was concerned about the optics and the and the imagery, and the whole thing I- I- that's how I describe it. I think, and I encouraged the president to just shake his hand.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But it was all in service of trying to rebuild America's alliances in this critical part of the world. That's where your head was.
BRETT MCGURK: Yeah, we were asking some--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --and the president's head was on the politics and the human rights issues.

BRETT MCGURK: Well, we were asking some very hard things to the Saudis that we needed for our core interests, and so I think the fist bump set us back. I will say we had a very good–overall–that was a very good and successful visit, and we- we built on it. But it's how imagery- you know, I was- Margaret, I was with President Bush in Baghdad when he came to Baghdad, I was sitting just off to his side. Kind of an extraordinary moment, I mean, what it took to get the president of the United States to come into Iraq at that time. You remember what it was like. And I was sitting, I don't know, six, seven feet away from him when the Iraqi reporter got up and threw two shoes at the president.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Mmhmm.
BRETT MCGURK: And I remember- whatever else happened on that visit--
MARGARET BRENNAN: That's all anyone--
BRETT MCGURK: --nobody remembers, and the- the fist bump kind of overshadowed all the what was actually the- the substance of that, of that visit and what, what came of it.

MARGARET BRENNAN: And just lastly, you know, I talked about some of the criticism of you. One of the things that I think you reveal, in a personal way, is how much of a toll this took on you. The time you spent away from your very young daughter. You write about the thoughts you had about that little Abigail. A little four-year-old who was taken into Gaza, and how you were having nightmares about her. That's something that maybe is a bit humanizing in a pretty tough situation. Why did you think that you needed to share that, that glimpse into your personal life?

BRETT MCGURK: I wrote this book– there was no other way to write it than to just pour it all down on the page, raw. I never thought to myself, "how is this going to be seen?" Or, I have no ambition for any future office or anything. It was just what happened and what was it like. And I- and to- and in the writing of it, it was impossible to- to write, in the flow of writing, without putting everything down. And I have those anecdotes because that's how it felt. And cognizant the whole time that lives were being lost every single day, and trying to stop it. So that- it was all-consuming. But that was the only way to write this book. This is not a book, Margaret, about dry policy, this is a book about the grittiness of war and diplomacy and the awfulness, the awfulness of it in every dimension, and not just making a speech or saying something should happen, actually trying to bring it to a close, and trying to bring Abigail home and thinking Abigail might be dead. Then you're living with that every day. And you get to know the families of the hostages, and you- you see the toll every single day in Gaza, and you're always a hair's breadth away from more American soldiers being killed or on the brink of a major war. It's what it was like in the day-to-day. And, so whatever side you might be on on this, this polarizing issue, I just hope readers will read it and take away and think for themselves, "what would I have done in this moment? What might I have done?" That's how I tried to write it. Just- I poured in a very raw, this is, you know, this is it. So yeah, I have those those anecdotes of Christmas Day being with my daughter, a quiet, you know, one quiet moment, realizing she's growing up in a way that I've missed a year, and then I get a call from the Situation Room that we have three Americans grievously wounded in northern Iraq, and I'm back at the White House. You know, that's just what this is like. And so I think it's a different type of book, and I hope people read it.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Thank you for your time.
BRETT MCGURK: Thank you, Margaret.
** Clarification: The Washington Post, not The New Yorker, reported then-Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin privately described Israel's actions as "playing with house money."

title: Iowa approves pricey foreign-owned steel plant project in swing district
summary: President Trump announced that the largest steel plant in U.S. history will be built in Iowa, touching off a week of debate.
story: "Stop the Steal" — or rather, steel — has an entirely new meaning for some Iowa voters in 2026.

Protesters at the Iowa statehouse Friday carried signs reading "No Steel Steal!" as lawmakers raced through a one-day special session to award Mesabi Metallics $1.36 billion over 10 years in tax incentives for a new steel plant in Lee County. Mesabi Metallics is owned by the Indian conglomerate Essar Group.
The Iowa House passed it 75-17, the Senate 28-19. Gov. Kim Reynolds signed it into law Friday night.

It comes after President Trump's Monday announcement that the largest steel plant in U.S. history would be built in Iowa. Mr. Trump promised the $15 billion steel plant would create 1,750 permanent jobs and roughly 6,000 construction jobs.

The announcement caught many in the state by surprise, including lawmakers who would be counted on to approve the tax incentives. When Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick told reporters at the White House "the deal is done" on Monday, lawmakers in Iowa still hadn't received details to review or timing for the special session held Friday.

Opponents of the $1.36 billion in incentives are largely supporters of the project, but they wanted more safeguards and guarantees of public benefits. The incentives roughly amount to about $777,000 in credits per permanent job over 10 years, a hefty price tag by any standards. Proponents argue that math leaves out roughly 6,000 construction jobs — which opponents point out are all temporary.
And at a time when many of Iowa's farmers are struggling, more than a billion dollars in tax credits for an India-based conglomerate is a hard sell for some.
Why Iowa?

There are places in the U.S. synonymous with steel, but Iowa has never been one of them. The state has a couple scrap-fed steel mills — a small fraction of the size Mesabi is promising — and no commercial iron ore. Mesabi Metallics is based in Minnesota, and its argument is that Iowa is conveniently downriver on the Mississippi.
But Iowa has something that Minnesota doesn't: One of the most tightly contested congressional races in the nation. The state also has close Senate and governor's races.

The plant's proposed location is Iowa's 1st Congressional District, where Republican Congresswoman Mariannette Miller-Meeks is defending one of the GOP's most at-risk seats. In 2024, the recount had her ahead of Democrat Christina Bohannan by just 798 votes. Sabato's Crystal Ball just moved the race from "toss up" to "leans Democratic" before the steel announcement.
Bankruptcy and broken promises

Mesabi and Essar Group have a long history of missed deadlines and unfulfilled job promises. In 2008, Essar announced a $1.6 billion iron ore mine and steel plant in Nashwauk, Minnesota, home to some of the country's richest iron ore deposits. It promised more than 700 permanent jobs. But the steel mill plans were dropped in 2015. Essar Steel Minnesota filed for bankruptcy in 2016, was renamed Mesabi Metallics under new owners, and later came back under Essar's control.
The India-based Essar has recueved billions of dollars in loans from the Russian state-owned bank VTB, according to local media. CBS News has not independently verified these reports.

There are also echoes of other regional mega-projects gone awry. No one in the Hawkeye state wants the steel plant to be the 2026 version of Foxconn. In 2017,  President Trump and Foxconn promised a $10 billion plant and create 13,000 jobs in the battleground state of Wisconsin. By 2021, the plan was scaled back to $672 million and 1,454 jobs. Republican Gov. Scott Walker championed the deal — and lost his 2018 reelection bid as public support for it soured.
Tricky politics
On Friday, Republican State Senator Kevin Alons told the Des Moines Register that lawmakers needed more time ahead of Friday's vote.
"The political extortion is breathtaking," he said.
But in the end, he voted for it.

State Sen. Dave Sires, also a Republican, voted no on the project, complaining the process was rushed. State Senator Dan Dawson, another Republican, called it the "largest corporate giveaway in the state of Iowa's history." And Republican State Senator Jeff Taylor raised concerns that the state was already in a real budget crunch.
Taylor was swapped off the Senate Ways and Means Committee at the last minute to ensure the bill would pass committee. It passed 10-8, with 6 Republican State Senators voting against the bill.

It's a careful political calculus for Republicans in the Iowa Senate. They're trying to thread a fine needle: follow their leaders and bring home jobs, without being seen as rushing more than a billion dollars in taxpayer money to a foreign-owned company with no time for review.

Republican gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn, who has campaigned against corporate handouts, made a case for supporting the bill. He called the idea of an Iowa steel plant a "once in a lifetime" exception.

Democrats have been navigating tricky political territory as well, trying not to oppose job creation while pushing back on the rush to issue nearly $1.4 billion in tax breaks before early voting starts on Oct. 14. Democratic nominee Rob Sand, currently the state auditor, called the steel plant "a promising idea for Lee County" but wanted to see more details first.

"You look at these data center deals that this administration has done over the last few years and we gave away the farm," Sand said. "I want to make sure this is a real opportunity, but also at the end of the day Iowa is getting served by it and not getting fleeced."
Iowa Senate Democratic Leader Janice Weiner said she wants good-paying jobs and investments in the state but balked at the rapid timeline that left taxpayers out of the conversation.

"If we were doing this the right way, we would be waiting until after the election," she told CBS News on Saturday. "We have a responsibility to our taxpayers to make sure our hard-earned dollars are well spent. If it's a good deal now, it will be a good deal in January when due diligence has been done."
Meanwhile, State Representative Dave Jacoby, a Democrat, voted yes, "with the hope that this plan is real," while still cautioning, "today is not a ribbon cutting."

The ribbon cutting, if it comes, is years away. The tax credits don't kick in until the plant is running, and Mesabi says that won't be before 2030. Iowans begin to cast their votes in just a few days. So the question on the ballot isn't whether Iowa gets a steel mill. It's whether voters believe it will — and if $1.36 billion was the right price to pay for it.

title: Trump announces AI "Super Intelligence Force"
summary: President Trump announced the formation of a "Super Intelligence Force" after meeting with leaders of the country's largest artificial intelligence companies last week.
story: Washington — President Trump announced Sunday the formation of a "Super Intelligence Force," after meeting with leaders of the country's largest artificial intelligence companies last week amid growing calls for guardrails on the technology.

"Following the Historic White House Accord on Super Intelligence, where the World's most important Technology Companies came together, and confirmed their responsibilities to the American People, I am announcing the formation of the Super Intelligence Force (SIF)," the president wrote in a post on Truth Social.

Mr. Trump said the task force will coordinate with the federal government to "ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence," the term which he directed the federal government to use instead of artificial intelligence. The president said the task force will lead engagement with consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, infrastructure providers and industry leaders, with Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton at the helm, among other leaders.

CBS News reported last week that Clayton was likely to be picked for AI czar, according to sources. Mr. Trump said Sunday that Andrew Ferguson, the chairman of the Federal Trade Commission, Emil Michael, the under secretary for research and engineering and chief technology officer at the Pentagon, and Scott Kupor, the director of the Office of Personnel Management, will also lead the force, and will report to him and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles.

The president told reporters shortly after meeting at the White House with the leaders of the country's top AI firms — OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, Nvidia and Elon Musk's SpaceXAI — that he planned to name an AI czar within three or four days. At the meeting, the leaders signed a set of voluntary safety standards.

Mr. Trump called the standards "morally binding," adding later that he was seeing "tremendous self-policing, and they understand that they have to self-police." According to a copy of the one-page accord that the president shared on Truth Social, the tech companies committed to "four layers of controls and audits" to ensure the AI models are acting as intended, including internal evaluations, audits by an external firm and reviews by each company's board of directors. The leaders also agreed to "meet regularly to establish standards and best practices to improve the safety of their systems."

title: Supreme Court to weigh energy companies' bid to end climate-change suit
summary: The Supreme Court will hear arguments Monday over a bid by Exxon Mobil and Suncor Energy to block a lawsuit filed by the city and county of Boulder over the effects of climate change.
story: Washington — When the Supreme Court returns to the bench Monday for the first time since late June, it will kick off its new term with a major case involving an effort by the city and county of Boulder, Colorado, to hold fossil-fuel producers accountable for the impacts of global climate change.

The lawsuit from Boulder is one of dozens filed by states and local governments against energy companies in state courts that seek money damages for past and future harms that they allege are caused by the buildup of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, which has led to global warming.

The long-running dispute brought by Boulder targets Exxon Mobil, the nation's largest energy company, and Suncor Energy, which operates two oil refineries in Colorado. The suit remains in its early stages, and the issue before the Supreme Court is whether the suit can proceed or is barred by federal law. A win for Boulder from the Supreme Court wouldn't mean it will ultimately prevail against the fossil-fuel producers in state court.

"This is not a judgment about whether these cases will succeed. It's a judgment about whether folks get to make their case," said Jonathan Adler, a law professor at William & Mary who has written about federalism and environmental law and filed a friend-of-the-court brief in support of Boulder. "And even if they get to make their case, the scope of what they can pursue could well be narrowed and might well be narrowed significantly."

Boulder's lawsuit dates back to 2018. Filed in state court, the city and county allege that Exxon and Suncor's conduct has caused or contributed to climate change, which has in turn forced Boulder to confront extreme heat, larger and more frequent wildfires and damage to the ecosystem, among other issues.

Boulder officials raised five claims under state law. They argue that the energy companies' production and allegedly deceptive marketing of fossil fuels has led to "unchecked" use of their products that has caused a rapid rise in the concentration of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere.

Exxon and Suncor attempted to move the case to federal court, but that effort was unsuccessful. The companies also asked the Boulder County District Court to dismiss the case on the grounds that federal law foreclosed the claims against them. When the state court denied that request, the companies asked the Colorado Supreme Court to step in.
The state high court sided with the city and county of Boulder, and Suncor and Exxon appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court.

In addition to considering whether federal law precludes Boulder's state-law claims, the Supreme Court asked lawyers for both sides to address whether it has jurisdiction to review the Colorado Supreme Court decision.

Only eight of the nine justices will participate in the arguments Monday, as the Supreme Court said last week that Justice Samuel Alito had chosen to recuse himself from the case. No reason was given for Alito's decision. His financial disclosure for 2025 shows that he had individual holdings in two energy companies, ConocoPhillips and Phillips 66. He did not report individual stocks in either Exxon or Suncor.
Alito's absence leaves open the possibility that the Supreme Court divides 4-4 in the case. If that happens, the decision of the lower court — the Colorado Supreme Court, in this case — would stand.
A "national problem"

Lawyers for Exxon and Suncor argued in Supreme Court filings that the Constitution and the Clean Air Act preclude claims that seek to address harms caused by interstate greenhouse-gas emissions. The Clean Air Act, they said, did not invite state law to apply to disputes involving interstate pollution.

If the Colorado Supreme Court's decision is upheld, "it would authorize all fifty States, the tens of thousands of municipalities, and even the hundreds of millions of individuals in our country to ask local courts to establish countless, conflicting climate policies for the Nation," Exxon and Suncor lawyers argued.

Additionally, the energy companies and the Trump administration, which supports Exxon and Suncor in the case, warned that efforts like Boulder's to secure relief for the effects of greenhouse-gas emissions — including those released abroad — undermine the government's control over foreign affairs.

"Such lawsuits would create an end-run around the United States' existing diplomatic channels for addressing climate change in favor of innumerable state judicial ones," lawyers for Exxon and Suncor said. "And the imposition of potentially devastating liability on fossil-fuel producers will undercut the government's pursuit of primacy in global energy production."

Because greenhouse gases emitted from sources in every state and around the world cannot be unmixed and traced, the companies warned that allowing all 50 states to apply their own laws would result in confusion. Only a "neutral, uniform federal law" can resolve disputes over the regulation of air and water, they said.
"It's a national problem, so it requires a national solution," Michael Williams, solicitor general of West Virginia, told reporters during a briefing Wednesday.

West Virginia and 25 other states are backing Suncor and Exxon Mobil and argue that Boulder's lawsuit jeopardizes their ability to achieve their own policy goals on energy production and environmental protection.

"We don't take issue with the idea that a state can actually regulate sources within its own borders. So if West Virginia wants to regulate a coal plant in West Virginia, we claim the right to do that," Williams said. "In the same way, if Colorado wants to regulate emissions coming from Colorado in Colorado, they're free to do that as well. What they're not free to do is say, hey you emitters, anywhere in the world … we're going to make you pay money for any of those emissions anywhere in the world."

But lawyers for Boulder urged the Supreme Court to dismiss the appeal on the grounds that it does not have jurisdiction. If the justices opt not to, they said the Colorado Supreme Court decision should be upheld.
"Does anything implicit in the Constitution bar this suit?" they wrote in a filing. "Nothing does."

Boulder noted there is often litigation to address the local impacts of problems that could benefit from international solutions, like food contamination, human trafficking and the fentanyl crisis. The city and county's effort to hold energy companies liable is just another example, they said.

"That climate change is a global problem does not disempower states from redressing its local harms either," they wrote in a filing. "This litigation is not an attempt to solve climate change; it merely asks that petitioners bear their fair share of local costs incurred in part because of their tortious conduct."

Boulder also pushed back on the energy companies' argument that the Clean Air Act preempts its claims, and said that law governs emissions, not the conduct of the upstream fossil-fuel producers. Plus, lawyers for the city and county said they did not sue for emissions, but over allegedly deceptive marketing and production, which the Clean Air Act does not regulate.

"Indeed, avoiding liability would not require reducing emissions at all — only telling the truth, so the public can make informed consumption decisions free of the distorting effect of petitioners' misrepresentations," they said.

The Trump administration argues that Boulder's suit invites "needless diplomatic friction" with the foreign countries where Exxon and Suncor produce and sell their fossil fuels. But Adler, the William & Mary professor, noted that the Trump administration has withdrawn from international agreements that seek to address global warming and greenhouse-gas emissions.

The foreign-affairs argument "seems to suggest that any time the executive branch claims that it would like to negotiate in a space that could be implicated by companies being held liable for damages that they may have contributed to, that would really give the executive branch the ability to preempt any sort of litigation that it wanted. That can't be the law," he said. "If there was an actual conflict between an actual treaty, of course that could preempt state law. But we don't even have that."

Adler also said that Congress could weigh in and restrict suits against fossil-fuel companies for the harms tied to their products. In fact, it took similar action in 2005 when lawmakers passed a federal law that shields gun manufacturers from civil lawsuits that seek to hold them accountable for harms stemming from the criminal misuse of their firearms.

"If Congress believes that what's going on here is a combination of plaintiffs' lawyers and activists trying to make energy less available or less affordable, or to otherwise create pressure on fossil-fuel companies, Congress has the tools to address that," he said. "That's a job for the legislature, not a job for the courts."
A decision from the Supreme Court is expected by summer of 2027.

title: Supreme Court gears up for new term with major cases on climate change, guns
summary: The Supreme Court kicks off its term Monday with cases involving climate change, President Trump's immigration policies and the Second Amendment among the most high-profile disputes.
story: Washington — The start of the Supreme Court's new term is quickly approaching, with cases involving climate change, President Trump's immigration policies and the Second Amendment among the most high-profile disputes the justices will hear in the coming months.

But waiting in the wings at the Supreme Court are several legal battles involving Mr. Trump's second-term agenda, which will be discussed by the justices in forthcoming closed-door conferences and, if taken up by the court, decided by the summer of 2027.

The Supreme Court kicks off its term Monday with arguments involving a lawsuit filed in state court by the city and county of Boulder, Colorado, that seeks to hold energy companies accountable for the effects of global climate change.
Here are the big cases that the Supreme Court is poised to decide so far in its upcoming term, which begins Oct. 5:
Climate change: Suncor Energy v. County Commissioners of Boulder County
On the first day of the new term, the Supreme Court will hear arguments in a dispute between Boulder and two energy companies, Suncor Energy and Exxon Mobil.

The question before the Supreme Court is a technical one: Whether federal law prevents Boulder County from suing energy companies in state court and claiming that the sale and allegedly deceptive marketing of fossil fuels violates state law.

The outcome of the case could have significant ramifications for dozens of similar lawsuits brought by states and localities that seek to hold fossil-fuel producers accountable for the effects of climate change. A decision in favor of the energy companies would block Boulder's lawsuit, which is still in its early stages and seeks money damages.

Lawyers for Exxon and Suncor warn that if the Supreme Court allows these suits to move forward and they are ultimately successful, they would effectively impose a carbon tax on fossil-fuel producers and "bankrupt" the industry.

In filings with the Supreme Court, they called climate change "one of the most complex public-policy challenges of our time," resulting from the buildup of greenhouse gases that are emitted by every state and every country. Those emissions, Suncor and Exxon lawyers said, "cannot be unmixed and traced to their individual sources."

The case landed at the Supreme Court on appeal from the Colorado Supreme Court, which allowed Boulder's lawsuit to proceed. The high court will also consider whether it has jurisdiction to review that decision.

The energy companies warned that if that ruling is upheld and adopted on a nationwide scale, it would give the green light to all 50 states and their municipalities "to ask local courts to establish countless, conflicting climate policies for the Nation."

Lawyers for Boulder County argued that the Constitution allows states to address the harms that arise within their own borders. Whether those harms should be better addressed at the federal level is a decision that rests with Congress, they said.
The county officials said the energy companies rushed to the Supreme Court and instead should wait until the state court has issued its final decision in the case before seeking review.

"That climate change is a global problem does not disempower states from redressing its local harms either," they wrote. "This litigation is not an attempt to solve climate change; it merely asks that petitioners bear their fair share of local costs incurred in part because of their tortious conduct."

Justice Samuel Alito will not participate in the case, according to a letter sent to lawyers for the parties Monday. The letter did not include a reason for his recusal. In his financial disclosure for 2025, Alito reported owning stocks in two energy companies, ConocoPhillips and Phillips 66, but did not list individual holdings in Exxon or Suncor.
Religious liberty: St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy

On Nov. 3, the justices will convene for arguments in a case involving a Catholic preschool in Colorado that argues it is unlawfully excluded from the state's universal preschool program. The dispute is the latest in which the Supreme Court will consider participation by religious entities in state-funded programs.

Colorado's program provides state funding for families to send their 4-year-olds to the preschool of their choosing. The program allows all children in the state to receive up to 15 hours of free preschool each week before they enter kindergarten. Families can send their children to public or private preschools, or to faith-based or in-home providers.

The law creating the program includes a nondiscrimination provision, which requires all schools to ensure children have the equal opportunity to attend regardless of their or their parents' religious affiliation, race, ethnicity, sexual orientation, gender identity, lack of housing or income level.

In 2023, the Archdiocese of Denver, which oversees more than 30 Catholic preschools, requested an exemption from the universal preschool program's nondiscrimination rule so it could admit only participating families who adhere to the Catholic Church's teachings, including on gender identity and sexual orientation.

But the Colorado Department of Early Childhood declined to provide the accommodation. In response, the Archdiocese, two parishes and a family with children who attend parish schools sued and argued they were entitled to an exemption under the First Amendment's Free Exercise Clause.

The plaintiffs said because the universal preschool program created exemptions to the nondiscrimination requirement, it was not neutral and generally applicable. The Supreme Court said in a 1990 decision called Employment Division v. Smith that laws burdening the free exercise of religion generally do not violate the First Amendment as long as they're neutral and generally applicable.

A federal district court sided with the state in June 2024, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit upheld that decision, finding that the program's nondiscrimination rule "exists in harmony with the First Amendment" and doesn't violate the plaintiffs' free exercise rights.
Gun rights: Viramontes v. Cook County and Grant v. Higgins
This latest Second Amendment dispute to arise following the Supreme Court's landmark 2022 decision expanding gun rights involves state laws banning AR-15s and similar semiautomatic weapons.

The two cases, which will be argued Dec. 2, involve a Connecticut law and an ordinance in Cook County, Illinois. Cook County's prohibition was put in place nearly 20 years ago, while Connecticut tightened its rules for semiautomatic firearms after the 2012 mass shooting at Sandy Hook Elementary School.
More than 10 states and the District of Columbia prohibit AR-15-style semiautomatic weapons.

In both of the cases from Illinois and Connecticut, lower courts upheld the bans. The appeals courts each applied the new standard for determining the constitutionality of gun restrictions that the Supreme Court laid out in 2022, which requires the government to show that a law is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearms regulation.

In its ruling then, the Supreme Court recognized for the first time that the Second Amendment protects the right to carry a firearm outside the home. The justices have been asked to take up a number of challenges to longstanding federal and state gun laws in the years since.

In 2024, the Supreme Court upheld a federal law that bars people subject to domestic violence restraining orders from having guns. Then, last year, it said that under the Second Amendment, the government cannot prosecute a habitual marijuana user for having a firearm. The high court also struck down a Hawaii law that required concealed-carry permit holders to receive permission before bringing their firearms onto private property that is open to the public.
The Supreme Court had turned away challenges to laws from Maryland and Illinois banning AR-15s and other semiautomatic weapons, leaving those restrictions in place.
Parental rights: International Partners for Ethical Care v. Ferguson
On Dec. 7, the Supreme Court will consider a case that involves laws from Washington state that expanded exceptions for when a youth shelter has to notify parents of a runaway teenager.

Under one of the new exceptions, if a child seeking or receiving medical treatments for gender dysphoria, including mental and physical health services, arrives at a shelter, it does not have to inform the parents that their child is there and instead must notify the Department of Children, Youth and Families.
The new measure also says the department must offer runaway teenagers those medical interventions at shelters if they seek that care without their parents' consent.

The question before the Supreme Court is whether parents have standing to file lawsuits challenging Washington's laws. The five sets of parents involved in the case all have children who they said have experienced gender dysphoria, and they allege the laws violate their constitutional right to direct the care and upbringing of their children.
A federal district court dismissed their case in 2024, finding that the parents lacked legal standing. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit upheld that decision.
Arizona's voting rules: Republican National Committee v. Mi Familia Vota

Amid President Trump's push for a federal proof-of-citizenship requirement to register to vote, the Supreme Court will weigh an Arizona rule that requires would-be voters to provide proof of citizenship when registering to vote using a state form. The case also involves the state's procedures for cleaning up its voter rolls. Federal law says any state program to systematically remove people from their voter registration lists must be completed 90 days before an election.
Arguments are set for Dec. 8.

Arizona's legislature approved the new voting policies in 2022. But soon after, Democratic groups including the Democratic National Committee filed lawsuits seeking to block their enforcement. The challengers argued that the requirements violated or were preempted by the National Voting Registration Act and a 2018 consent decree between Arizona's secretary of state and the Maricopa County recorder.

A federal district court said that under the consent decree, local election officials could not reject state voter registration forms that lacked proof of citizenship. The court also said that under the NVRA, Arizona couldn't systematically cancel voter registrations within 90 days of an election.
The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit upheld that decision last year.

Arizona's voting rules have been before the Supreme Court before, though at an earlier stage in the case. In August 2024, the Supreme Court allowed the state to enforce the proof-of-citizenship requirement for the general election. But the high court did not let the state enforce rules requiring proof-of-citizenship to vote for president or by mail.
Third-country deportations: Department of Homeland Security v. D.V.D.

The Trump administration implemented a policy in March 2025 that allowed for the swift removal of migrants to countries that they do not come from — so-called third countries — if those nations have provided credible assurances that deportees will not be persecuted or tortured.

The administration has argued that the third-country removals are an "essential tool" to remove certain migrants, including those who have criminal records. But last year, a group of four migrants subject to final orders of removal filed a class-action lawsuit arguing that their due-process rights would be violated if they were denied sufficient notice and an opportunity to challenge their removals before they were deported to a third country.

A federal district judge in Boston ruled that the Department of Homeland Security's guidance likely violated their due process rights, and he ordered immigration officials to provide migrants with written notice of the third country of removal, as well as a "meaningful opportunity" — at least 10 days — to assert a fear of removal.
The case ended up at the Supreme Court during an earlier stage, and the high court allowed the Trump administration to resume the deportations to third countries while litigation continued.

Then, in February, the judge in Boston ruled that the Trump administration's policy of deporting migrants to third countries without giving them notice is unlawful and said it must be set aside. A federal appeals court largely upheld that decision last month and said immigration authorities must offer detainees "a meaningful opportunity to contest" their deportations to countries that are not their own.
The Justice Department filed an emergency appeal with the Supreme Court and asked it to block the district court's decision.
The high court granted that request, allowing DHS to resume third-country removals for now, but also said it would decide the legal merits of the case. Arguments will take place Dec. 9.

Among the questions that the Supreme Court has asked the Justice Department and lawyers for the migrants to answer is whether the administration's guidance on third-country removals is unlawful under federal immigration law, the Constitution's Due Process Clause and protections against torture.
Immigration detentions: Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha
At issue in this case is the Trump administration's policy of detaining immigrants in the country illegally during their removal proceedings without access to bond hearings.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement rolled out the policy last year when it reinterpreted an immigration law from the 1990s and determined detainees facing removal are no longer eligible to be released on bond if they entered the country unlawfully, even if they have been in the U.S. for years.

Since then, as part of the president's crackdown on immigration, tens of thousands of immigrants have been detained by immigration authorities and held indefinitely. Many have filed petitions in federal court challenging their detentions and seeking release or a hearing. Hundreds of federal judges across the country have granted those requests and rejected the Trump administration's policy.
Two federal appeals courts have allowed noncitizens to be subject to mandatory detention without bond, but nine others have ruled against the Trump administration.

The case before the Supreme Court involves a Brazilian man, Ricardo Aparecido Barbosa da Cunha, who came to the U.S. illegally more than 20 years ago. Barbosa da Cunha has never been convicted of a crime, according to court papers. He applied for asylum in 2016 and was granted a valid work permit.
But last year, during a traffic stop in Massachusetts, Barbosa da Cunha was taken into custody by ICE officers, and the Department of Homeland Security initiated removal proceedings against him.

Barbosa da Cunha requested a bond hearing, but an immigration judge denied the request on the grounds that he was subject to mandatory detention without the possibility of bond under a provision of federal immigration law.

He then filed a petition in federal court alleging that his detention without access to a bond hearing was illegal and a violation of the Constitution's Due Process Clause. A federal judge sided with Barbosa da Cunha, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit upheld that decision, rejecting the Trump administration's mandatory detention policy.

In its decision, the 2nd Circuit panel of judges said accepting the administration's interpretation of immigration law would "send a seismic shock through our immigration detention system and society, straining our already overcrowded detention infrastructure, incarcerating millions, separating families, and disrupting communities."
Arguments in the case will likely be held early next year.
More big cases looming
The Supreme Court could also decide to take up several new cases that involve Mr. Trump's policies and actions taken during his second term.

Solicitor General D. John Sauer has asked the justices to decide the constitutionality of the Department of Defense's policy prohibiting transgender people from the military. An appeals court ruled that the ban discriminates against transgender individuals. But the Trump administration argues that the military has the power to decide who can serve in the armed forces and cannot be prohibited from exercising that authority.

The solicitor general, who argues on behalf of the U.S. government before the Supreme Court, has also appealed lower court decisions that have blocked Mr. Trump's appointments of acting U.S. attorneys in New York and Nevada.

The Trump administration has sought to install his allies as second-in-command, a position called first assistant U.S. attorney, of those offices and then elevate them to serve as the acting U.S. attorneys. But lower courts have said that those prosecutors, John Sarcone in Albany and Sigal Chattah in Nevada, were unlawfully appointed since they were not serving as the first assistant when the U.S. attorney position became vacant.

Mr. Trump has used the same mechanism to put his preferred picks atop U.S. attorney offices in New Jersey and Los Angeles, circumventing the Senate confirmation process required for those prosecutor positions. But lower courts have all said the appointments were unlawful.
Sauer has also asked the Supreme Court to decide whether Mr. Trump's efforts to effectively suspend asylum at the U.S.-Mexico border is lawful.

Mr. Trump, in his personal capacity, has asked the Supreme Court to review an $83.3 million defamation judgment stemming from statements he made about E. Jean Carroll and whether presidential immunity applies to those remarks.

Separate from the cases involving the president, the Supreme Court could also take up challenges to laws from Texas and Louisiana that require the Ten Commandments to be displayed in public school classrooms. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit has upheld the Texas law.

The high court has also been asked to take up a legal fight over a plea agreement reached by military prosecutors and two of the men allegedly behind the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks, including accused architect Khalid Sheikh Mohammed.

title: Latino Dems urge investment in Hinojosa campaign as Texas governor's race tightens
summary: Latino Democratic leaders are renewing calls for the Democratic Governors Association to invest more heavily in Texas after a new poll showed Gina Hinojosa narrowly leading Republican Gov. Greg Abbott.
story: Latino Democratic leaders are renewing calls for the Democratic Governors Association to invest more heavily in Texas after a New York Times/Siena College poll showed Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa narrowly leading Republican Gov. Greg Abbott.

The poll released Saturday found Hinojosa ahead of Abbott by three points, a result within the poll's margin of error. It comes as Hinojosa continues to face a huge financial disadvantage against the three-term Republican governor.  Abbott's reelection campaign and his Republican allies are outspending her by roughly 10-to-1.

More than 70 Latino Democratic leaders from across the country sent a letter this week urging the DGA and its chair, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, to invest $10 million in the Texas governor's race. The New York Times first reported on the letter, which CBS News has confirmed.

Beshear, a potential 2028 presidential contender, has been constrained by the DGA's commitments to first protect incumbent Democratic governors seeking reelection, though some of those incumbents are currently in strong positions.

Julián Castro, who served as secretary of housing and urban development in the Obama administration, renewed the push Saturday following the release of the New York Times poll. Castro, the former mayor of San Antonio and a 2020 presidential contender, took to social media to call for the DGA and Beshear to support Hinojosa "in a real way."
"How much more evidence" of Hinojosa's "strength in Texas" will Beshear and the DGA "have to see before they support her in a real way?" Castro wrote. "She can win!"

The renewed pressure comes as Democrats increasingly see the Lone Star state as competitive in the closing weeks of the campaign, even as Hinojosa continues to face a substantial spending disadvantage --- what some Republicans are describing as a "firewall" --- in a state that President Trump won by nearly 14 points in 2024.

title: Trump urges daylight saving time bill supporters to personally call Sen. Cotton
summary: President Trump urged supporters to call what appears to be the senator's personal cellphone number.
story: President Trump on Saturday pressured Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas to support a bill to make daylight saving time permanent, urging Americans to call what appeared to be the personal cellphone number of Cotton, the chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee.
The Sunshine Protection Act passed the House in July in a 308 to 117 vote. Mr. Trump called the passage of the bill "Great News for America!" at the time.

The bill still faces roadblocks in the Senate, where some Republicans are strongly opposed. Proponents, including the White House, argue that the change would provide more daylight during the times that Americans are most active.

Detractors said permanent daylight saving time would lead to darker and potentially more hazardous winter mornings when children will be waiting for school buses and parents will be driving to work in darkness.
The president has changed his position on the issue throughout the years. Mr. Trump has called both for daylight saving time to be eliminated and for it to be made permanent.

Daylight saving time is the period between spring and fall when clocks in most parts of the United States are set one hour ahead of standard time. Not all states observe it — and under the bill, states can opt out of the change if their respective legislatures act to do so before the bill's enactment.

"For some reason, Tom is stopping the Bill and, in the Senate, it's very easy to do, it only takes one!" Mr. Trump wrote on social media, noting that passing the bill would give professional golfers more time on the greens. "So, everyone in Arkansas, a State I love, and won 3 times, the last by by 34 points, tell Tom to, GET IT DONE! It will be appreciated by all," Mr. Trump said.
Mr. Trump included a phone number with an Arkansas area code. This is not the first time the president has released personal information about a senator.

While competing for the 2016 Republican presidential nomination, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham of South Carolina described Mr. Trump as "unfit for office" after Mr. Trump denigrated the military service of Sen. John McCain of Arizona. Mr. Trump then released Graham's personal cellphone number. That prompted a viral video in which the senator dramatically destroyed a series of flip phones. Graham later became a close ally of Mr. Trump.

Cotton, a member of Republican leadership, reiterated his opposition to permanent daylight saving time in a social media post of his own Saturday afternoon, though he is not the only Republican who opposes it.

"No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Savings Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter," Cotton wrote. "Arkansans don't want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I'll always put Arkansas first."

Mr. Trump responded: " If Tom Cotton were putting Arkansas first, he would give them an extra hour of daylight and, more importantly, they wouldn't have to run all over their houses, farms, work places, and everywhere else, twice a year, having to change their Clocks, and often forgetting to do so."

Members of Congress have long been interested in the potential benefits and costs of daylight saving time since it was first adopted as a wartime measure in 1942. The Senate passed a bill four years ago to make daylight saving time permanent, but it stalled in the House.
