MARGARET BRENNAN: I'm Margaret Brennan in Washington.
And this week on Face the Nation: One month away from midterms, and the pressure on the president to do something about high prices is building.

With control of the House and Senate at stake, President Trump has been on a red state road trip to get Republicans to the polls. He now concedes that his party might have a messaging problem when it comes to the economy.
(Begin VT)
DONALD TRUMP (President of the United States): We're doing a phenomenal job, but maybe we're doing a bad job in selling it.
(End VT)

MARGARET BRENNAN: And our new CBS poll has troubling news for the president's party, with nine in 10 voters saying they rate the economy on the basis of prices. Seven in 10 say that Trump's policies are making food and grocery prices go up. And nine in 10 say the conflict with Iran is making U.S. gas and oil prices either a lot or a little higher.
With early voting now under way, is it too late for Trump to turn things around?

We will talk with Energy Secretary Chris Wright about new efforts to get gas prices down. Plus, we will ask Zach Lahn, the Republican running for governor in Iowa, and Arizona Democratic Senator Mark Kelly what they're finding out on the campaign trail.
All that and more is just ahead on Face the Nation.
Good morning, and welcome to Face the Nation.
We begin with one of the Trump administration officials tasked with working to lower those high gas and oil prices, Energy Secretary Chris Wright.
Good morning to you.
CHRIS WRIGHT (U.S. Energy Secretary): Good morning, Margaret.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So, it's good to have you here.

You said this past week that Americans can expect lower gasoline prices and diesel prices by Election Day. The Wall Street Journal editorial board has a piece outlining that the campaign to squeeze Iran financially is working, but they can still knock out significant Gulf energy infrastructure.
They could be planning an October surprise before the U.S. midterms. We are still seeing Iranian attacks on ships now. I mean, how can you be so confident prices are headed down?
SECRETARY CHRIS WRIGHT: Well, because we've got increasing supplies coming out of the Strait of Hormuz, and they've continued to rise over the last months, over the last recent weeks.

We've got U.S. gasoline production today at record high. We have demand for gasoline as we come out of the summer driving season starting to go down. Similar stories with diesel. Diesel's mostly been impacted by the Russia- Ukraine war and also by China's decision not to export diesel or gasoline into the marketplace.

And, of course, we're living with two refineries that were recently closed, large refineries in California that Gavin Newsom forced the closure of, and, frankly, 15 years of Democrat policies that have been energy subtraction, trying to close coal plants, close refineries, and shrink our capacity, which means, when you get in crisis, we're just less resilient than we should be.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But you still think that, in the next four weeks, prices are going to go down?
SECRETARY CHRIS WRIGHT: Absolutely. Diesel prices have been going down. Gasoline prices have been going down. I expect that to continue.
MARGARET BRENNAN: I want to talk about diesel in a minute, but I – I was reading that the U.S. was sending more defensive equipment to the Gulf countries to protect their oil infrastructure.

I see there was a gathering of national security advisers at Camp David on Friday to talk about Iran and the conflict in Yemen. Can you share any outcome from that? I mean, is – is the U.S. about to escalate? We did just see a third carrier strike group get sent to the region.
SECRETARY CHRIS WRIGHT: Look, the president has – has taken a strong stand that Iran, the world's greatest terrorist regime – regime, cannot and will not have nuclear weapons.

So, of course, we're looking at every avenue to achieve that goal, economically, to be prepared for what comes militarily. But we cannot pass to the next administration an Iran armed with nuclear weapons. Not only is that a threat to peace and stability.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Right.
SECRETARY CHRIS WRIGHT: That's a massive long-term threat to energy prices.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Right, but he's also said that they're not seeking a nuclear weapon. He said that just the other day that they might have actually already stopped.

But in the immediate sense of threats to our neighbors who have refinery and production capacity, how do you guarantee that there is no October surprise that sends those prices going the opposite direction?
SECRETARY CHRIS WRIGHT: Hey, well, there's no guarantees. There's no guarantees in conflict. There's no guarantees in life.

But everything we're doing is to grow the supply of diesel, to grow the supply of gasoline, and, frankly, again, to reverse years of policies that have been directed exactly the opposite, to shrink our ability to produce, refine, and deliver hydrocarbons.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Can you say whether the president has decided he will escalate post-Election Day? That's when that third carrier strike group will be arriving, mid-November.
SECRETARY CHRIS WRIGHT: Oh, I'm definitely not going to get in front of the president's plans or policies. But remember…
MARGARET BRENNAN: He's thrown that out there himself.
(CROSSTALK)

SECRETARY CHRIS WRIGHT: … he's – he's always planning for contingencies and he's always negotiating. How you communicate, what you – what you lean in on, it sends a message to the other side. He's been a master, a master at doing that.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So he's got both tracks still going, diplomatic and military pressure?
SECRETARY CHRIS WRIGHT: Of course, of course, at all times.
MARGARET BRENNAN: OK, you talked about diesel.

The world's wealthiest countries, the G7, this past week agreed to release 100 million barrels of fuel over four months. They're going to front-load it with a lot of diesel in the next 20 days. I know you asked our friends and allies to consider doing this. How significant a price impact and for how long?
SECRETARY CHRIS WRIGHT: It's a big deal. It's a big deal.

Europe has very large diesel stores. They – you know, they don't refine enough diesel to supply their own economies, so naturally they store a lot of diesel. They're very keen to see American diesel continue to flow to Europe. They've got a lot of diesel in stores. Why not release some of that?

This is what you store diesel for, when all the Russian exports of diesel are shut down, when the Chinese have said, we're not going to deliver any more diesel, and you still have a reduction of diesel flows coming out of the Gulf. But we're restoring those. But that takes time.

This is just common sense. This lowers diesel prices, not just in the United States, but it lowers them in Europe and around the world. But it will drive diesel prices down as those releases come. It'll drive diesel down through the winter in the United States and around the world.
And – and, by then, we'll be in another place. We'll have more refining capacity online. I – I suspect we'll continue to see diesel decline as we go into next spring as well.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So, below six bucks, which is where it is?
SECRETARY CHRIS WRIGHT: Yes.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes, by post-midterms, or where…
(CROSSTALK)
SECRETARY CHRIS WRIGHT: Well, down.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Just down.
SECRETARY CHRIS WRIGHT: It's down a little over 20 cents so far.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
SECRETARY CHRIS WRIGHT: I think you'll see it continue to go down. Yes, you should see it below $6 before too long. But exactly when, I certainly don't know that.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So the allies did this after President Trump said he was considering a diesel export ban. You had so many quotes where you were telling people, this is not a good idea. Let's not do a diesel export ban.
But the president kept saying it was a consideration. Has he completely ruled out an export ban at this point?
SECRETARY CHRIS WRIGHT: Look, every day, he's throwing out ideas. He's engaging with discussions with me, others in the administration.
(CROSSTALK)
MARGARET BRENNAN: Even when you're saying it's not a good idea?
SECRETARY CHRIS WRIGHT: Absolutely.
(LAUGHTER)
SECRETARY CHRIS WRIGHT: No, he – he – he's a thinker.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But you're the expert.
SECRETARY CHRIS WRIGHT: He says – well – well, but there's different ways to slice this cat. There's different ways to look at it.

He's always looking, how do I lower energy prices? How do I lower heating prices, electricity prices, gasoline prices, diesel prices? In fact, I would say his constant communication of that may have been quite helpful in achieving – in achieving the deal we just struck.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Because people thought he might actually not listen to you and go ahead and do it?
SECRETARY CHRIS WRIGHT: I…
MARGARET BRENNAN: That was the – the ploy, essentially?

SECRETARY CHRIS WRIGHT: It – it wasn't a ploy. It's just a constant dialogue about the many levers we have. How can we drive down diesel prices and drive down gasoline and – and other prices along with it?

MARGARET BRENNAN: So we checked, and it looks like, because of this Lindsey Graham bill that gives the president more sort of powers to punish the buyers of Russian fuel, he has to make a decision by October the 18th as to whether he's going to put tariffs on the biggest buyers. That would be China, and that would be India. Is he going to do that?
SECRETARY CHRIS WRIGHT: Look, he – he leaves every decision until the end. He'll evaluate the trade-offs. He has worked ceaselessly to try to end this war.

Not only would end – would ending this war end the killing of – of tens and of thousands of people every month. It would dramatically lower energy prices. He's wanted to end that conflict, yes, since before he was president.
So – and – and there is constant, constant dialogues with both sides in that to try to bring that war to an end.

MARGARET BRENNAN: But, at this point, like, what's the direction here? You just had this big state visit. Are we actually in a position where the U.S. might put tariffs on China for buying Russian oil? Are we actually going to see that? And what impact would that have?
SECRETARY CHRIS WRIGHT: Again, I won't get in front of the president on that. We're trying to have the best relations we can.
MARGARET BRENNAN: I'm sure you've looked at the projections on what it would do for pricing.
SECRETARY CHRIS WRIGHT: Of course we're trying to have great relations with China and move that ball forward. I think things are going reasonably well there.
But then the flip side is, you've got to look at every leverage you've got to bring a murderous conflict to an end.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Mm-hmm. So, he may? And you would encourage him to?
SECRETARY CHRIS WRIGHT: I'm not going to say. I'm not going to say on either one of those.
MARGARET BRENNAN: OK.
SECRETARY CHRIS WRIGHT: He's – he's looking to how to end that conflict and how to lower prices for Americans every day.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.

Well, the date just stood out, you know, weeks before the midterms, doing something that could arguably push prices back up, and so if it's a national security decision – decision versus a political one. Be interested to know your point of view.
SECRETARY CHRIS WRIGHT: Hey, if his decisions were political, he would have just kicked the can down the road and delivered a nuclear-armed Iran to the next president. You've got to respect that.

That's an incredible move to lean in and say, I'm not going to let them become nuclear-armed. He knew it was going to elevate energy prices in the short run. He said, I'm going to take a hit there, but I got to do the right thing.
MARGARET BRENNAN: You did tell him that, that there would be a huge energy price spike, when he made this decision?

SECRETARY CHRIS WRIGHT: He – he was well aware of – of the risk to energy flows that were coming out of the Persian Gulf region. He said, I simply cannot – the world cannot sustain a nuclear-armed Iran, and I'm not going to do it.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Secretary Wright, thank you for your time today.
SECRETARY CHRIS WRIGHT: Thank you, Margaret.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Face Nation will be back in a minute. Stay with us.
(ANNOUNCEMENTS)

MARGARET BRENNAN: Our new CBS News Battleground Tracker poll finds that, if the election were held today, Democrats have a lead in that battle for control of the House. It would give them a 229-seat majority, with Republicans at 206 seats.
Anthony Salvanto is our executive director of elections and surveys and joins me now.
So, Anthony, when you look at this, the president's argument that he has the best economic numbers of any president in the history of the world don't seem to be persuading.
ANTHONY SALVANTO: It all comes back to prices, which is how people evaluate the economy.

Number one, the Democrats are winning more of the votes of people who say that they are hard-hit by prices. But this affects Republicans too in this way. Republicans tell us they're less likely to turn out than Democrats say.

And that's important. It's driving a lot of that lead that you just described. But then you look at the Republicans who are saying that. The ones who give the president relatively worse marks on handling inflation than they do for other matters, the ones who were most hard-hit themselves by prices, they're not necessarily switching over and voting for Democrats.

They're just saying they're going to sit this one out. And that's a big part of this. It's also, when you pull back the lens and look wider at what the electorate wants, you see opposition to a candidate in principle who supports tariffs. They don't want a candidate who supports data centers, because they think AI is going to take jobs, and they want a candidate who opposes the Iran conflict, because they think that's driving up gas prices.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Hispanic voters were so pivotal in 2024 for Republicans. Where are they now?

ANTHONY SALVANTO: Hispanic voters have moved more towards the Democrats than they were in 2024. And what that means is that the Republicans will not necessarily get the gains out of redistricting that they had hoped for if they can't keep those Hispanic voter gains that they made in 2024, Hispanic voters just as concerned about the economy and also a little more concerned about the president's focus on deportation.
MARGARET BRENNAN: And, even with a majority, it's a narrow one. That creates all sorts of political challenges.
Anthony, fascinating.
ANTHONY SALVANTO: Thanks.
MARGARET BRENNAN: We turn now to Arizona Senator Mark Kelly. He joins us from Charleston, South Carolina, where he is campaigning for his fellow Democrats.
Good morning to you, Senator.
SENATOR MARK KELLY (D-Arizona): Good morning.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Our CBS polling shows that Democrats have reason to be optimistic about taking the House, but how much harder will it be in the Senate?

SENATOR MARK KELLY: Well, Margaret, there is a lot of energy in the states I have been to recently, whether it's Ohio or Iowa, Kansas, Georgia, now here in South Carolina. I think we have real opportunities in a lot of places.

But, also, I mean, this could be, you know, close elections in many of these states. But I will tell you this. People are frustrated and they're fed up with Washington D.C. right now, and they know that this president is not addressing, you know, any of the needs that affect them and their families.
I mean, the cost of living is way too high. The price of everything just keeps going up.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
SENATOR MARK KELLY: And people can't afford their lives.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, President Trump announced Friday he's going to send $90 payments to 20 million older Americans this month, Medicare Part B enrollees. That's in addition to sending $500 in terms of checks to ACA refunds to a million people.
Also said, if Republicans win, then he'll send everyone 5,000 bucks. Do you support any of that? And what exactly is the Democratic message on lowering costs for Americans?
SENATOR MARK KELLY: Well, certainly, trying to help some working-class people and seniors on a fixed income.

But you got to remember this is a guy that gave a big tax cut to the wealthiest Americans, to billionaires and millionaires, and then, to partially pay for it, he's kicking people off of their health care, off of Medicaid. He's taken food benefits away from people that are having a hard time affording food, even children, in order to help out his family and his friends.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Mm-hmm.

SENATOR MARK KELLY: So I think people should see this for what it is, especially this $5,000 payment if Republicans maintain control of the House and the Senate. I mean, this is just a – a payoff, and he's trying to buy votes.
I mean, are you surprised with this president, who, in my view, is the most corrupt occupant of the Oval Office ever? I'm not surprised, but it's not right.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But what is the affirmative Democratic message here, other than, we're not him?
SENATOR MARK KELLY: Well, we're going to lower costs for the American people.
MARGARET BRENNAN: How?
SENATOR MARK KELLY: We've got to win the House and/or the Senate.

Well – well, how will we do this? I have legislation with – with Chris Van Hollen. We've got to get Republicans on board. It raises taxes for people who make over a million dollars a year in income, and it provides tax cuts for people, individuals and even couples up to – who make up to about $160,000 a year. That's some relief.

Ending this war in Iran that he started without a – any kind of a strategic goal or a plan has jacked up prices for the American people. Ending that would help. Getting this tariff policy reversed, these ridiculous tariffs that have also jacked up prices, the American people pay this.
For some reason, the president thinks that foreign countries are paying for these tariffs. That is not true.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
SENATOR MARK KELLY: So, there are things, a lot of things, we can and will do once we win back the House and/or the Senate.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, Republicans have pulled funding, as I understand it, from North Carolina's Senate race. They've redirected it out to Kansas, not typically a place a Republican would have to spend money to – to keep an advantage.
But what seats specifically are you optimistic you can turn blue?
SENATOR MARK KELLY: Well, there are a lot of them.

I spent some time in Kansas with Adam Hamilton. He's a pastor. He's – he's a great guy. He is the right person for Kansas. He understands what Kansans are dealing with. Josh Turek in Iowa, similar kind of situation, where that's a very winnable race, Mary Peltola in Alaska, Troy Jackson in Maine, Sherrod Brown in Ohio.

I'm going to do an event, you know, here today with Annie Andrews in South Carolina. Yes, I understand it's South Carolina, but she is a pediatrician. She's working incredibly hard. She's raising the resources to be successful.

And then there are the House races. Admiral Nancy Lacore – I did an event with her yesterday here in South Carolina – can be critical to Democrats winning back the House of Representatives. She's a – she's a three-star admiral, a Naval aviator, like myself, who was fired by Pete Hegseth early in this administration.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, a number of Senate Republicans have expressed some concern about Secretary Hegseth's firing. He also announced this past week he's going to cut by 20 percent the number of generals and admirals, he says, in order to try to change the culture. And what the media calls a purge, he says is simply a matter of accountability.
Do you have any insight into who he will be targeting in these cuts? And, if Democrats take some control, do you have any ability to stop it?
SENATOR MARK KELLY: Well, he often fires people because of the color of their skin or because they're women.
He also seems to be looking for…
MARGARET BRENNAN: He would deny that.
SEN. MARK KELLY: … loyal – of course he would deny that. I think anybody would deny that.

But it's pretty obvious. When you have a list of seven people who don't promote from one-star to two-star, and five of them are either black or women, it's pretty obvious. Also, right off the bat, firing C.Q. Brown without giving any reason, without any particular reason why one of the most qualified professional aviators, but a four-star general, chief of staff of the Air Force, fired.
Lisa Franchetti…
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
SENATOR MARK KELLY: … the chief of Naval operations, fired. The commandant of the Coast Guard, also a woman, was fired. The – the list goes on, Margaret.

This is a pattern with this secretary of defense. And it's damaging our readiness. And when you hurt readiness, it means that all of us, everybody watching the show, you and your family, are less safe, because we have the most unqualified secretary of defense we've ever had in this country's history.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, he gave a big speech this past week. The secretary said that every military branch has hit its recruiting targets ahead of the end of the year. He also argues military sexual assaults are on the decline.
I know they have been on the decline for a few years now. But what is your response to his argument that he's doing something right?
SENATOR MARK KELLY: Well, he's doing very little right.

Remember, Margaret, this is a guy that gets on a stage in front of the senior leadership of the U.S. military and runs around talking about killing people and lethality and that the rules of engagement – I'm going to paraphrase, but he talks about how he wants to eliminate or reduce the rules of engagement.
And you see the consequences of that in Iran. And he…
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
SENATOR MARK KELLY: His plan is what we went into Iran with, and he has bombed or attacked over 15,000 targets, depleting our munitions supply.
This thing has been a disaster because the secretary of defense has no idea what he's doing.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
SEN. MARK KELLY: And, to some extent, he's also a yes – a yes-man for the president. Nobody seems to want to push back against this president, who…
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
SEN. MARK KELLY: … who I – I think is checked out from even trying to do this job…
MARGARET BRENNAN: OK.
SEN. MARK KELLY: … got us into another war with – without – without a plan and without explaining – explaining to the American people, what are we going to get out of this?
MARGARET BRENNAN: Senator, I'm sorry to cut you off, but I'm out of time. I have to leave it there. Thank you.
We'll be right back.
(ANNOUNCEMENTS)
MARGARET BRENNAN: Tomorrow is the first Monday in October, which marks the start of a new Supreme Court term.
Our Jan Crawford sat down with Justice Samuel Alito in an interview for CBS News about his new book, "So Ordered." Here's a preview.
(Begin VT)

JAN CRAWFORD: When you have political leaders on both sides talking about the Supreme Court as though justices are just nothing more than political actors trying to deliver victory to their team, how damaging is that to the court?
SAMUEL ALITO (U.S. Supreme Court Associate Justice): I think it's damaging. I think it can be quite damaging.

There's been a great change in what presidents have said about the court when they are unhappy about our decisions. Traditionally, what presidents would say is, the Supreme Court, it's made its decision, I disagree with it, but we have to abide by it. And that was it.
That's what presidents said. That's what members of the Cabinet said. That has changed. And…
JAN CRAWFORD: Did Trump change that?
JUSTICE SAMUEL ALITO: It's been bipartisan. It's a bipartisan effort.
JAN CRAWFORD: But what's – in terms of presidents, I mean, the language that we're hearing from President Trump is different, certainly with social media.
JUSTICE SAMUEL ALITO: He has his own way of saying things.

But the criticism of the court – I mean, I want to be even-handed on this. The criticism of the court by President Biden and justices by President Biden and his administration was very harsh. And President Trump has been very harsh.
JAN CRAWFORD: But when you – when you see the president of the United States – and you're saying you're following the law whichever way it leads you.

But when you see the president of the United States talking about you and some of your colleagues as being part of his political MAGA movement, that you're – you're trying to make America great again, does that bother you?

JUSTICE SAMUEL ALITO: Well, we are not part of any political movement. And we are not attempting to further any political agenda. We are trying to interpret the Constitution as best we can and apply it in the cases that come before us.
(End VT)

MARGARET BRENNAN: You can see more of Jan's interview Monday on CBS Mornings and the CBS Evening News, and you can read all about it on CBSNews.com later today. Her preview piece drops at 3:00 p.m. Eastern.
(ANNOUNCEMENTS)

MARGARET BRENNAN: We will be right back with an update on that terrifying attempted hijacking of a Flydubai flight last week and an interview with Brett McGurk, the former national security official who worked to negotiate the release of the Israeli hostages and others being held by Hamas.
Stay with us.
(ANNOUNCEMENTS)
MARGARET BRENNAN: Welcome back to "FACE THE NATION."
We turn now to the Republican running for governor of Iowa, Zach Lahn. He joins us from Bell Plain.
Good morning.
ZACH LAHN (Republican Candidate for Iowa Governor): Good morning, Margaret.

MARGARET BRENNAN: We look at diesel prices. They're north of six bucks. President Trump's trade war with Canada and China have made things expensive for farmers. You know that well in Iowa. Are the president's policies a headwind for your party?

ZACH LAHN: Well, I think when you talk about what's going on with affordability for farmers – and, by the way, this is something we launched our campaign on in the beginning. You have to take a step back and really understand what's been going on for decades in the agriculture industry, where we've seen consolidation after consolidation of businesses taking choice and competition away from farmers. We've reached monopoly stages there.

And now what we're seeing with some of the increased prices on diesel, it's kind of just another one of these pieces that's adding up to that. And we've been focused, you know, in the state on how do we cut the gas tax and other priorities to help farmers have more affordable fuel when they go into harvest.

So, this has been a part of our campaign since the very beginning. And I really think farmers understand that for a long time they have been treated as price takers. And, really, the deck has been stacked against them. And now when you add in the higher cost of diesel, we really have a problem.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, it – you just mentioned there, big ag. You are campaigning with a promise to break up big ag monopolies. You said you're going to tax the heck out of Wall Street hedge funds that own farmland. Those sound more typically like progressive policies than conservative ones. How do you convince Iowa Republicans?

ZACH LAHN: Well, I just say that, you know, breaking up monopolies was first done by Republicans. The Sherman Anti-Trust Law is Republican. Teddy Roosevelt broke up two of the biggest companies in existence. Monopoly is a failure of the free market. I think we forgot that in large part and now we're paying the consequence for it. So, my priority is to increase the funding to the attorney general's office, to take on these anti-competitive lawsuits, because farmers across the country are waiting for someone to take the first step here and really give them a fair deal.
And so, I think that these are ideals of the Republican Party, but really they're just the right ideas, the right thing to do.

MARGARET BRENNAN: It's an interesting position, though, given that the party has typically been very close to the agriculture industry. I know you have focused in, in your campaign, on the cancer rate in Iowa. It has the second highest cancer incidence in this country. You say it's nitrates and pesticides, including glyphosate that caused it.
President Trump signed an executive order to boost production of glyphosate-based herbicides. How do you reconcile those presidential decisions from the policy you have?

ZACH LAHN: Well, I would just say first that I was one of the first people to come out and say that this was the wrong move to sign that executive order. I think that if we could give the president the advice on that, that he would understand that better.

But what – we are focused on a campaign that's focused on Iowa issues specifically. And this is something that Iowans are facing. We have the fastest rate of new cancer anywhere in the country, number one. And if you move out of the state of Iowa to say a state like Nevada, your chance of getting cancer in a given year goes down by 40 percent. These are very specific Iowa-based issues and we've been focused on them. High nitrate load in water is one of the top causes of colon cancer, bladder cancer, ovarian cancer, and we've got some of the highest levels in the country, if not the highest level.

So, we are focused on providing incentives to farmers, real incentives, to adopt different types of practices, to allow them the ability to really change what they're doing, to stop these products from getting into the streams in the first place, clean up our water at the source, and help farmers make sure that they're not losing money by doing it, by providing real incentives that help them actually make money by adopting these practices. Because it really goes back to, farmers are operating on razor- thin margins right now. And the idea to experiment with something new is not very appealing when you could be the first in a line of five generations that loses your family farm.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Right. Right. And that's one of the arguments for continuing to use this herbicide that has arguably ties to cancer is that it's just frankly cheap.
Your position –
ZACH LAHN: OK (ph).

MARGARET BRENNAN: You just said, if the president had more information, maybe he would make a different decision. Just for the record, RFK Jr., the HHS secretary, says he opposed it, told the president he opposed it, and the president did it on national security grounds. But he has been out there, the HHS secretary. He's been campaigning for you. Many of your platform issues are very popular with the MAHA movement. Should America view your race as a test of Kennedy's popularity?

ZACH LAHN: Well, I think that Kennedy is very popular in Iowa. He's very popular across the country. But it's more so the principles that he represents, which are similar principles to what I represent.

Look, we all want healthy kids. We want clean water. We want to make sure we have less medications for our kids. We want to solve these issues that have been causing a rise in, you know, chronic illness and autoimmune conditions, not just amongst kids but amongst adults. And we believe that food is medicine. That it's the first line that you need to be looking at, is what food are we putting into our body?

And this is one of the reasons that – a top priority of mine. My moon shot for the state of Iowa is to see a day in which 80 percent of the food served in our public schools is grown in the state of Iowa. And we can do that. It will take time, but this might be, you know, the only nutritious meal a kid has all day. And Iowa has the best farmland in the world. The best farmers in the world. We can do this and lead the country on it. And this is one of the first steps that we can take to really make sure that we're cleaning up our food supply, we're getting kids healthy food.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, we will continue to watch your race and see if Iowa, as you say, is an outlier here and maybe starting something new.
Thank you, Zach Lahn, for your time today.
We'll be right back.
(ANNOUNCEMENTS)
MARGARET BRENNAN: We're learning new details about the attempted hijacking of a FlyDubai flight over Saudi Arabia. Our Matt Gutman reports from Abu Dhabi.
(BEGIN VT)

MATT GUTMAN (voice over): CBS News has learned that Israel now believes the attack and suspected hijacking of Flight 1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv was likely a lone wolf attack. Now for the first time, hero Captain Smit Machchhar tells his version of what the UAE is calling a terrorist attack when his copilot tried to crash the plane with 172 people on board into the Arabian Desert. He spoke by phone to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday.

CAPTAIN SMIT MACHCHHAR: While he was praying, out of respect, I was just looking at the front and not at the back. And suddenly there was a big blow to the back of my head. My first thought was that there was a catastrophic damage to the aircraft. After that, the blows kept coming, one after another. And that's when I realized that it's not the aircraft, it's the other guy who was in the cockpit with me.

MATT GUTMAN (voice over): The UAE says the copilot used a crash ax, found in the cockpit of most commercial airliners. Sources tell CBS News, co- pilot Hamam al-Hammami had been banned from flying for Oman's national carrier after its government discovered he was visiting radical websites. That as Israeli authorities acknowledged they did receive a list of Flight 1073's crew members, which reportedly included al-Hammami.
As Israeli dentist Dr. Shota Musaev rushed to treat Captain Machchhar's wounds, he also spoke to co-pilot al-Hammami.
DR. SHOTA MUSAEV, HELPED CAPTAIN AFTER ATTACK: After two minutes he – he said to me, kill me. Kill me. And said to Yanif (ph), kill – kill me, sometimes. That's – that's it.
MATT GUTMAN: He said, kill, kill me, multiple times?
SHOTA MUSAEV: Yes. Yes, yes.

MATT GUTMAN: That alleged attacker is now being interrogated here in the UAE, as both the UAE and Israel are facing questions about how a pilot with known extremist views was allowed to fly that route from Dubai to Tel Aviv.
(END VT)
MARGARET BRENNAN: That's Matt Gutman reporting from Abu Dhabi.

Three years ago this week, Hamas massacred 1,200 people in Israel and took 254 people hostage. As national security council coordinator under former President Biden, Brett McGurk, worked to secure their release, a challenge he writes about in his new book, "Brink."
We spoke with McGurk last week.
(BEGIN VT)

MARGARET BRENNAN: You wrote that the U.S. had no clear warnings, nor did the Israelis, from what they told us. But you leave open the idea that there were missed signals. Was this a total intelligence failure?

BRETT MCGURK (Former White House National Security Council Coordinator for the Middle East and North Africa): So, we have really looked at – we did not have any – anything in our system that would have been a warning and indicator.
MARGARET BRENNAN: No U.S. intelligence?

BRETT MCGURK: No U.S. intelligence of a warning or indicator. I can't speak to whether the Israelis – the Israelis still have, to this day, not had a commission of inquiry. We had the 9/11 Commission that made a number of reforms that have helped keep our country safe since 9/11. The Israelis still have not done that. I think they have – they should do that.

But from what I, in dealing with all of these guys in Israel, security echelon, political echelon, I think they had an assumption that was deeply engrained that Hamas was deterred, assuaged, and was not about to do something massive on any scale like this. I think that was a false assumption in their system, failure of imagination, and it was tragic.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Let me ask you about the Israeli prime minister. In February of 2024, you talk about a meeting you had with him. You were very focused on these hostages and trying to get them out. You said, "for more than 30 minutes, he never mentioned the hostages. Netanyahu was animated in discussing the military campaign and far less so when discussing the hostages, when he chose to discuss them at all."
BRETT MCGURK: Yes.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Why? Why do you think that is?

BRETT MCGURK: Netanyahu was focused far more on the military campaign and assuring Hamas can never retain power in Gaza. Believing the military campaign and the pressure on Hamas would lead to a deal that released all the hostages, whereas we were trying to focus on a phased deal that at least let's – get some of the hostages out first. And Netanyahu always believed that more military pressure will actually deliver a better deal, whereas Sinwar believed more time would put more pressure on the U.S. and others to deliver him a better deal. That's what makes this almost an impossible situation to deal with.
MARGARET BRENNAN: You felt the U.S. was putting more value on those lives than the Israeli government did?

BRETT MCGURK: The U.S. role in this, in all dimensions, we were trying to stop a war and get the hostages home. And the two were – the two were completely linked. And to reduce human suffering as much as possible in Gaza.

You know, Netanyahu, I describe him as, obviously, very confident in his assumptions. And he has a brother who was killed in the Entebbe raid, very confident in terms of his belief and how to deal with these groups. And yet I believe a lot of times there were miscalculations.

MARGARET BRENNAN: National Security Adviser Jake Sullivan has publicly suggested that the U.S. focus was so much on the hostages that it was almost a trap, as he put it, in thinking that we can get to a ceasefire and a hostage deal, and other things were sublimated to that objective. I mean, in hindsight, do you share that feeling?
BRETT MCGURK: The war would not have stopped without the hostages. I don't – I don't believe that.

About a month into the war we had – we had a deal with Hamas. Not easy. I describe what it was like to get, for all women and children, it's very clear, all women and children hostages are going to come out. And in exchange for a number of Palestinian prisoners. And we had a ceasefire for eight days. And about 100 hostages came out. Three of those women that did not come out, because on the eighth day Hamas said, we're not going to release the younger women, actually. We released the young toddlers, like Abigail, the young American girl. We released the 80-year-old grandmothers. We're going to hold on to the younger ones. They said, we can't find them, which was completely untrue. So –
MARGARET BRENNAN: Wasn't part of the excuse that they were military age too?
BRETT MCGURK: No. Well, they said some – they claimed that.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.

BRETT MCGURK: But they said, let's keep a ceasefire and talk about the older men. And in the book I go through this night, midnight here in Washington, December 1st, and it's a moral quandary. And this is what a hostage taker does. Hamas is as good as Iran is. They're masters at this. They put the moral onus on the other side. Do you skip the younger women, start talking about older men, keep the ceasefire, or say, no, you broke the deal?
(END VT)
MARGARET BRENNAN: We'll have more from Brett McGurk when we come back.
(ANNOUNCEMENTS)
MARGARET BRENNAN: We pick up our conversation with Brett McGurk about the negotiations with Hamas in 2024 to release the hostages and end the Gaza war.
(BEGIN VT)

MARGARET BRENNAN: All of what you were trying to do was happening at the same time as the American political cycle here, a presidential election. And there appeared to be unquestioning U.S. support for Israel and providing military support to Israel. And this became a political issue, particularly among Democrats. Then, the Republican candidates, including now President Donald Trump, were criticizing that you weren't strong enough in support of Israel. How aware were you of the politics of the moment, as you're making decisions like this?

BRETT MCGURK: I'm very independent. So, I've worked with Republican presidents, Democratic presidents. I was a law clerk for two judges appointed by Republicans, one by a Democrat. And – but let me bring you into the Oval Office and kind of, in a scene in which I think encapsulates this very issue.

April 4, 2024. President Biden, it's his re-election. He's on the campaign trail. Obviously frustrated about the situation. Unable to articulate, because the hostage talks have now collapsed. They recently collapsed for a number of reasons I go through in the book.

He's frustrated by being unable to point to how are we actually going to try to bring this to a close. We had a horrific air strike from the Israelis that killed nine aid workers with World Central Kitchen, Jose Andreas –
MARGARET BRENNAN: An Israeli drone hit the clearly marked convoy.

BRETT MCGURK: And – which – which was so tragic – so horrific. And so, we have a call with – between Biden and Netanyahu. And Biden is just like, you know, completely fed up. And at the same time, however, Iran is planning to launch – we have intel – intelligence that Iran is about to launch a massive ballistic missile drone attack directly against Israel, which is totally unprecedented. And – which if those missiles get through, you're talking about thousands of casualties.

So, this is how kind of everything converges. And I think at that moment, if not for that impending missile attack, which we then had to deploy military forces. We built an unprecedented coalition with air partners, European partners and, of course, the U.S. military and General Kurilla (ph), who was kind of putting this together. If not for that, I think on that – in that moment, I think we would have taken some pretty draconian measures against Israel.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Really?
BRETT MCGURK: Yes. I do not –
MARGARET BRENNAN: Draconian how? What do you mean?

BRETT MCGURK: Well, I think we would have – you just mentioned cutting off weapons and other things. That was very much on the table. But also at that time in April, Congress bipartisan – a massive bipartisan majority approved a $26 million aid package for Israel, right in April, right in that moment. But the – the focus very quickly shifts to, how do we defend Israel from this – from this missile attack. It ended up being 120 ballistic missiles, 170 drones, 30 cruise missiles, all launched to land at the same time.

MARGARET BRENNAN: But on the World Central Kitchen event, the – people remember that. There was outrage around that. You wrote that, "President Biden told Bibi Netanyahu," the prime minister, "that he could, in theory, cut Israel from military aid at a finger snap –
BRETT MCGURK: Yes.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Leaving Israel on its own. You think I'm Santa Claus? No Santa in Israel, pal?"
BRETT MCGURK: Yes.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But he didn't. He didn't cut.
BRETT MCGURK: Well, I mean, we –
MARGARET BRENNAN: Did he actually mean that as a threat?

BRETT MCGURK: We selectively – we talked about it in that – in the Oval Office around that time. We selectively, after that call, the president stopped all sales and deliveries of heavy payload munitions, 2,000-pound bombs. We stopped –
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, he delayed them, ultimately.
BRETT MCGURK: We didn't deliver them and we didn't approve any other sales. President Trump reversed that immediately after coming into office.

MARGARET BRENNAN: It was such a public debate at the time about America's role in the world, the standards America is held to, and whether America is complicit in how our weapons are used. And under the Leahy Law, as you know, you know, countries that receive U.S. weapons have to avoid committing human rights violations or risk losing the weapons supply.
Blinken said –
ANTONY BLINKEN (Former Secretary of State): It was reasonable to access that in certain instances Israel acted in ways that are not consistent with international humanitarian law.
MARGARET BRENNAN: And that "Israeli civilian harm mitigation efforts were inconsistent, ineffective, and inadequate."
Do you agree with that State Department memo?

BRETT MCGURK: No aid to any country is unconditional, including – including to Israel. And – but security assistance is a – is a complex, multi-institutional, multi-branch endeavor. And again, these – most of these appropriations were appropriated by massive, bipartisan majorities in Congress at the time. But – and the – and the State Department has a role and the Pentagon has an important role.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Right. He was saying hit the brakes on deliveries. Or reexamine (ph).

BRETT MCGURK: Again, we hit the brakes on some – on some deliveries, again, selectively. But to have a broad-based stoppage of support, again, for Israel, at a time – I don't know what the timeframe was for that statement, but I can –
MARGARET BRENNAN: It was in May, in 2024.
BRETT MCGURK: So, in May – yes, so in May, we just had the largest ballistic missile and drone attack ever in history. We helped the Israelis defeat it.
We say to Netanyahu, Biden's quote in that meeting is, "I just saved your ass." We're getting back to the hostage deal, OK?

We spent the month of May putting together a detailed, four-page, three- phase agreement, single space, every detail there. We go to the Israelis and to Netanyahu and say, we need you to sign up. And it went very far in the direction of Hamas. Frankly, it was a better deal for Hamas than what they have right now.

And Netanyahu, on May 27th, signed onto that deal. On May 31st, because what were we doing in May? On May 31st, President Biden laid out that deal to the world in a speech. And he said, Israel has accepted this deal. Hamas, say, yes, let's end this war. The U.N. Security Council endorses that deal. It's May 31st.

What happens? In early June, after this is on the table, we can stop the war right now if Hamas says yes. Khamenei, supreme leader of Iran, gives a defiant speech praising October 7th, and basically Iran is telling Hamas to not – to not compromise in any of – of the terms. Hezbollah launches its largest attack of the war, 250 rockets into northern Israel. This is – when we have a ceasefire deal on the table.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
BRETT MCGURK: We don't get an answer from Hamas until July 2nd, almost five weeks later. And they put all sorts of things in it that set the talks back.
So, I say this because we were working to end this crisis and end this war. And if you want – in May, June, and we had the deal on the table to do it.

My approach would have – is, this deal is on the table to stop the war. All pressure, everything, public, everything else, has to come down on Hamas and their enablers to say yes to end this deal – or to end this war.

But Hamas did not say "yes." and they kept stringing this out. And they would put an issue on the table, then Israel would take a hard position. But that's what was happening in May. And if you go to that – you know, Biden goes to the world and says, this is the deal. He had a phone call with I think 18 heads of state because these hostages are from countries all around the world. They all said – they called on Hamas to take the deal, and Hamas did not take the deal. I mean we were working at that time to end the war through a deal. And I think, again, all vectors of pressure should have been on Sinwar to say yes.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But you're not saying –
BRETT MCGURK: And the war would have stopped.
MARGARET BRENNAN: You're not saying that the Democratic Party pressure and calling out compliance with U.S. law was enabling Hamas? That's not what you're saying?
BRETT MCGURK: No, no, no. I – but I'm not – and also not –
MARGARET BRENNAN: But you're saying it's almost like naive?

BRETT MCGURK: And I'm also not getting into internal party debates. I've never been a part of that. I'll let – I'll let political parties have their debates. Not my role at all. I come back to the question, how do you end this crisis?
MARGARET BRENNAN: Uh-huh.
BRETT MCGURK: And I think the record shows, if you just stop American support for Israel, that is not going end to the crisis. It's going to make it worse.
(END VT)
MARGARET BRENNAN: Our full conversation's on our website, facethenation.com, and our YouTube page.
We'll be right back.
(ANNOUNCEMENTS)
MARGARET BRENNAN: That's it for us today. Thank you all for watching. Until next week. For "FACE THE NATION," I'm Margaret Brennan.

title: Energy Secretary: Trump was "aware of the risks to energy flows" before Iran war
summary: Energy Secretary Chris Wright said that President Trump was "well aware of the risks to energy flows" before launching the war in Iran earlier this year, but argued "the world cannot sustain a nuclear-armed Iran."
story: Washington — Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Sunday that President Trump was "well aware of the risks to energy flows" before launching the war in Iran earlier this year, but argued "the world cannot sustain a nuclear-armed Iran."
"He knew it was going to elevate energy prices in the short run, he said, 'I'm going to take a hit there, but I got to do the right thing,'" Wright said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."

Americans have been feeling the financial squeeze of soaring gas and diesel prices in recent months. But the Trump administration has pointed to the potential threat a nuclear-armed Iran could pose, and how it could represent a long-term threat to energy prices. Wright defended the president on Sunday, arguing that Mr. Trump has taken a "strong stand that Iran, the world's greatest terrorist regime, cannot and will not have nuclear weapons."

Wright expressed confidence that prices will fall, pointing to increasing supplies coming out of the Strait of Hormuz, U.S. gasoline production, the summer driving season slowing, among other factors. Asked whether he expects prices to go down over the next four weeks — as Republicans eye a tough environment in the lead up to the midterm elections — Wright said, "absolutely."
"Diesel prices have been going down, gasoline prices have been going down," Wright said. "I expect that to continue."

Diesel prices soared of above $6.50 a gallon in recent weeks, squeezing farmers, who rely on diesel to run agricultural machinery, along with industries from construction firms to food banks, which rely on diesel to fuel their vehicles and delivery trucks. Wright noted that diesel prices are down a little over 20 cents so far in recent days, adding that he expects the prices to continue to go down.
"You should see it below $6 before too long," he said. "But exactly when, I certainly don't know that."

Wright said "everything we're doing is to grow the supply of diesel, to grow the supply of gasoline, and frankly, again, to reverse years of policies that have been directed exactly the opposite-to shrink our ability to produce, refine, and deliver hydrocarbons."

Wright wouldn't weigh in on the president's plans and whether things would escalate militarily after the midterm elections. But he said Mr. Trump is "always planning for contingencies and he's always negotiating," and both diplomatic and military tracks remain open.

The energy secretary said securing the agreement from the Group of Seven countries last week to release 100 million barrels of fuel over four months is a "big deal." He called it "common sense" and said it will drive diesel prices down in the U.S. and around the world through the winter.

"Europe has very large diesel stores. They don't refine enough diesel to supply their own economies, so naturally they store a lot of diesel. They're very keen to see American diesel continue to flow to Europe. They've got a lot of diesel in stores. Why not release some of that?" Wright said. "This is what you store diesel for when all the Russian exports of diesel are shut down, when the Chinese have said we're not going to deliver any more diesel, and you still have a reduction of diesel flows coming out of the Gulf. But we're restoring those, but that takes time."

Asked whether the president has ruled out an export ban on diesel, which Wright has opposed, Wright said "every day" Mr. Trump has been "throwing out ideas," and the president remains engaged in discussions.

"There's different ways to look at it. He's always looking, 'How do I lower energy prices? How do I lower heating prices, electricity prices, gasoline prices, diesel prices?' In fact, I would say his constant communication of that may have been quite helpful in achieving the deal we just got," he said.
Wright added, "It's just a constant dialogue about the many levers we have, how can we drive down diesel prices and drive down gasoline and other prices along with it?"

story: The Emmy Award-winning "CBS News Sunday Morning" is broadcast on CBS Sundays beginning at 9:00 a.m. ET.  "Sunday Morning" also streams on the CBS News app beginning at 11:00 a.m. ET. (Download it here.)
Hosted by Jane Pauley
WATCH THE FULL OCTOBER 4 BROADCAST!

COVER STORY: Letting go: Why holding onto grudges can be damaging | Watch VideoStudies have shown that people who hold grudges have greater levels of cardiovascular trouble, and higher levels of depression and anxiety. But according to one survey, four out of five adults harbor some lingering resentment towards others, sometimes over the smallest of reasons. Correspondent Susan Spencer talks with experts about why some people can maintain grudges for years; how holding grudges can be counterproductive; and what it takes to have forgiveness overcome lingering ill will.

READ AN EXCERPT: "Narratives" by Nancy ColierIn her latest book, the psychotherapist writes about how the stories we tell ourselves about ourselves can hold us back from living a more truthful and connected life.

HEADLINES: Hero passenger on FlyDubai flight: "I decided that we are going to survive" | Watch VideoThis past Wednesday, the co-pilot of FlyDubai's Flight 1073, flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv, attacked the captain and tried to crash the Boeing 737 Max, the jet plunging 14,000 feet in a matter of seconds. Passengers subdued the attacker and another pilot righted the plane with moments to spare.  Correspondent Matt Gutman talks with some of the passengers who heroically helped avert disaster.

CULTURE: Ken Kesey's original "Furthur" bus on its latest trek | Watch VideoIn 1964 writer Ken Kesey and his band of "Merry Pranksters" rode a 1939 school bus, named "Furthur," across the country, fueled by music, alcohol and LSD. It became an icon of the burgeoning counterculture movement, and a symbol of liberation. But in the decades since it has fallen into a rusted state. Now the bus is on display in San Francisco, part of an ongoing journey to help restore it to its former, magic glory. Jonathan Vigliotti reports.

MOVIES: Aaron Sorkin on "The Social Reckoning": "Maybe we can't handle the truth" | Watch VideoAaron Sorkin's Oscar-winning screenplay for "The Social Network" helped define Mark Zuckerberg in the public imagination. Sixteen years later, Sorkin turns from Facebook's origins to its consequences. He wrote and directed "The Social Reckoning," inspired by whistleblower Frances Haugen's leak of thousands of internal documents to Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz. Correspondent Jo Ling Kent talks with Sorkin and Haugen about Facebook's power – and what it means for all of us.

title: Iowa approves pricey foreign-owned steel plant project in swing district
summary: President Trump announced that the largest steel plant in U.S. history will be built in Iowa, touching off a week of debate.
story: "Stop the Steal" — or rather, steel — has an entirely new meaning for some Iowa voters in 2026.

Protesters at the Iowa statehouse Friday carried signs reading "No Steel Steal!" as lawmakers raced through a one-day special session to award Mesabi Metallics $1.36 billion over 10 years in tax incentives for a new steel plant in Lee County. Mesabi Metallics is owned by the Indian conglomerate Essar Group.
The Iowa House passed it 75-17, the Senate 28-19. Gov. Kim Reynolds signed it into law Friday night.

It comes after President Trump's Monday announcement that the largest steel plant in U.S. history would be built in Iowa. Mr. Trump promised the $15 billion steel plant would create 1,750 permanent jobs and roughly 6,000 construction jobs.

The announcement caught many in the state by surprise, including lawmakers who would be counted on to approve the tax incentives. When Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick told reporters at the White House "the deal is done" on Monday, lawmakers in Iowa still hadn't received details to review or timing for the special session held Friday.

Opponents of the $1.36 billion in incentives are largely supporters of the project, but they wanted more safeguards and guarantees of public benefits. The incentives roughly amount to about $777,000 in credits per permanent job over 10 years, a hefty price tag by any standards. Proponents argue that math leaves out roughly 6,000 construction jobs — which opponents point out are all temporary.
And at a time when many of Iowa's farmers are struggling, more than a billion dollars in tax credits for an India-based conglomerate is a hard sell for some.
Why Iowa?

There are places in the U.S. synonymous with steel, but Iowa has never been one of them. The state has a couple scrap-fed steel mills — a small fraction of the size Mesabi is promising — and no commercial iron ore. Mesabi Metallics is based in Minnesota, and its argument is that Iowa is conveniently downriver on the Mississippi.
But Iowa has something that Minnesota doesn't: One of the most tightly contested congressional races in the nation. The state also has close Senate and governor's races.

The plant's proposed location is Iowa's 1st Congressional District, where Republican Congresswoman Mariannette Miller-Meeks is defending one of the GOP's most at-risk seats. In 2024, the recount had her ahead of Democrat Christina Bohannan by just 798 votes. Sabato's Crystal Ball just moved the race from "toss up" to "leans Democratic" before the steel announcement.
Bankruptcy and broken promises

Mesabi and Essar Group have a long history of missed deadlines and unfulfilled job promises. In 2008, Essar announced a $1.6 billion iron ore mine and steel plant in Nashwauk, Minnesota, home to some of the country's richest iron ore deposits. It promised more than 700 permanent jobs. But the steel mill plans were dropped in 2015. Essar Steel Minnesota filed for bankruptcy in 2016, was renamed Mesabi Metallics under new owners, and later came back under Essar's control.
The India-based Essar has recueved billions of dollars in loans from the Russian state-owned bank VTB, according to local media. CBS News has not independently verified these reports.

There are also echoes of other regional mega-projects gone awry. No one in the Hawkeye state wants the steel plant to be the 2026 version of Foxconn. In 2017,  President Trump and Foxconn promised a $10 billion plant and create 13,000 jobs in the battleground state of Wisconsin. By 2021, the plan was scaled back to $672 million and 1,454 jobs. Republican Gov. Scott Walker championed the deal — and lost his 2018 reelection bid as public support for it soured.
Tricky politics
On Friday, Republican State Senator Kevin Alons told the Des Moines Register that lawmakers needed more time ahead of Friday's vote.
"The political extortion is breathtaking," he said.
But in the end, he voted for it.

State Sen. Dave Sires, also a Republican, voted no on the project, complaining the process was rushed. State Senator Dan Dawson, another Republican, called it the "largest corporate giveaway in the state of Iowa's history." And Republican State Senator Jeff Taylor raised concerns that the state was already in a real budget crunch.
Taylor was swapped off the Senate Ways and Means Committee at the last minute to ensure the bill would pass committee. It passed 10-8, with 6 Republican State Senators voting against the bill.

It's a careful political calculus for Republicans in the Iowa Senate. They're trying to thread a fine needle: follow their leaders and bring home jobs, without being seen as rushing more than a billion dollars in taxpayer money to a foreign-owned company with no time for review.

Republican gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn, who has campaigned against corporate handouts, made a case for supporting the bill. He called the idea of an Iowa steel plant a "once in a lifetime" exception.

Democrats have been navigating tricky political territory as well, trying not to oppose job creation while pushing back on the rush to issue nearly $1.4 billion in tax breaks before early voting starts on Oct. 14. Democratic nominee Rob Sand, currently the state auditor, called the steel plant "a promising idea for Lee County" but wanted to see more details first.

"You look at these data center deals that this administration has done over the last few years and we gave away the farm," Sand said. "I want to make sure this is a real opportunity, but also at the end of the day Iowa is getting served by it and not getting fleeced."
Iowa Senate Democratic Leader Janice Weiner said she wants good-paying jobs and investments in the state but balked at the rapid timeline that left taxpayers out of the conversation.

"If we were doing this the right way, we would be waiting until after the election," she told CBS News on Saturday. "We have a responsibility to our taxpayers to make sure our hard-earned dollars are well spent. If it's a good deal now, it will be a good deal in January when due diligence has been done."
Meanwhile, State Representative Dave Jacoby, a Democrat, voted yes, "with the hope that this plan is real," while still cautioning, "today is not a ribbon cutting."

The ribbon cutting, if it comes, is years away. The tax credits don't kick in until the plant is running, and Mesabi says that won't be before 2030. Iowans begin to cast their votes in just a few days. So the question on the ballot isn't whether Iowa gets a steel mill. It's whether voters believe it will — and if $1.36 billion was the right price to pay for it.

title: Michael Lewis on "Blockers": Profiling government workers confronted by DOGE
summary: The latest book by the bestselling author of "The Big Short" and "Moneyball" profiles federal workers targeted by President Trump and his mega-donor Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE).
story: Author Michael Lewis believes most Americans do not know that civil servants in the federal government take an oath of office. "I didn't know," he said. "I don't think I knew even after I'd written a whole book about them. So, I assume not."

"I, ___, do solemnly swear (or affirm) that I will support and defend the Constitution of the United States against all enemies, foreign and domestic; that I will bear true faith and allegiance to the same; that I take this obligation freely, without any mental reservation or purpose of evasion; and that I will well and faithfully discharge the duties of the office on which I am about to enter. So help me God."– Civil Service Oath of Office, U.S. Code § 3331.

For Lewis, pursuing knowledge is a calling. He has conjured up bestsellers and box-office hits out of deep-dives into data, from Wall Street ("The Big Short," "Liar's Poker"), to the NFL ("The Blind Side"), to baseball ("Moneyball"). Lewis likes to challenge assumptions, including those about the occupants of Washington's federal buildings – government workers, sometimes derided as faceless bureaucrats. "That's the stereotype," Lewis said.

He believes people who distrust government don't understand what it does: "They don't like the government, or they think they don't like the government. They think they don't trust the government, but in fact they just don't know how much they trust the government. They take the trust for granted. Every time they drink water out of the tap, or fly on an airplane, or eat food, or put dollars in their bank account, they're trusting the government.

"And I thought, who are these people? We live in a society that is largely focused on personal ambition. It's a free market capitalist society and people are really interested in money and fame," he said. "To find people who are some of the most valuable people on the planet, who are interested in neither money nor fame, but have found some other purpose, who have a sense of public spirit, who are not selfish –  and the government is a place where you can really do stuff that makes a difference, and it attracts these people. And thank God for them."

Lewis' latest book, "Blockers: Rebels in the Deep State" (to be published Oct. 6), profiles workers confronted by DOGE – the Department of Government Efficiency, championed by President Trump and his mega-donor, billionaire Elon Musk.
Musk promised massive savings of "at least $2 trillion" from cutting government, and targeted government workers he called "blockers."

"It's an insult," Lewis said. "A 'blocker' is a word that Elon Musk likes to toss around. He told all the 20-year-olds who came to work for him in DOGE to go find the 'blockers,' the people who would get in the way of doing what he wanted to do, and get rid of them."
"I was blocking people from violating the law"
A central character in "Blockers" is Kathleen Walters. "I mean, if you want to say I was blocking people from violating the law, then I guess that's a fair term," she said.

Once a top executive in the Internal Revenue Service, Walters was responsible for protecting taxpayers' personal information. She said, of President Trump's executive order creating DOGE, "Executive orders are normal. And as long as they're lawful, our job is to administer them."
So, she wasn't trying to block executive orders? "No, no, no," Walters said. "I've been in the government for every administration since Bush, so I've worked for them all, and that's normal."

But after DOGE's arrival, nothing seemed normal to Walters. She says Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) began asking for information on undocumented workers who had been paying taxes to the U.S. Treasury. ICE would later specify in a memo they were only seeking information on individuals under criminal investigation. "They came out and said, 'Well, we're thinking of approximately, probably seven million [people],'" Walter said. "And I questioned in my head, I did not believe there could be seven million active criminal investigations going on."
Walters says she resisted for months, and ultimately she resigned. "After I left, the IRS handed over the data," she said.

The Treasury Department's Inspector General has since found that ICE did not meet "safeguarding standards"; and federal courts have ruled that privacy rights were violated. [The Trump administration continues to argue it has acted within the law.]

Walters said, after trying to stop what she saw as a violation of the law, she left the IRS when she felt she could not stop it.  Asked how tough of a choice that was for her, she replied, "In one respect, it was a simple choice. But simple isn't easy always, and it was challenging, because I'd been there almost 20 years. I was 23 days shy of qualifying for early retirement. And I'm a mom to an elementary-aged child."

Walters described her daughter's reaction to watching her mother struggle: "Well, she's a smart little kid, and I told her high level that I was asked to violate the law and I couldn't do it, so I left. And then later that week, I went into my bedroom and there was a $10 bill on my shelf. And she said, 'Mom, I just wanna help out at home.' And she wouldn't let me give it back, so I had to sneak it – hopefully she doesn't see this! – had to sneak it into her piggy bank again. And so, I know she's proud and she understands why I did what I did. And so again, I can sleep at night well knowing that my decision was the right one even though it was hard."

As for DOGE, there is intense debate over its impact. The Government Accountability Office, an independent nonpartisan federal watchdog, found in an audit that DOGE overstated its savings or could not verify them, and fell far short of its goals.
The Trump administration's Office of Personnel Management (OPM), which manages the federal workforce, praised DOGE in a statement to "Sunday Morning":

"The President is committed to stewardship of taxpayer dollars in delivering services to the American people," said Scott Kupor, director, Office of Personnel Management. "DOGE was a catalyst for these reforms that are now being institutionalized through the Vice President's leadership on fraud, waste and abuse and OPM's and OMB's cross-government focus on organizational efficiency."

But for Michael Lewis, this story is about more than numbers or budgets; it's about people. And he would like people who are skeptical of government to read this book: "Oh my God, yes. That would be my favorite reader."

Asked why some people might not see government as he sees it, Lewis replied, "Because they haven't spent the time to get to know it. This isn't knowledge I was born with. If we don't see that these people who don't make any money, and aren't famous, and don't like to talk about what they do but are working their tails off for us have value for our society, we're in trouble. And that's the message that I'm trying to get across."
Story produced by Ed Forgotson. Editor: Jason Schmidt.

title: Detecting deepfakes, in a world where even reality is suspect
summary: Hany Farid, a leading expert on deepfakes and digital manipulation, estimates that half of the content widely viewed on the Internet is fake. What does this mean for our ability to detect images generated or hallucinated by artificial intelligence?
story: Last February, a Tomahawk cruise missile struck an Iranian elementary school, killing more than 150 people, most of them children. President Trump initially suggested that it could have been somebody else's Tomahawk: "Whether it's Iran or somebody else, the fact that a Tomahawk – a Tomahawk is very generic, it's sold to other countries, but that's being investigated right now," he said.

When Iran put out video as evidence that it was a U.S. missile, Hany Farid, one of the world's foremost experts on deepfakes, was contacted by several media outlets to determine if it was real or fake.

A professor at Dartmouth College, Farid is also co-founder of GetReal Security, a cyber security firm. "What was difficult about this case was you had very little to work on," he said. "We had a very grainy, shaky video. The missile is extremely small. And we had to reason about the physical plausibility of that missile striking the ground."

But he also had certain aspects that he could study scientifically, involving the speed of sound, the speed of light, and the size of the missile: "And those three things were enough for us to say that this is physically plausible," he said. "And this is the important part: all evidence led us to the belief that the video was authentic, and there's been no refuting of that."
But that's the world we live in: Reality itself, so perfectly mimicked by artificial intelligence, that even reality is suspect.

Farid said, "Here's the thing that makes me a little crazy, as a scientist in particular: I don't think you should be able to go into a court of law and say, 'Here is some evidence that is damning enough to put this person to death,' and then the judge says, 'Well, how do you know it's real?' And I say, 'Well, because the computer told me so.' This is not an answer

"And if I can't explain to you, to a judge, and to a jury, what is happening here – because the lighting, because the shadows, because the geometry, whatever it is – that's what we need to be able to do."
A case in point: Alex Pretti, who was killed by an ICE agent in Minnesota. If you remember the scene last January 24, it was chaotic. Several ICE agents with guns surrounded Pretti.

Farid showed us a blurry photo of Pretti that was taken from the original video. "Somebody took this and 'enhanced' it," he said. According to Farid, the crispness of this "enhanced" image makes the scene feel "more real, but what it also did is when it enhanced it, it seems to have put a gun in [Pretti's] hand. If you go back to this video, the camera's panning a little bit and what's happening is, there's a shadow behind his hand on the street. And what the AI did is that it hallucinated this."

Farid says artificial intelligence has learned, "When you see photos like this with three men with guns, everybody's got a gun." And now, when you do Google searches for events like Pretti's killing, it shows the "enhanced" image.

By Farid's estimate, half of the content that's widely viewed on the Internet is fake, basically a toss of the coin. Much of it has its own sneering label: "AI slop." Footage of airplanes skidding on the tarmac, toddlers dancing a two-step, Elvis. "AI slop is a broad term that defines people generating content using AI just to grab eyeballs, video after video after video driving engagement," Farid said.

For the most part, Farid limits his examinations to the really serious stuff, the deepfakes. Even so, he's inundated. He said, "We're seeing deepfakes being weaponized in many, many different ways, from the creation of child sexual abuse material, to non-consensual intimate imagery, to full-blown state-sponsored disinformation campaigns, to what the North Koreans have done, [which] is to have their IT workers interview for jobs remotely. And they conceal their accent using AI. They can conceal their identity using a deepfake, where they change their identity from eyebrow to chin, cheek to cheek, in real time over a video call. They can conceal their geolocation. And they interview for jobs. I will tell you, just about every single Fortune 500 company has hired one or more of these, whether they know it or not.

"And now, the question you want to ask yourself is, what's next? Well, so one CEO said, 'Okay. No more virtual interviews. No more remote work.' That's insane. … We're gonna start flying people across the country? That can't be the answer. I mean it's exhausting. Let's be honest. I mean, if we're always looking at our shoulder over every email, every text message, every voicemail, every phone call, every video call? It's exhausting. I'm exhausted, and I do this for a living."

Asked if he has nightmares over deepfakes, Farid replied, "I look at content all day long. And usually the things I look at are not pleasant. I'm looking at bad things that involve horrific crimes, and when you view these things over and over and over again, they sit with you and you can't get them out of your head.

'And number two is, I don't want to be wrong. And five years ago I felt a lot more confident about our ability to distinguish real from fake. It's gotten harder. And then I worry more. I feel like the ground is constantly shifting," he said.

It builds – the stress, the pressure. After seven years on the West Coast, Farid returned to Dartmouth College, where he had previously spent 20 years on faculty. His wife, Emily Cooper, is also a professor there. The two of them bought a rural property in neighboring Vermont, where Farid mows acres of meadows, and cuts enough wood to feed their stoves through the winter. It's enough mowing and cutting to rinse some of those disturbing images away. It's isolated – there's no mail delivery, no garbage pickup –  but it's peaceful.

Certain work-related issues linger. Social media? Farid loathes it: "You can look at social media, at online platforms and say there is measurable harm coming to young kids, to adults, to seniors, across the boards. And I think we have been so mesmerized by these products which are, by design, meant to be addictive.

"I think we did an experiment on an entire generation of these young kids coming up, putting these devices in their hands. And now we've woken up and we're like, 'Oh, my God. This is terrible.' This generation right now has lower learning outcomes than any generation in history. Go to Palo Alto at the fanciest private schools where all the tech billionaires send their kids. There's no devices in those classrooms. They know."
That $17 billion settlement that Meta reached a few weeks back includes some safeguards, like a two-hour time limit for users under the age of 18. Farid thinks that's a start, but not nearly enough.
"The darkest vision I have is that everybody lives in their own information ecosystem, and nobody knows how to talk to each other anymore," he said.

On platforms where algorithms prefer fake to real content, Farid thinks all of us should stay off social media, or at the very least take those apps off our phones, to resist the temptation. As for those websites that promise to detect AI fakes, he says it's not that simple: "Here's what I think is next (and by saying next, I mean in the coming year), which is most of the deepfakes that we are seeing today have a human somewhere in the process. Somebody's hands are on the keyboard. There's still a human in the loop. But what's gonna start happening is AI agents are gonna start creating their own fakes."

And what is an AI agent? "An agent just has more autonomy, and what we have started to see is when you give it a problem to solve, it will find creative ways to do it, including creating a fake identity to interact with a human to get a human to do something and then it will lie about it," he said.

AI agents have been in the news recently for going rogue in testing trials, intensifying the global debate over AI safety and the very course of humanity. These are issues Hany Farid grapples with every day.

"I think there is a near-future where people will have an AI agent that they grow up with," he said, "and it will know them better than anybody else who knows them. And I think that thing can live on forever.

"My wife and I have been talking about this," he said. "She's younger than I am. We've been talking about, should we be incorporating into an AI agent my voice, my likeness, how I think, how I talk, the type of questions I ask her in the morning, how I respond to her when she's sad, how I respond to her when she's happy? Do I think AI can mimic that to near-perfection? Yes."

Asked if – should Farid be hit by a truck – an AI agent of him might be an adequate replica of him for his wife, Farid said, "I think, for my generation, the answer is probably no. But the next generation, the generation after that, that will think about these things differently? I don't know."
