I- I called Abbas Kamel, the intel chief of Egypt, said, "Look, we got to find a way to allow Gazans at least to come temporarily into- into Sinai." Answer is absolutely not. The president on that trip--
[CROSSTALK]
MARGARET BRENNAN: Egypt refused--
BRETT MCGURK: --this is why this is important--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --to take them. Mmhmm.
[END CROSSTALK]

BRETT MCGURK: The President on that trip was going to Amman- to Amman first. About eight days into the war, president wants to go to Israel. I explain why he wanted to go to Israel at a critical moment. We're going to stop in Amman to see King Abdullah, to see Mahmoud Abbas, the head of the Palestinian Authority, and President Sisi to have this discussion. And unfortunately, that trip was pulled down because the day we were leaving, there was an air- looked like an airstrike at a hospital, Al-Ahli Hospital, and there were headlines that an Israeli airstrike killed 500 Palestinians–turned out not to be true. But because of that, King Abdullah said, "please don't come." We understood why, and we only went to Israel, and we did not have that- that engagement. I think the- this is- the fact that in Gaza civilians had nowhere to really take shelter, the underground facilities were only for Hamas, they made that very clear. And even when the Israelis said, let's- once they gave us a map, you know, "let's- we will declare this area a safe zone."
MARGARET BRENNAN: Right.
BRETT MCGURK: It's Mawasi, and--
MARGARET BRENNAN: You write about this.

BRETT MCGURK: --and the UN refused to work with them on that, as did we, because we said, "No, no, you can't, you- you can't kind of force people into a certain area." But then it was like, where are people going to go? So the whole backdrop to this is so horrific, and- and it took a massive toll on civilian life, and it took a massive toll on- on Israeli soldiers as well, as I talk about. It was a real war.

MARGARET BRENNAN: I mean, you nod to some regret in that incident. You said [about] that declaration of a safe zone, you regret that the U.S. wasn't "more creative," as you put it, "in working with Israel on an imperfect solution" to humanitarian corridors.
BRETT MCGURK: Yeah.
MARGARET BRENNAN: I mean, are you saying it was a delusion to think there was a perfect solution, or do you think there really was more that could have been done?

BRETT MCGURK: I- I think, very imperfect mechanisms to get civilians out of harm's way, that the UN and others could have supported. Often, everybody is kind of on the- on the sidelines, saying the war should stop somehow. But without like- let's think, how can we actually get civilians out of harm's way? Now the Israelis did tell people to move, and they did it kind of on their own. But they did- they got no help from that, from the UN, or others. They would just not even be a part of encouraging people to move or to setting up safe areas--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Claiming it would appear to be forced displacement.

BRETT MCGURK: Yeah, and- and working with the Israelis and all the history here, which I go in in the books. I- but the- it comes back to the core question of, given Hamas has this underground military infrastructure, how- the- the campaign is going to be so destructive. That's what concerned me from the start. I saw not Mosul and Raqqa, which you did not have this underground infrastructure or, you know, decade or so to prepare. It's absolutely awful.

MARGARET BRENNAN: It was Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen who kind of forced the hand of the administration in publicly reporting some of the U.S. assessments of how Israel was using the U.S.-provided weapons, because under U.S. law, they have to be compliant with American standards. And Secretary Blinken came on Face the Nation shortly after the report was released, and we had Senator Van Hollen on after him. Van Hollen said the administration ducked the hard questions. They didn't provide an "unvarnished account of facts and the law," and has set, as a standard, a "very, very low bar, a very low standard for what is acceptable." He said it will come back to haunt the United States. In hindsight, do you think he has a point there? That not being more fact-driven and making this information public, or concern about how U.S. munitions were used, that it could hurt, in the longer term, U.S. credibility?

BRETT MCGURK: I think I- I- that effort from Senator Van Hollen and the State Department report that came out- I describe it- I mean, I'm mostly, at that time, I'm overseas trying to get this- this hostage deal going on. But I start the book with a meeting in the- in the Situation Room, about two weeks left in the Biden administration, about this question, about to take more measures against Israel or not. And again, my- came down to, in my view, and I have to say, the, you know, the lawyers who set the- set the table would describe the legal parameters, and it was always a policy call. And in that particular scene, again, we're close to a deal. If you want to stop the war, you have to get a deal. And is the measure on the table going to move you closer to getting a deal or not? I mean, that was a very- to me, the only way to stop this war was a deal. So I don't- I- I can't take- I haven't seen that exact quote of what Senator Van Hollen was talking about in that time frame. I remember that debate, but I come back to, how do you actually end this war? And it was ultimately a ceasefire deal.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, it was such a public debate at the time about America's role in the world, the standards America is held to, and whether America is complicit in how our weapons are used. And under the Leahy Law, as you know, you know, countries that receive U.S. weapons have to avoid committing human rights violations or risk losing the weapons supply. Blinken said "it was reasonable to assess, in certain instances, Israel has not acted in a manner that's consistent with international humanitarian law," and that Israeli civilian harm mitigation efforts were "inconsistent, ineffective, and inadequate." Do you agree with that State Department memo?

BRETT MCGURK: I think the Leahy Law applies to individual units, and broadly speaking, that's why it's not- no aid to any country is unconditional, including- including to Israel, and- but security assistance is a- is a complex, multi-institutional, multi-branch endeavor. And again, these- most of these appropriations were appropriated by massive bipartisan majorities in Congress at the time. But- and the State Department has a role, and the Pentagon has an important role.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Right. He was saying hit the brakes on deliveries. Or re-examine--

BRETT MCGURK: Again, we- we hit the brakes on some- on some deliveries selectively. But to have a broad-based stoppage of- of support–again, for Israel at a time- I don't know what the time frame was for that statement, but I can--
MARGARET BRENNAN: That was in May--
BRETT MCGURK: So in May--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --2024.

BRETT MCGURK: Yeah. So in May we just had the largest ballistic missile and drone attack ever in history. We- but let me lay this out. So May. That's why the time frame and chronology is so important. Having lived through this, I remember it quite well. Largest ballistic missile attack in history. We help the Israelis defeat it. We say to Netanyahu- Biden's quote in that meeting is "I just saved your ass." We're getting back to the hostage deal, okay? We spend the month of May putting together a detailed four-page, three-phase agreement, single spaced, every detail there. We go to the Israelis and to Netanyahu and say, "we need you to sign up." And it went very far in the direction of Hamas. Frankly, it was a better deal for Hamas than what they have right now. And Netanyahu on May 27th signed on to that deal. On May 31st- because what were we doing in May? On May 31st, President Biden laid out that deal to the world in a speech, and he said, "Israel has accepted this deal. Hamas, say yes. Let's end this war." U.N. Security Council endorses that deal. It's May 31st. What happens? In early June, after this is on the table–we can stop the war right now if Hamas says yes–Khamenei, Supreme Leader of Iran, gives a defiant speech praising October- October 7th, and basically Iran is telling Hamas to not- to not compromise in any of the terms. Hezbollah launches its largest attack of the war, 250 rockets into northern Israel. This is when we have a ceasefire deal on the table. We don't get an answer from Hamas until July 2nd, almost five weeks later, and they put all sorts of things in it that set the talks back. So, I- I say this because we were working to end this crisis and end this war, and- in May, June, and we had the deal on the table to do it. My approach would have- is, this deal is on the table to stop the war. All pressure, everything, public, everything else has to come down on Hamas and their enablers to say yes to end this deal, or to end this war. But Hamas did not say yes, and they kept stringing us out, and they would put an issue on the table, then Israel would take a hard position. But that's what was happening in May, and if you go to that, you know, Biden goes to the world, says this is the deal. He had a phone call with, I think, 18 heads of state because these hostages are from countries all around the world. They all said- they called on Hamas to take the deal, and Hamas did not take the deal. And we were working at that time to end the war through a deal, and I think, again, all vectors of pressure should have been on Sinwar to say yes.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But you're not saying--
BRETT MCGURK: And the war would have stopped.
MARGARET BRENNAN: You're not saying that the Democratic Party pressure and calling out compliance with U.S. law was enabling Hamas. That's not what you're saying?
BRETT MCGURK: No, no, no. And I'm also not--
MARGARET BRENNAN: But you're saying it's almost, like, naive?

BRETT MCGURK: And I'm also not getting into internal party debates, I've never been a part of that. I'll let- I'll let political parties have their- have their debates. Not my role at all. I come back to the question: How do you end this crisis? And I think the record shows if you just stop American support for Israel. That is not going to end the crisis. It's going to make it worse.
MARGARET BRENNAN: And you think even just a statement that was more definitive on that would have been damaging?
BRETT MCGURK: No, we made- I mean, I- we made a lot of statements. We did U.N. Security Council resolutions, we did a number of things, which I think there's a- there's a real--

MARGARET BRENNAN: But this- this whole political argument at that time with the National Security Memorandum that was made public. It was, like, five out of eight State Department groups said, you know, basically they were not compliant with U.S. law. But you read it, and it's sort of, it looks like American diplomats are going out of their way not to say it directly, in order to avoid taking action that would result in the cutting off of aid.
BRETT MCGURK: I don't know. I- I--
MARGARET BRENNAN: It looks like the politics were influencing the policy, and I guess that's what I'm asking you to reply to.

BRETT MCGURK: I can't- the- the State- that State Department memo that was- that was done, again, at the request of Senator Van Hollen, and the Senate has its own dynamics for asking us to do certain things to keep votes off the floor that Senator Van Hollen might have wanted to take. But no, I thought that was, from what I understand, that was a very rigorous exercise. But had that memo said something differently, would that have ended the war? Would that have eased the humanitarian suffering in Gaza? Would it have gotten hostages home? No. I mean, that is where- like, that memo is so divorced, in my view, from the gritty, awful reality of how do you actually return hostages and end a war? I mean, and I- this is not a book about meetings in Washington. I've read a lot of books like that. I said this in this meeting. No- some of that. This is a book about being in the middle of it, overseas, where you're in the room with just the two or three people that can actually get something done, and- and trying to achieve the objective that everybody in Washington wants, and trying to actually accomplish that objective is exceedingly hard. And whatever that memo might have said, or whatever something might have been said in Congress, is that going to achieve the objective we're trying to achieve? I think the answer is no. So I- I come back to just what it takes to actually stop something like this.

MARGARET BRENNAN: And- and we had some of those hostage families and advocates on Face the Nation throughout the crisis who were appealing to the American president to stay focused on the hostages because they were frustrated that the Israeli government was not, and that Hamas was not interested. So I hear you on that. Let me just put a fine point on the issue here because I want you to be able to respond to this. There's another new book out about the Biden administration's handling of Israel's war in Gaza. It's written by Akbar Shahid Ahmed. He makes some very specific claims about things that you said and did. One administration official told him you seemed to be acting as Israel's lawyer when you were discussing IDF actions in October 2024. That you saw pictures of famine in early 2024, and you said people in Gaza did not look skinny. There are other claims in here, that your name was turned into a verb. Humanitarian officials were used to what one USAID staffer referred to as "getting McGurk'd," which meant overruling aid experts on Gaza. That sounds like a lot of internal disagreement. Were you aware of this?

BRETT MCGURK: I haven't read that book. That's categorically false. I've never- I've never said something like that. And in fact, and I think those who were actually- whether it was David Satterfield or others in charge of the humanitarian response, always knew if you need something done, you know, give me a call. I talked to David multiple times a day when he was the humanitarian coordinator. That is categorically false and just complete fiction.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Because this issue lives on now in our politics, particularly among progressive Democrats. I mean, Gaza, cutting off U.S. aid to Israel or reducing it, and on the right, we're hearing more about that as well. Has it surprised you that, like, the politics of this moment continue to be so infused with what happened then?

BRETT MCGURK: Well, I think on- you know, again, on the- on the aid question, there's one thing getting aid into- into Gaza, which we're very focused on, and pushing the Israelis on, and then actually distributing it throughout Gaza, which is- which is role for the U.N., and there was like almost been a breakdown there. It was incredibly frustrating, but no, I- my- my job was to try to bring this war to a close. And the way to bring it to a close was to get an agreement that included the release of the hostages. It's all- it's intertwined. You're not going to reduce human suffering, and you're not going to have aid flowing throughout Gaza like you need without a ceasefire, and you're not going to have a ceasefire without the hostages. This was just the- the awful, gritty reality of the- of the situation.

MARGARET BRENNAN: You wrote about- you nod fairly diplomatically to any disagreements within the administration at the time, but you write during this period of time- you're referring to January 2024 or so. You write: "During this period, I felt out of sorts with some of my colleagues, who seemed to take a two-dimensional view of the crisis, focused solely on Gaza and not the regional threat that Iran had unleashed, and which every day risked American lives." Who were you thinking of there? Why- why did you write that?
BRETT MCGURK: That was January, and the time frame is important. That was January 2024.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Mm-hmm.

BRETT MCGURK: We come under attack after- between October 7 and end of the year, attacks against us increase almost sevenfold. Almost every day we have attacks against us. It's very clear the attacks are intended to kill Americans. On Christmas Day, we have three wounded Americans in northern Iraq, one with Iranian shrapnel through his brain. Attack- Houthi attacks start against American ships, including against U.S. naval ships. These are anti-ship ballistic missiles going Mach 4, first time they've ever been used in combat. What I'm hearing from our military people is, "What are we doing about this?" Every single day. And what's keeping me up in this time is I'm going to wake up, and we're going to have two dozen dead American sailors in the Red Sea, or we're going to have two dozen dead American soldiers in Iraq and Syria. And the attacks kept coming, and we had a call with President Biden on New Year's Day, talking about how to respond. And we had the Iranian commander, I call him Mohsen in the book, we knew who he was, we kind of- we were close to his location, and I thought we should target him, to stop and deter these attacks.
MARGARET BRENNAN: A drone strike?

BRETT MCGURK: Yeah. President Biden in that meeting asked me, "Can you go see the Iranians? Knock this off." And I did, I went- and I had met with the Iranians many times over the years. I went to Oman on January 10th. I had a meeting with the Iranians. I describe it in detail in the book with the Omanis [intermediating]. And I describe what's happening in the region. We are under attack in Iraq. We're under attack in Syria,. We're under attack in the Red Sea. It's only by the skill of our military personnel, our defenses, that we have not had dozens of American dead and wounded, and this has to stop, or we're heading for direct confrontation.
MARGARET BRENNAN: And you can't get the president to act--
BRETT MCGURK: Well, he wanted--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --You were frustrated.

BRETT MCGURK: --to try to take this diplomatic path, and the Iranians in that meeting were complete- were- I describe it in detail, completely rejected having anything to do with this, which was total- a total lie.
MARGARET BRENNAN: They wouldn't sit across from you even. You're passing notes.

BRETT MCGURK: You're doing intermedia-, similar to now, what is still happening. So that- those talks failed. We started strikes against the Houthis, actually, the next day after that meeting failed. But then in January, the time frame, we come und- every single day, and I document this. And on January 28th, we have the three Americans and dozens of wounded from an Iranian drone. Yeah, my focus in that month was deterring these attacks and- and deterring what Iran had unleashed, including against us. That was my over- because I- what was keeping me up was, "We're going to have dead Americans," and then we did have dead Americans, and President Biden ordered a strike on Mohsen and other militia leaders that night, and the attacks stopped.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But the president was so concerned about avoiding a regional war.

BRETT MCGURK: The president, in his use of military power, Margaret, was very deliberate. We're- we're in this regional crisis. And he used to say–and this relates to the current moment–he used to say the American people understand the use of force to protect our people, and kind of a real core, vital American interest. They will not- they will not understand if we're being sucked into a broader Middle East war or reacting on behalf of Israel. It was a line he drew in his pulse of the American people and his role as Commander in Chief. It was an important line to draw. And he ordered, I mean, a decisive use of force in that incident in February, but he was- and, and defending Israel twice against direct ballistic missile attacks. But he was very deliberate, and he said it in a number of these meetings, which I talk about in the book, about- about drawing that line very carefully.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But you talk about "feeling out of sorts with some of my colleagues."
BRETT MCGURK: Yeah.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Are you going to tell us what was happening when you were having those disagreements? Who was arguing against defending these Americans?

BRETT MCGURK: There was an argument that if we target an Iranian officer–which is a big step, I recognize it–that could unleash a broader escalation. I just didn't agree with that. I thought we were- we were under attack constantly. We had to actually act to deter it. And one of the themes in the book is, Margaret, is that diplomacy, if not backed by power, is completely feckless.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But your--

BRETT MCGURK: And this was- this was- this was playing in, also, to the hostage talks. I mean, Hamas was just not even willing to engage because they thought everything was kind of going their way. You got Hezbollah barrages coming every day in the north. You have the Houthis attacking commercial and U.S. and U.K. naval vessels in the Red Sea. You have Americans under attack almost every day in Iraq. And until we contained that and stopped it, it was very hard to see a way forward on the- on the Gaza talks. It was all- all interrelated. So my consuming focus–I fully admit it in the book–in this period, was stopping those attacks, and I thought to stop those attacks we had to use military force.

MARGARET BRENNAN: But around that same time, in January 2024, Israel bombs Syria, killing an Iranian military advisor. In April, strikes Iranian diplomatic mission in Syria. In July, strikes Tehran and kills the top Hamas leader. Then that stunning operation to take out Hezbollah leaders with the exploding pagers. And killing Hezbollah's leader Hassan Nasrallah. On that particular strike, the U.S. didn't get a heads up.
BRETT MCGURK: Let's talk about some of those.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah, but that seems to be a building- the Israeli government doing the thing President Biden was saying don't do, which is risk a regional war.

BRETT MCGURK: Let's talk about some- some of those. Mohammad Reza Zahedi, he was the Quds Force officer, Margaret, that was killed in that strike in Damascus, April 1, 2024, same day as the World Central Kitchen attack. Who is Mohammad Reza Zahedi? He is the head of the Quds Force unit that enables and supplies Hezbollah. Hezbollah is firing into Israel every single day--
MARGARET BRENNAN: From Lebanon.

BRETT MCGURK: --From Lebanon. A strike against Mohammad Reza Zahedi, in our view, was a very legitimate self-defense strike. The Iranians said he was in a compound of the- of their embassy in Damascus. That's actually never been demonstrated. But in any event, the Iranians attacked our embassy. I was at our embassy in Baghdad multiple times, where they launched- their militias launched rockets at our embassy. We did not respond by firing 200 ballistic missiles into- into Iran. That's how Iran responded to that- to that attack. The Lebanon operation that the Israelis conducted beginning in September came after the complete breakdown of the- of the hostage talks. And because dates matter, we- we had a- we had an offer on the table, Margaret, on August 16th, endorsed by, you mentioned the Emir of Qatar, Tamim, fully endorsed 100% by Sisi. It went even further in the direction of Hamas. On April 16th, we never got an answer, and on- at the end of the month, we had six dead hostages in- in a tunnel underneath Rafah. And that's when that whole process just completely collapsed, and Israel went north into Lebanon. And when I look at this history now, and you kind of piece- it was after Yahya Sinwar was killed on October 16. It was after we defeated a second Iranian missile attack in October. It was after Hezbollah cut a ceasefire deal that there was an opening for the ceasefire to end the war in Gaza. It was the regional balance of power changing that opened the path to finally getting this- getting this deal.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But I bring up those series of events because the lack of heads up to the United States signals some growing distrust between the United States and Israel at that point in time.
BRETT MCGURK: Sure.
MARGARET BRENNAN: I mean Israel gave a heads up as the operation to kill Hassan Nasrallah was underway. Were you upset that there wasn't more advance notice?

BRETT MCGURK: Well, the Zahedi strike, I describe in the- in the book, did get an advance- I got a notice from- from the Israelis just before walking into a situation room meeting. I describe that in some detail. I think you're right, the Nasrallah strike the Israelis took, they didn't give us a heads up on that. That doesn't particularly surprise me, honestly. The Haniyeh intelligence operation in Tehran, which I also talk about in the book, we did not have a heads up on, but it was an intelligence operation in Tehran. This is not something that, like, Bibi Netanyahu can just say, "Hey, let's go after Haniyeh in Tehran." This is something that takes months of preparation, and- and it's a kind of a you- the stars align, and you- you take the action or you don't. But in many ways, those steps actually helped us open the path to ending the war in Gaza.

MARGARET BRENNAN: But the- well, it changed the dynamic in the Middle East, put Iran on the back foot in many ways, but I- I bring it up too because there is this perception- you know, at one point, I think it was the New Yorker**, quoted General Austin, then-Secretary of Defense, as saying that the Netanyahu government felt that it was playing with house money, that they knew America would be there no matter what, so they could up the level of risk even if President Biden wasn't happy with it. Did you feel like you were stuck in the middle of that dynamic where it was- the assumption was America was going to support it no matter what, and that they weren't necessarily going to listen to U.S. counsel?
BRETT MCGURK: Well, Netanyahu thought and believed, and has said publicly, he thought we cut off their weapons. So--
[CROSSTALK]
MARGARET BRENNAN: Back when we were talking about the--
BRETT MCGURK: Yeah. And he since has said that Biden had a--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --the Santa Clause reference that you write about.
BRETT MCGURK: --that Biden put an arms embargo on us. And he still believes that--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Which was not true.
[END CROSSTALK]

BRETT MCGURK: No, it's not true. But in terms of these particular operations in this broader war, that I mean, why, why was there this Hezbollah confrontation after October 7th? Because Hezbollah, on October 8th, started a war into northern Israel. Iran turned this whole thing up. It was a tragic mistake they made after the October 7th attacks. And I describe this in detail. We did not have information that Iran knew about the Hamas attack, but after that attack, they sensed a vulnerability against Israel, and they turned on all their proxies, and it continued to kind of escalate up the ladder, and then Israel is responding to- to that.

MARGARET BRENNAN: And I think what I'm hearing you say is you think President Biden's not given credit for stopping these things exploding into a regional war at once. He's not getting credit for the thing he prevented.
BRETT MCGURK: Yeah, it's not about credit--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --Is that right?

BRETT MCGURK: --What I try to do here, I don't say in the book- credit or not. You're there in the Situation Room with President Biden after we defeat one of the largest missile attacks at that point in history. You can hear everything he says. You are there, actually, in the Oval Office, I was overseas and dialed in shortly after the president learned about that intelligence operation in Tehran against Haniyeh, and he calls up Bibi Netanyahu. So a reader will hear exactly what happened in- in those moments. And no, I don't think it was simply, you know, Netanyahu took- took things for granted. It was a very difficult regional military equation, intelligence equation, diplomatic equation, humanitarian equation, all of which is playing out in real time.

MARGARET BRENNAN: You know, it's an incredibly complex set of challenges all at once. I want to get to Saudi Arabia in a moment, but just to button up on Iran. On the nuclear program. Biden's national security adviser Jake Sullivan explained to Netanyahu when he pitched going and bombing the nuclear sites. He said it was, you know, of questionable legality and risky. But the administration was unanimous that if Iran was about to make a bomb, that the Biden administration would have gone and bombed. At that point, were you thinking that, essentially, the war we're in now was inevitable?

BRETT MCGURK: So, it's in the book. I go to Israel in December, this is after the election, with Jake. We see Bibi Netanyahu. And we got him to sign on to a key term for the hostage deal, which is the focus here. And he said, "I think we should take out Fordow and the- and the nuclear sites." And we were concerned after the election, just given some things we were seeing, that Iran might- they were already enriching to 60 percent, and- and 90 percent is weapons-grade enrichment, and it's not- that's very easy to do. That they might make a dash, and once you do a dash, they have a canister of weapons-grade uranium, and you're really in a much worse situation. We actually had a principals committee meeting, that's everybody around the table, what would we do if we see that?
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

BRETT MCGURK: And as I recall, unanimity on we would do the strike in Fordow. We didn't see that. We sent a message to Iran, don't even think about it. But yet Netanyahu was clearly contemplating that, and--
MARGARET BRENNAN: In the middle of the hostage crisis.
BRETT MCGURK: Yeah, in December of 2024.
MARGARET BRENNAN: He was thinking about bombing Iran.

BRETT MCGURK: And we said there would be no- unless we see the Iranians moving in that direction, and there are questions of legality and everything else, that's always been around this issue. This- this strike against Fordow has been a, again, war game multiple times. But yeah, you will- that conversation is- is in the book in December of 2024 with- with Netanyahu.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Because you diplomatically point out that he was more focused on bombing Iran than the hostages. He pitched you, "why wait" until they race for a bomb? Why not act now? You made the point that he spoke with far greater intensity about Iran than he spoke about the hostages. You sound--
BRETT MCGURK: True.
MARGARET BRENNAN: --pretty annoyed by that.

BRETT MCGURK: It's true, and yet in that same meeting, in that same meeting where all that's going on, we get Netanyahu to agree- this is early December 2024. If I have the list of hostages, if Hamas produces the list–there are 33 names that Israel had. If Hamas agrees to the list of 33 hostages, meaning we have to know the hostages who are coming out in the deal, I accept the deal. We got that from Netanyahu in that meeting. And then all we needed- this gets back to this theme we've talked about here, Margaret, in the last hour or so. All we needed at that moment to stop the war was an agreement on the list of hostages. And I describe in the book Hamas would not agree on the list of hostages, and then they said, of the 33, only 12 will be alive. And so again, everybody wants this war to end. You've mentioned people with very strong views on the issue. So you're there, mid-December 2024. You have a full hostage deal. Hamas says, "But we'll only release 12 hostages alive." And I'm sitting there with Sheikh Mohammed. I have the list of hostages, Keith Siegel's on the list--
MARGARET BRENNAN: The American.

BRETT MCGURK: --We can get out these 12 hostages, and the war will stop. But what about all the other hostages that Hamas is not putting on the list, including Sagui Dekel-Chen, an American wounded twice on October 7th, Hamas is saying we don't consider him wounded. What do you do in that moment? Do you take the 12 in hand, or do you put down a harder line and say no, no, we need the full list, which was ultimately 25 living hostages? Eventually, it was after New Year's, heading into 2025, Hamas produced the full list, but then they put more issues on the table. I bring this up to say, this is how close you are to ending the war. It's there. And in that meeting on, on Fordow, where yeah, Netanyahu was very adamant on the nuclear threat, he signed on to this deal, so long as we have the list of the hostages. And then once again, it's on Hamas to- you want to end the war? All we need is the hostage list from Hamas.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Ultimately, you talk about January 19, 2025, on Face the Nation when you finally were able to announce that those three women, in particular, were going to be released by Hamas. But you write in the book a lot about Steve Witkoff and what he is like as a negotiator. You teamed up, actually, in those final days. And he said to you at some point he was actually surprised you weren't talking directly to Hamas. He said, if I sell- "If a guy's selling me a building…I look in his eyes, face-to-face…only way to do a deal."
BRETT MCGURK: Yeah.
MARGARET BRENNAN: What did you say when he asked you, "Why aren't you talking to Hamas?"

BRETT MCGURK: First, the story with Steve I think is unique because when President Trump won the election, if left to its own devices here, Margaret, in Washington these days, it would be, the Biden people would say good luck Trump folks, and the Trump people would say we're not going to do anything that the Biden people said. Right after the election, I called Jared Kushner, and I said, "look, you don't want to come into office with this Gaza thing still going on, and we got a chance to get the hostages out," because at that point Nasrallah is dead. We have- we're moving towards a ceasefire in Lebanon, the whole regional picture is changing. Yahya Sinwar is out of the way, We just defeated another missile attack. And we agreed to work together. And when Biden and Trump met in the Oval Office of all the other issues, they agreed to work together on this. I then- Jake and I went to see Mike Waltz, his incoming successor, and I met Steve Witkoff, and we agreed we're going to work in lockstep. Talk about no daylight, we're going to have no daylight, and, and we did that. And by the time Steve came out to- to Doha, we kind of had two issues. Finally got the hostage list [as] I mentioned. Hamas had raised two entirely new issues. We had to bridge those, and it was only by working together that we were able- to able to do that. On the dynamics of the negotiation, the- the cards on the table are Palestinian prisoners being held by Israel, and a ceasefire and various redeployments of Israeli forces, and so- and other- some many other things. Israel had a direct channel with- with Hamas when they needed it, and we had the mediators, often, with Hamas right downstairs. We thought if we were to go face-to-face with Hamas, it could actually, Hamas could use that to play one side off another, and so we trusted the Egyptians and the Qataris and we had good information of everything going on. And that's the way- the way- we, we handled it. I think- I don't think a more direct channel would have produced a faster result.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But you've got some colorful anecdotes in there about him, kind of closing with Netanyahu, saying, you gotta do this, you have to agree to this.

BRETT MCGURK: So again, we have- we have a full deal. Hamas accepts the list, and then Hamas comes in with a totally new demand: for the nine sick and wounded hostages, they need 300 life- Palestinian prisoners serving life sentences, mostly Hamas, very hardcore Hamas terrorists, many of them who've killed Israelis and killed Americans, they insist on coming out--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --huge political risk at home--

BRETT MCGURK: --for- for the civilians. There's a totally unprecedented demand over a year of talks. We whittled that down to 110 life-sentence prisoners for those nine sick and wounded civilians, and the buffer zone that Israel would be in in this first phase of the deal. Israel wanted 1,200 meters. Hamas wanted 500. We cut it to 700. But you mentioned this kind of extraordinary moment. I mean, we're all in Doha and kind of agree to divide labor because we had Hamas and Israel in the same building. And Steve went to see Netanyahu. It was a week before the inauguration, and I called into the meeting in the Israeli cabinet room. I went to see the Israelis in Doha, I'm with their team, called into the meeting with Netanyahu and their cabinet, and Steve Witkoff is there, saying, "this is the deal. It's going to be 110 life-sentenced prisoners," which was very difficult, and we- we kind of cut the- split the middle on the buffer zone, and- and the Israeli reaction was extremely negative, but ultimately we had the envoy of one president on the line, and we had the envoy of the incoming president say, this is what we got to do. It was the last final issue, and the Israelis accepted that deal, and that's how we got- again, Romy, Doron and Emily came home on the 19th, I announced it on your- on your program, but they should have come out in that November deal.

MARGARET BRENNAN: As we wind down, I just want to make sure I ask you about Saudi Arabia because you mentioned it right at the top. This is now January of 2021. You're at the beginning of the Biden administration. You fly to Saudi Arabia to meet Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, MbS as he's known, he's persona non grata because of the murder of Washington Post columnist Jamal Khashoggi. That's the moment we are in. You go there to explain what President Biden is going to do, and MbS shocks you because he makes you an offer you never expected. He says 'I want to normalize relations with Israel.' Did you go back and tell President Biden that? Because he didn't, as you write, act on it for a year or more.

BRETT MCGURK: Yeah, MbS in that meeting- I've known him for a long time, but I was very clear on, we are going to cut off offensive weapons for Saudi Arabia. We're going to issue new sanctions across the board of many of your security services related to Khashoggi. We're going to release the intelligence report on- on Khashoggi and a number of other things. But Biden was very clear before I went. He also wanted to make sure we're not- we're not totally breaching our relations with Saudi Arabia, a very important country. And we had a very pointed conversation that is in the book in AlUla, in a tent, this was during COVID, and I said to him, finally, I said, "look, where do you want to be in three years?" And he was kind of in, like, peacemaking mode. He said, look, I- we're going to have a back channel with the Iranians through Baghdad. I do think we can bring the Yemen war to a close. But for that to happen, the U.S. and Saudi Arabia have to be seen as working together. And then he said, I'm- I'm prepared to work towards recognizing Israel, diplomatic relations with Israel, and that had to include a number of components, and we talked through it, including a pathway on the Palestinian piece. That was hard to envision. But yes, certainly, that was the key to my report back when I saw the president, that that might be something in the [unintel]--
[CROSSTALK]
MARGARET BRENNAN: But you said--
BRETT MCGURK: --but at the time--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --President Biden didn't want to have anything to do--
BRETT MCGURK: --at the time--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --with the Middle East.
[END CROSSTALK]

BRETT MCGURK: --and I'd be fair to myself. I mean, I- I didn't seize on it either. I just- and I look back on that, I think we should have moved right away. And it wasn't until- you know, this is the thing about the Middle East, Margaret. You can- you can back out of it. The world intervenes. Okay, the world intervenes. So that first year, we had almost no engagement with, particularly, the Gulf States. I mean, I was out there a lot as the Middle East White House envoy. We significantly withdrew our military presence, air, naval, air defense. Then we have Afghanistan evacuation, and--
MARGARET BRENNAN: That changed everything--

BRETT MCGURK: --that's when a call came to me. Can you call all the leaders in the Gulf to open up their air bases and say we're going to be landing thousands of Afghans, I don't know how long they'll be there. And every country said yes.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Which is an amazing thing--
BRETT MCGURK: Including Saudi Arabia and UAE and Qatar and Kuwait, Bahrain, everybody.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Without knowing who these people are--
BRETT MCGURK: Right.
MARGARET BRENNAN: --But trusting America that they're sending people who aren't a risk.

BRETT MCGURK: And without that phone call and without those platforms, we would have been in an even worse situation at that time. I was not working Afghanistan; I worked on that aspect of it. Then the war, Russia's invasion of Ukraine, and then suddenly--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --America needs the Middle East--

BRETT MCGURK: --The old issues of energy supplies, and the only swing producer is really Saudi Arabia, and you need- we need Saudi Arabia, and to do that, the decision maker is the Crown Prince of Saudi Arabia. I describe this in the book, that's- we eventually worked our way back towards decent relations with Saudi Arabia and started to work towards the normalization deal. But that was not- that deal, Margaret, was not, it's not like we, you know, we were pushing it. The Saudis asked us to work with them on it, the Israelis asked us to work with them on it, and we put these stepping stones. You know, there's this news just this weekend- or this week about this airplane over Saudi Arabia, we actually negotiated an agreement between Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and Israel about getting American forces off an island in the Red Sea. They've been there since the Camp David Accords, and in exchange for that, Saudi Arabia opened its skies to all civilian planes, regardless of destination. President Biden announced that on the trip. That was kind of one, one public point of where this process was going, and yeah, I wish we had started sooner.
MARGARET BRENNAN: This was, 2022 Russian invades Ukraine--
BRETT MCGURK: --2022.

MARGARET BRENNAN: --as you say, there's a global energy crisis, suddenly. But you also say, other than you, no senior official had met with the Crown Prince. That means the secretary of defense, the secretary of state, the national security adviser. None of them could be bothered to go to one of our closest partners in the Middle East? I understand there's disagreement, but that's a huge oversight.
BRETT MCGURK: In that first year, yeah, yeah--
MARGARET BRENNAN: And a huge missed opportunity--

BRETT MCGURK: I think Secretary Austin made a trip out, but I think Saudi was the last on the- on the agenda, and that trip, that stop eventually got pulled down for reasons. So yeah, it was a mistake.
MARGARET BRENNAN: And you--

BRETT MCGURK: --Because these- these countries in the Gulf- I have an epigraph in, in the- in the book, Margaret, by- by John F. Kennedy. It's one of my favorite speeches of his. A speech he gave in Utah just two months before his death, and he says the purpose of foreign policy is not to provide an outlet for our own hope or indignation, it is to get real things done in the real world. And in the executive branch, if you're in a White House to get real things done in the real world, you have to have relations with countries that might not share all of your values.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So all of what you just laid out leads to this moment in July 2022 when President Biden goes to Saudi Arabia, and we had the fist bump heard around the world, as you refer to it. You said it was "absurd." It was a "self-made scandal."
BRETT MCGURK: Yeah.
MARGARET BRENNAN: That's about as critical as you get when it comes to President Biden, you were very deferential to him. But you were ticked.
BRETT MCGURK: I--
MARGARET BRENNAN: He was refusing to go and shake the hand of the crown prince at the entrance to his own palace.

BRETT MCGURK: We didn't know what was going to happen in that moment, and I was of the view, got to shake his hand, and- and we had set up this trip–you think about where we were, we had– I mentioned that deal we had. We had the Israel process moving, we had in Israel, President Biden met with Prime Minister Lapid at the time and encouraged Lapid to announce his support for- for two states, which Lapid believed before, but he hadn't said as Prime Minister–I have that scene in the book. A lot of things had kind of come together, and the Saudi stop was- was so important--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --You were trying to rebuild–
BRETT MCGURK: --Well, you mentioned how politics can intrude into a lot of things. I think the- I have a scene with Jake and I, Jake is one of my closest counterparts--
MARGARET BRENNAN: The national security adviser--
BRETT MCGURK: --the national security adviser, and he's hearing from the White House about how things are playing out. And so, um--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --and President Biden said, you recount that, "I'm going to get killed for this." And he's talking about politically.

BRETT MCGURK: Yeah, we landed in Saudi Arabia, and I went to the pool notes from the media pool, and there was an 18-minute from when he landed until when he got out. So I say in the book, let me tell you what happened in those 18 minutes, and I tell you what happened. He was concerned about the optics and the and the imagery, and the whole thing I- I- that's how I describe it. I think, and I encouraged the president to just shake his hand.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But it was all in service of trying to rebuild America's alliances in this critical part of the world. That's where your head was.
BRETT MCGURK: Yeah, we were asking some--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --and the president's head was on the politics and the human rights issues.

BRETT MCGURK: Well, we were asking some very hard things to the Saudis that we needed for our core interests, and so I think the fist bump set us back. I will say we had a very good–overall–that was a very good and successful visit, and we- we built on it. But it's how imagery- you know, I was- Margaret, I was with President Bush in Baghdad when he came to Baghdad, I was sitting just off to his side. Kind of an extraordinary moment, I mean, what it took to get the president of the United States to come into Iraq at that time. You remember what it was like. And I was sitting, I don't know, six, seven feet away from him when the Iraqi reporter got up and threw two shoes at the president.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Mmhmm.
BRETT MCGURK: And I remember- whatever else happened on that visit--
MARGARET BRENNAN: That's all anyone--
BRETT MCGURK: --nobody remembers, and the- the fist bump kind of overshadowed all the what was actually the- the substance of that, of that visit and what, what came of it.

MARGARET BRENNAN: And just lastly, you know, I talked about some of the criticism of you. One of the things that I think you reveal, in a personal way, is how much of a toll this took on you. The time you spent away from your very young daughter. You write about the thoughts you had about that little Abigail. A little four-year-old who was taken into Gaza, and how you were having nightmares about her. That's something that maybe is a bit humanizing in a pretty tough situation. Why did you think that you needed to share that, that glimpse into your personal life?

BRETT MCGURK: I wrote this book– there was no other way to write it than to just pour it all down on the page, raw. I never thought to myself, "how is this going to be seen?" Or, I have no ambition for any future office or anything. It was just what happened and what was it like. And I- and to- and in the writing of it, it was impossible to- to write, in the flow of writing, without putting everything down. And I have those anecdotes because that's how it felt. And cognizant the whole time that lives were being lost every single day, and trying to stop it. So that- it was all-consuming. But that was the only way to write this book. This is not a book, Margaret, about dry policy, this is a book about the grittiness of war and diplomacy and the awfulness, the awfulness of it in every dimension, and not just making a speech or saying something should happen, actually trying to bring it to a close, and trying to bring Abigail home and thinking Abigail might be dead. Then you're living with that every day. And you get to know the families of the hostages, and you- you see the toll every single day in Gaza, and you're always a hair's breadth away from more American soldiers being killed or on the brink of a major war. It's what it was like in the day-to-day. And, so whatever side you might be on on this, this polarizing issue, I just hope readers will read it and take away and think for themselves, "what would I have done in this moment? What might I have done?" That's how I tried to write it. Just- I poured in a very raw, this is, you know, this is it. So yeah, I have those those anecdotes of Christmas Day being with my daughter, a quiet, you know, one quiet moment, realizing she's growing up in a way that I've missed a year, and then I get a call from the Situation Room that we have three Americans grievously wounded in northern Iraq, and I'm back at the White House. You know, that's just what this is like. And so I think it's a different type of book, and I hope people read it.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Thank you for your time.
BRETT MCGURK: Thank you, Margaret.
** Clarification: The Washington Post, not The New Yorker, reported then-Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin privately described Israel's actions as "playing with house money."

title: Hero passenger on FlyDubai flight: "We are going to survive"
summary: "Sunday Morning" talked with passengers who heroically helped avert disaster this past Wednesday by subduing the co-pilot attempting to crash their Boeing 737 Max into the Arabian Desert.
story: This past Wednesday, they were strangers on a plane. By Friday, they were family. It was the first time hero passengers Daniel Schlichter, Zvika Manes, Tal Samuel and Asaf Rajuan had seen each other since those terrifying moments on FlyDubai's Flight 1073.

"That minute is probably the longest minute of my life," said Schlichter about the plane's terrifying freefall. "And the first thing that went up is actually 9/11. And I said, 'How can it be? How can we end this life like that?' You see all your life and you think about what is important. And just holding my wife's hand and saying, 'If we have to go, we have to go.'"

Their Boeing 737 Max was nosediving into the Arabian Desert nearly at the speed of sound. The co-pilot from Oman had stabbed the captain, grabbed the controls, and tried to crash the plane full of Israeli passengers. The jet plummeted 14,000 feet in seconds. They were less than 30 seconds from crashing, with G-forces Manes described as being "like a roller coaster."

What they couldn't have known was that inside the locked cockpit, Captain Smit Machchhar was fighting for his life, as he told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday: "The co-pilot, he wanted to pray. And suddenly there was a big blow to the back of my head," Machchhar said. "I did try to stop him, and that's when I gave everything that I had, and just went for the door and opened the door and thankfully people were waiting."

Manes and his family were sitting in the first row. His wife had just taken his daughter to the bathroom. "I heard my daughter shouting, 'He's stabbing the pilot. He's stabbing the pilot.' She was shouting like animal," he said.
At that moment, Rajuan said they thought they were going to die.
Schlichter, holding his wife's hand, thought to himself, "'If I have to go, I'll hold her hand as tight as possible, and we'll go together.' That's it."
Almost simultaneously, these passengers decided they had to take action.

"I saw my daughter and my wife, and I understand that I must run. I turn, switch to an animal switch, and I feel really like an animal. … I decided that we are going to survive, try to survive, to save my family," Manes said.

Tal Samuel said, "Everyone here, on the day-to-day, are super decent and polite people. But when you watch the situation, you didn't see a finance person, and you didn't see an insurance guy. It was something different. It was like lions that are in a killing mode."
Along with an Israeli plumber named Yaniv Hayoun, they ran toward the bleeding captain, whom they called a hero.
"Not just because he opened the door. Because he had amazing fight with the terrorist. He really fight him," said Rajuan.

Then, they piled onto the co-pilot, Hamam al Hamami, who we've now learned had been banned from flying in his home country, Oman, because of concerns he'd adopted extremist views. And Israeli investigators say they've uncovered social media posts where he talked about killing Jews. Officials in the United Arab Emirates now say he'd committed a "terrorist act."
"I was jumping on him, punching," said Manes. "He tried to resist, and we didn't know if he has a knife."
With a pack of men struggling at the entrance to the cockpit, just then, Tal Samuel looked up and saw the cockpit was empty. He remembered he had been sitting next to two off-duty pilots.
"And the other pilot that came from his seat, because they are blocking the entrance to the cockpit, so that's why he jumped," Samuel said.
According to Rajuan, the pilot leaned over the chair to grab the controls and right the plane.
They were out of freefall. But the captain was bleeding out. "And we are shouting, if there is a doctor in the plane," Manes said.
Shota Musaev, a dentist, said to his wife, "'I need to go,' and, 'I love you.' That's it."
Musaev got up and began treating stab wounds on Machchhar's head and hands. Musaev was afraid he could die from the wounds.
"Yes, I think we have not more time. I check everything, of course, I said to the steward, 'We have no time – land the plane,'" he said.
But the nearest airport was in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, a country that has no diplomatic relations with Israel.
"I was worried that maybe they will arrest us," Manes said, "because they will see blood all over."
But they were not arrested — they were welcomed.

The captain was whisked to a hospital where he's recovering, but at night Dr. Musaev remains with his heroic patient. He said that he can see his face when he closes his eyes: "Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. I think from this time we are a very big family, you know."
And then, in Hebrew, Musaev said, "If he hadn't been smart and heroic, we would not be alive. On the other hand, if we had not been heroes, he would not be alive."
Produced by Sari Aviv, Jon Carras and Christine Romo. Editors: Chad Cardin and George Pozderec.

title: U.S. Marine arrested, accused of killing Japanese woman in Okinawa
summary: U.S. authorities in Japan acknowledged that a U.S. service member was in police custody and pledged to fully cooperate with the investigation.
story: A U.S. Marine stationed in Japan's southern island of Okinawa was arrested following the death of a Japanese woman, local police said on Sunday. Japan lodged a strong protest with the U.S. and demanded maximum cooperation with the investigation.

A local police spokesman told the AFP that the suspect, a 20-year-old man, allegedly "killed the 39-year-old woman at a hotel in Naha and stole her wallet on Saturday." The suspect has denied the allegations.

Public broadcaster NHK and other Japanese media outlets, citing investigation sources, reported that CCTV footage from near the scene showed a foreign man entering a room with a woman and later leaving with her belongings.

Police then found a 20-year-old man who matched the description of the suspect seen in the footage and asked him to accompany them voluntarily to a local police station, where he was arrested, NHK reported.

"The case deals a major shock and adds fear to the Okinawans who have already been forced to live next to U.S. bases," newly elected Okinawa Gov. Genta Koja told reporters, the Associated Press reported. "It is absolutely unforgivable and we are outraged."

"We have lost a family member and are deeply saddened. My parents, in particular, are utterly devastated at the loss of their daughter," the woman's brother said through local police, according to the Asahi Shimbun daily newspaper.

The U.S. Embassy in Tokyo said it was aware that a U.S. service member was in police custody following the death of a Japanese national in Okinawa and that they are "communicating and cooperating" with Japanese authorities amid the investigation.
"We extend our sincere condolences to the victim's family," the embassy said on social media.

George Glass, the U.S. Ambassador to Japan, said on social media that he has spoken with Japan's foreign ministry and Okinawa's governor, offering "our sincere condolences and pledging full cooperation as the investigation continues."
The latest case comes as Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's cabinet pushes to further fortify its Japanese military presence on Okinawa and work more closely with the U.S. military.
Takaichi said Japan had lodged a protest with U.S. authorities and called the crime "exceptionally brutal and vicious."
"The occurrence of the heinous crime is extremely regrettable," Takaichi said in her message on social media.

She said Tokyo has urged the U.S. to "provide maximum cooperation with the investigation, enforce stricter discipline among U.S. military personnel, and take thorough measures to prevent the recurrence of similar crimes."
The U.S. Marine Corps said in a statement to the AP that the suspect is assigned to the III Marine Expeditionary Force on Okinawa and that it is fully cooperating with Japanese authorities.
"The Marine Corps takes these allegations very seriously and expects every Marine to adhere to the highest standards of behavior," the statement said.
The U.S. has around 54,000 military personnel stationed in Japan, mostly on Okinawa, which the U.S. held from the end of World War II until 1972.

Crimes, including rapes, assaults and drunk-driving accidents committed by U.S. personnel have been a thorn in relations between the close security allies. The number of arrests related to U.S. service members and their families exceeded 100 last year, according to prefectural police.
"Incidents and accidents involving U.S. military personnel cause great anxiety among the local community and must not be allowed to happen," Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said.
Last year, a Japanese court sentenced a U.S. Marine accused of choking and attempting to rape a woman in her 20s to seven years in prison.
In 2017, a former U.S. Marine and civilian military base worker was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local woman in Okinawa.
The same year, U.S. Forces Japan banned all personnel from consuming alcohol after an intoxicated US Marine crashed his vehicle into a mini-truck, killing its 61-year-old local driver.

title: U.K.-Iranian national released on bail after arrest in security incident near base
summary: The 25-year-old man was arrested in London, and police searched two properties in the U.K. capital, Counter Terrorism Policing said.
story: A dual U.K.-Iranian national who was arrested earlier this week on suspicion of plotting a terror attack following a security incident at the U.S.-run RAF Fairford air base in England that British authorities have linked to Tehran was released on bail Saturday.
The 25-year-old man was arrested in London on Thursday, and police have searched two properties in the U.K. capital, Counter Terrorism Policing said in a statement.
On Saturday, Counter Terrorism Policing announced that the man had been released on bail.
"The investigation into the circumstances surrounding events in Gloucestershire is continuing," the agency said in a new statement.

British police also initially reported that a second 26-year-old British national had been interviewed by investigators "under caution," meaning the interview was recorded and could be used in future prosecutions. However, they later disclosed that this was "not correct and has been removed" from their statement.

On Oct. 27, five men, all British nationals in their 20s and from London, were also arrested on suspicion of explosives and terror offenses close to the RAF Fairford air base, which has been used by American bombers to strike Iran. The suspects have also since been released on bail.
Their quick release drew criticism from President Trump and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio. But it also prompted questions in the U.K. as to whether the authorities had overreacted.
Police say they found a quantity of an accelerant – gasoline – in three vans linked to the five suspects, but no explosives.
Vicki Evans, the senior national coordinator for counter terrorism policing, said the investigation "is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of inquiry."
"As we've made clear, we're looking at all possible angles - including possible foreign state involvement," she said.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the U.K. sees "strong indications" that Iran played a part in the incident. Iran denies involvement.

"There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford, but of course it remains an ongoing, complex and serious police investigation, and of course we are working closely with our colleagues in the United States of America," the prime minister told the BBC.
The base 100 miles west of London has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East, including this year's war with Iran.

Iranian authorities have warned that any bases used to attack the country would be considered legitimate targets, but the Iranian Embassy in London said in a statement shared Monday on social media that the regime "categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran" to the incident.

Burnham said authorities have the investigation under "the strongest grip and the closest control," and British officials had been "talking to counterparts in the United States all week to explain what is happening here, how things are being done."

U.K. officials say proxies linked to Iran have been behind a string of arsons and other attacks in Britain and other countries, many of them targeting the Jewish community and intended to sow fear. They have previously warned that Tehran could expand its targets in the U.K. if conflicts in the Middle East continue.

title: U.K. police accuse 2 Iranian men of planning terror attack on Jewish community
summary: Two Iranian men have been charged with plotting a terror attack on the Jewish community in Manchester, British police said.
story: Two Iranian men have been charged with plotting a terror attack on the Jewish community in Manchester, British police said Friday.

The suspects appeared in Westminster Magistrates' Court Saturday, where neither entered a plea, the Associated Press reported. The judge ordered them held until an Oct. 23 appearance at the Central Criminal Court in London.

The arrests come nearly a year after a deadly knife and gun attack on the Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation Synagogue in northern Manchester, where worshipers had gathered for Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar. Two people died in that Oct. 2, 2025, attack.
U.K. Metropolitan Police said in a news release that 36-year-old Salam Ahmadyan of Liverpool and 34-year-old Rahman Salehi of Salford, both Iranian nationals, were arrested in Manchester on Sept. 20.
"It is alleged that the two men were in contact with an overseas third-party who may be in Iran in relation to the plot," the Met wrote.
The Associated Press reported that the third party provided instructions on making a homemade chlorine bomb.
"We do not believe there to be any ongoing threat to the public in relation to this matter," Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans said in a statement.

"This news will be deeply distressing for our Jewish communities, coming so soon after Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur," British Home Minister Shabana Mahmood said in a statement. "I know this will be especially true in Manchester, as we mark one year since the terrorist attack at Heaton Park Synagogue."

Mahmood also added in her statement that "both suspects" had "arrived by small boat several years ago," which she said was a "reminder of the importance of our relentless work to tackle illegal migration into this country." Salehi was granted asylum and Ahmadyan has a pending asylum claim, the Associated Press reported.
The past year has seen a spate of attacks in the British capital targeting Jewish or Israel-linked locations.

This also comes after five British nationals, all men in their mid-20s, were arrested on Sept. 27 in a southwest English village near the British air force base RAF Fairford on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act. The base has been used by American bombers to launch attacks on Iran during the war in the Middle East. The men were later released on bail.

On Thursday, British authorities arrested a 25-year-old dual U.K.-Iranian national in London on suspicion of plotting a terror attack near the RAF Fairford air base. He was also released on bail Saturday, the U.K. Counter Terrorism Policing agency announced.
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that the British government believes Iran "played a part" in the Sept. 27 incident. Iran's government has denied any involvement.

title: FlyDubai pilot tells his survival story in emotional call with Indian leader
summary: The FlyDubai captain attacked by his co-pilot tells his harrowing survival story to India's leader in an emotional video call from his hospital bed.
story: The FlyDubai captain attacked by his co-pilot on a Wednesday flight to Israel says his faith gave him the courage to seize what he believed to be a last chance to save himself and the 173 other people on board the plane.

Flight captain Smit Machchhar told India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi in an emotional video call from his hospital bed in Saudi Arabia on Thursday that, despite multiple stab wounds, he managed to open the cockpit door to let in passengers who subdued the attacking co-pilot, likely saving the 174 people on the Boeing 737.

"I was fighting for my life," said Machchhar, who is an Indian national. "When I was lying on the floor I could feel the aircraft was going down. I knew exactly that this would be the last push. I told myself that if I didn't get up, there would be a problem. I managed to open the door, and then everyone else came in."
Machchhar told Modi how, in his darkest moments, he repeated Hindu religious chants and clung to his faith, believing "God would save us."
He apologized for breaking down in tears as he told the Indian leader he had never really been "proud of myself, but today I am."
The first question Modi asked Machchhar was how he was feeling, to which Machchhar, wearing a bandage around his head and with an oxygen tube still in his nose, replied simply: "All good, sir."
"I am not thinking about the wounds that much," the captain said. "I look at this as a journey. I am confident of my recovery and return."
"Get better and healthy, the whole nation is with you," the Indian leader told him. "I don't want to bother you much. My best wishes are with you."
Co-pilot transferred to UAE for questioning

The co-pilot of FlyDubai flight 1073, who has not been identified by authorities, was transferred Thursday from Saudi Arabia to the United Arab Emirates for questioning by Israeli, UAE and Saudi officials, an Israeli official confirmed to CBS News on Friday.

"As time passes, the picture is becoming clearer; the attacker underwent Islamist radicalization. He came to crash the plane with its passengers," Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Friday. "We are investigating whether he was dispatched, and whoever sent him will pay a very heavy price."
Saudi officials said Wednesday that the co-pilot was hospitalized after the incident and treated for unspecified injuries.
An Omani official confirmed to CBS News that the copilot was born in Oman and currently holds Omani citizenship, but Oman's government has not publicly confirmed his nationality.

Netanyahu said Thursday that Israel knew he had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination" based on "personal information" gathered during initial questioning. He offered no further information on the alleged indoctrination Thursday or Friday, but told Fox News on Thursday that the alleged attacker was "suicidal," and that after he was subdued by other crew members and passengers, he shouted: "Kill me, kill me!"
President Trump on Thursday suggested the co-pilot was linked to Iran, going further than Netanyahu, who had said it was still "too early to say" if Iran could have been involved.

"We're working on it right now," Mr. Trump said Thursday at the White House when a reporter asked if the co-pilot had links to Iran. "They're being very open with us. I would say the answer, based on what I'm hearing, is yes. But we're working on it right now."
Asked if the co-pilot could have been working for or with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps or radicalized some other way, Mr. Trump replied that he "could've been, yeah."

title: Some topics are off limits in Chinese AI, researchers find
summary: A popular Chinese AI program, Qwen, has no memory of Tiananmen Square and no tolerance for Winnie the Pooh.
story: An AI model downloaded over 3 billion times and used by U.S. firms like Airbnb and Uber is embedded with China-friendly narratives and programmed for censorship, new research shows.

Qwen, a freely available model made by Chinese conglomerate Alibaba, doesn't acknowledge the violent suppression of protests in Hong Kong in 2019 or Tiananmen Square in 1989; it calls the Chinese government-maligned religion Falun Gong a "dangerous cult," and curiously won't talk about Winnie the Pooh, it's thought because dissidents have compared the fictional bear to Chinese President Xi Jinping.
The apparent censorship inserted into Qwen of events and issues not approved by the Chinese authorities was identified by Hirundo, an Israeli cybersecurity startup.

The firm says its scientists have found a way to remove the model's bias using sophisticated technology that amounts to "AI brain surgery," and are now set to publish what they call a "Westernized" version of Qwen.
This year Qwen became the most popular free AI model in the world, following a meteoric rise in the use of Chinese-made artificial intelligence.
But researchers warn that its  international popularity also risks spreading and entrenching its bias toward the Chinese government.

When we asked Qwen, "Are there forced labor camps for Uyghurs in China?" it replied, "No, there are no forced labor camps for Uyghurs in China," adding that there are "vocational skills education and training centers in Xinjiang."

In fact, human rights organizations, governments and international bodies have found hundreds of thousands of people in the Muslim ethnic minority working against their will in factories surrounded by barbed wire fences, and even accused the Chinese government of genocide.

Qwen often refuses to respond to questions about the events in Tiananmen Square on June 3, 1989, when the Chinese military massacred several hundred people at protests in Beijing  — and ominously "remind[s] you that your questions should comply with the relevant laws and regulations."

The Chinese government effectively banned Winnie the Pooh from the country after dissidents began satirically comparing Xi to the fictional bear and using Pooh as a euphemism for the Chinese president in social media posts to avoid government censors. When CBS News asked Qwen a factual question about it, it responded with a warning to "use respectful language" and directed the user to "other questions about China's development."
Qwen's creator, Alibaba, did not respond to a request for comment.

Despite evidence of embedded bias in the program, U.S. firms have been increasingly switching to use "open-weight" models offered by Chinese companies, which allow them to download and use AI for free or use giant, powerful models at lower costs than U.S. competitors such as Anthropic's Claude or OpenAI's ChatGPT.

Uber Eats' search and delivery functions are built "on a Qwen backbone" according to an April blog post by the company. Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky told the LA Times last October that his company is "relying a lot on Alibaba's Qwen model" for its customer service chatbot.
Neither company responded to a request for comment.

Chinese open-weight models grew from under 2% of global usage in late 2024 to more than 45% by June this year, according to usage data of all AI models from the software developers' platform OpenRouter.
By August, Qwen had eclipsed all other open models, including those made by Facebook owner Meta and Google owner Alphabet, rising to more than 3 billion downloads globally.
Experts at security firm CrowdStrike and consultancy Booz Allen have warned American firms about using Chinese models after their separate studies found bias and security flaws.

Booz Allen published results in June saying that when they asked Qwen to write computer code and told it the project was for the U.S. government, the code it produced had 130% more security vulnerabilities.
"The Chinese models that we tested failed to demonstrate trustworthy behaviors and should be banned," the report said.

CrowdStrike conducted a similar study last November on another popular Chinese model, DeepSeek. When they told the model that its coding task was for an adversary of the Chinese government, the code it produced had 50% more security vulnerabilities.
Hirundo says it tested Qwen on 500 prompts across 15 topics and then removed the bias its analysts found to create what they call a "Westernized" version.

"On sensitive political prompts, the original Qwen produced censorship, propaganda-aligned framing or political bias 89.8% of the time," Hirundo CEO and founder Ben Luria told CBS News. "The Westernized model does so 2.8% of the time, with the capability preserved at-large across reasoning, coding, instruction following and math tasks."

In a white paper on the technology shared with CBS News, Hirundo says it edits the "model weights" — the neurons of the AI's digital brain — rather than previous, less effective attempts to remove bias that merely ask the AI to follow new rules that it often ignores.

"Everything in a model is entangled with a lot of other things, similar to our brains," Luria said. "That's why it's so hard to pinpoint what specific neurons are representing the things you don't want in your AI models."
He said his team's goal was "realigning the model to Western standards to make them safer for deployment in Western enterprises."
"The trend is clear. Chinese models are on the rise," he added.
"We need to acknowledge the risks, and then we can go to solve them."
