"I live in Texas, and I’ve been here for a really long time, and it’s time for a change, a positive change," she said. "And I think Talarico is definitely going to bring that."
"We just have to vote," Kiara added. "We can’t complain about the problems if you don’t want to vote to fix them."
Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

title: Supreme Court kicks off new term with fresh questions over its legitimacy and its future
summary: The Supreme Court opens its new term with major cases on gun rights, voter citizenship and religious liberty amid record-low public approval ratings.
story: Former Deputy Assistant Attorney General John Yoo analyzes the constitutional challenges surrounding birthright citizenship and executive authority under the 14th Amendment on ‘America’s Newsroom.’
The Supreme Court begins its new term Monday, with renewed public and political concern over their recent rulings, the justices' personal safety and even their future makeup.

Chief Justice John Roberts, surrounded by his eight colleagues, will call the court into public session precisely at 10 a.m. EDT with a pair of scheduled oral arguments. Their first case from the bench will be a major one: a federal-state environmental dispute over holding oil and gas companies liable for climate change harms.
Other high-profile appeals are already on the argument docket:

Religious liberty and whether states can exclude religious schools from a taxpayer-funded preschool choice programGun rights and state bans on certain semi-automatic rifles like AR-15sVoting rights and efforts to require proof of U.S. citizenship when registering to vote
Religious liberty and whether states can exclude religious schools from a taxpayer-funded preschool choice program
Gun rights and state bans on certain semi-automatic rifles like AR-15s
Voting rights and efforts to require proof of U.S. citizenship when registering to vote
NEWSOM PROMISES NEW LEGAL FIGHT AFTER TRUMP GETS SUPREME COURT VICTORY ON MAIL-IN VOTING
The Supreme Court opens its new term Monday with major cases involving executive power, gun rights, religious liberty and voting rules. (Leah Millis-Pool/Getty Images)
But the Supreme Court under Roberts' leadership continues to struggle against negative public attitudes over their reputation as a non-political actor upholding the law and Constitution.

"The chief justice is in a tough position in that he is an institutionalist and a traditionalist at a time in our nation's history where a lot of institutions and traditions have come under pressure like they haven't in a long time," said Thomas Dupree, a leading appellate attorney and former top Justice Department official. "And so in many ways, he is trying to kind of buck a lot of the tide right now by really insisting and hewing to these traditions of the institutions that have governed Washington for a long time."
Trump on the docket

The new term will feature more constitutional disputes over the power of the executive, with current or anticipated fights over immigration, federal bureaucracy reforms and possibly the White House ballroom and Kennedy Center construction projects.
And if recent history is any predictor, the justices are likely to offer a mixed, nuanced series of rulings both for and against President Donald Trump's ambitious agenda.

The last term saw him and his allies lose over sweeping reciprocal tariffs, birthright citizenship and removal of Federal Reserve governors; but prevail on various immigration policies, mid-decade redistricting and political gerrymandering, and federal campaign spending.

For the most part, the 6-3 conservative majority has greenlighted the administration's power, especially in a series of preliminary decisions from its so-called "shadow docket" that allow Trump to move ahead – for now – on a range of issues.

The Trump Justice Department has won over 70% of its emergency cases before the Supreme Court since 2025 – applications that ask a challenged executive policy be enforced temporarily, while the larger issues are further litigated in the lower courts.
Those included new federal rules for verifying a voter's citizenship status ahead of the November midterms; and approval for continued construction of the ballroom.
Court legitimacy and public perception
Decisions in Trump's second term have him and Republican lawmakers sharply criticizing their judicial losses on one hand, and Democratic leaders sounding the alarm when their side does not prevail.
The judiciary has always weathered such criticism, but the personal tone of the attacks has only increased, as have the calls for sweeping accountability.
Those on the right have demanded impeaching federal judges who block White House policies, while those on the left have renewed calls for drastic changes to the court's structure.
The president himself amped up the tensions dramatically, after losing a key decision over federal efforts to restrict mail ballots for the midterm elections.
In a wild Truth Social post, he took aim at the three members he appointed to the bench – Justices Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett.

"These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court, they are merely a shell of their original selves," wrote Trump after the Sept. 14 ruling, adding, "The Court’s inability and unwillingness to do the right thing for our Country will go down, in a very negative way, in the annals of History."

Those on the left have their own beefs. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries told the National Association of Black Journalists that "dramatic Supreme Court reform is necessary... there's a variety of different options that are on the table and I think that we can't foreclose any single one of them."
As the midterms approach, angry and energized Democrats hoping to take control of the House and maybe the Senate have tried to rally the base during the midterm races.
Among their proposals are renewed calls for 18-year term limits for the justices, expanding the number on the bench to 13 or more from the current nine, and an independently enforced code of ethics.
All this has added to increasing public perception the high court is motivated by something other than its constitutional obligations.

A Washington Post/Ipsos poll in July found 46% of Americans think the justices rule on Trump administration policies based on their political views, while just 25% see the court as ruling based on the law.

Gallup's July poll showed the Supreme Court's job approval slumped to a record low of 33% and a record high 61% disapproval, driven by a steep drop in Republicans' backing of the court since last year.
And the most-recent Fox News survey revealed a 38% public job approval for the court, and a record high 45% believing the justices are too conservative.
That was up from 34% in 2022, and a low of 16% in 2015 and 2010.
Safety matters
Numbers aside, the amplified partisan rhetoric is having real-world consequences.
Several federal judges have told Fox News that budget shortfalls have compromised their physical security, at a time when they say threats against members of the bench have become more concerning.
The U.S. Marshals report 370 threats made to federal judges as of July 1, a 31% year-over-year increase.
"Extraordinary safety measures" have been taken in some cases by federal law enforcement, one federal judge told Fox News, without offering details.

While "criticism is fair game, intimidation is a different thing entirely," Justice Elena Kagan told a congressional panel in July. "When political figures of any stripe are trying to intimidate judges and justices to do things that they like rather than the things that they don't, that's where we really have crossed a line."
Justice Barrett told the same House committee, "The threat level is really high."
On at least one occasion, she has had to wear a bulletproof vest away from the court, and was a victim of a swatting incident over the summer at her home.
TRUMP'S WHITE HOUSE BALLROOM CONSTRUCTION GETS ANOTHER LIFELINE FROM SCOTUS AMID HEATED LEGAL FIGHT
Chief Justice John Roberts and the Supreme Court return to the bench as disputes over President Trump’s agenda remain a major focus. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)
Roberts' rules
The job of managing the court's docket falls to Roberts, who has faced bipartisan criticism for perceived partisanship.
Appointed by a Republican president, he more than any conservative on this current bench has been willing to rule against Trump and his Republican supporters.
That mixed record has been especially acute in recent days, where his influence was apparent in a series of decisions on midterm election matters, separately favoring both political parties.
That includes fights over congressional redistricting, mail ballots, a DHS database for voter eligibility and campaign ad spending.
More such emergency disputes are expected to reach the high court in coming weeks, pre- and post-election.
His colleagues have come to the chief justice's defense.

"I don't see this as a court that is just like: We're just going to rubber stamp what the current administration does. You know, quite the opposite," Kagan said at a judicial conference in July. "I think that that is a bad rap."
Roberts himself in May defended the court against accusations of partisanship.
"We’re not simply part of the political process, and there's a reason for that, and I'm not sure that people grasp that as much as is appropriate," he said at a judicial conference.
Looking ahead
The court's new term will continue to be defined by various Trump executive actions being challenged by progressive states and private groups.
That includes pending appeals over transgenders in the military, tariffs, private data access and federal agency cuts.
Other upcoming challenges include mandated Ten Commandments displays in public schools, free speech fights and abortion access.

Much of what the court decides to tackle will likely turn on whether Democrats can gain control Congress after November, and their ability to legislatively tame Trump's aggressive assertion of presidential power.

"This term is once again, set to deliver us a series of decisions concerning some of the most fundamental aspects of our government, including the relationship among the three branches of our federal government, and the relationships between the federal government and the states," said legal analyst Dupree. "I think we're also going to see in the near future a lot of election-related cases about the right to vote, how you protect it, and how we ensure the integrity of our election. So this is a term that promises a lot of big decisions and frankly, something for everyone."
TRUMP BLASTS SUPREME COURT 'DISASTER' AFTER JUSTICES RULE AGAINST HIM ON MAIL-IN VOTING

The Supreme Court begins a consequential new term as the justices confront major constitutional disputes and continued scrutiny of the institution. (Jay Janner/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images)
Add to that the possibility of a Supreme Court vacancy in coming months, with much of the speculation centered on 76-year-old Justice Samuel Alito.
Fox News was the first to report earlier this spring he would stay on for another term that effectively ends in late June, and he plans to be on the bench Monday.

This despite public and private pressure from many Republicans – aware they may lose the Senate in November – that he step aside now to give the president a chance to name a fourth member to the court.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Sources close to Alito tell Fox News considerations of his future are driven more by personal practicality rather than politics. They say for now he enjoys the work, and feels he is able to serve with commitment and focus.
Shannon Bream currently serves as anchor of FOX News Sunday. She joined the network in 2007 as a Washington, D.C- based correspondent covering the Supreme Court.

title: Southern Baptist president calls on pastors to 'step up' ahead of midterm elections
summary: Willy Rice says pastors must "step up" on abortion, marriage, gender identity and immigration, arguing these political issues are deeply theological.
story: Southern Baptist Convention President and Pastor Willy Rice called on pastors across the country to "step up" into the political process as midterm elections near.
Southern Baptist Convention President and Pastor Willy Rice called on pastors across the country to "step up" into the political process as midterm elections near.
While some Christian leaders advise against wading into politics from the pulpit, Rice argues pastors have long played a key role in American politics.
Members of the theological and political left have shown no hesitance to mix religion with their politics and evangelicals should not either, he says.
DETROIT PASTOR SAYS PROGRESSIVE CANDIDATES ARE TRYING TO 'VIRTUE-SIGNAL' TO CHRISTIAN VOTERS
Parishioners worship during Sunday service at Clayton Baptist Church in Clayton, Ga., on June 9, 2024. (AFP via Getty Images)

"Should pastors engage in the political process? They absolutely should. Because there are many political issues that are, at their heart, theological issues and moral issues that strike at the very center of what we believe to be true and what we believe people need to know in order to flourish personally and as a culture."
"I think the pastors need to step up. I think throughout American history, pastors have had a strong voice at key moments in American political history," Rice said.
'JESUS WAS A RADICAL': PROGRESSIVES INVOKE CHRIST TO SELL LEFT-WING AGENDA ON CAMPAIGN TRAIL
Worshipers arrive for Easter Sunday services at Second Baptist Church in Houston on April 5, 2026. (Houston Chronicle via Getty Images)
Rice lamented that many Christians have been encouraged in recent decades, from both external and internal forces, to "be more quiet" and "withdraw from the political process."

"Now, the interesting thing is that those on the theological and political left did not [withdraw], and they had no intention of doing so. And in fact, statistics show that people on the political and theological left are actually more politically engaged than those on the right," Rice said. "So what you had was, for a period of time, I felt like you had an almost a vacuum that kind of developed, a silence that was there with a lack of Christian leaders leaning in."
PRO-LIFE GROUP RAMPS UP NC GROUND GAME AS REPORT FINDS FED ABORTION MESSAGE GIVES GOP CANDIDATE BIGGEST BOOST
The midterm elections heat up as voters return to the polls in 2026. (Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Melissa Sue Gerrits/Getty Images)
Rice highlighted abortion, the definition of marriage, gender identity and immigration as issues where Christians should feel compelled to vote in a certain way.

"These issues are deeply, profoundly theological issues. They go back to the creation; they go back to Genesis 1 and 2. They go back to our understanding of what it means to be a human being, and our understanding of what God's creative purpose is for us as human beings," he said.
BIDEN ADMINISTRATION FORCED A FALSE CHOICE ON AMERICANS ABOUT IMMIGRATION

Voters cast their ballots at the Utah County Health and Justice Building on Nov. 8, 2022, in Provo. After months of candidates campaigning, Americans are voting in the midterm elections to decide close races across the nation. (George Frey/Getty Images)

Rice argued that Christians also face "manipulative" arguments when it comes to immigration. He admits that the immigration issue does present a "challenge" for Christians but argues there is nothing wrong with enforcing America's laws.

"There is a value of compassion, a value of wanting to care for the least of these people who are poor and oppressed and wanting to help," Rice said, noting that Christians do more of that charity than any other group in the U.S.
FEDERAL APPEALS COURT COMPARES TRUMP MIGRANT DETENTION POLICY TO JAPANESE AMERICAN INTERNMENT

"But there is also the importance of the rule of law," he continued. "The protection of people who are in this country. And what you've had is sometimes a very cynical use by some people in power of trying to manipulate Christians by saying, since you must demonstrate compassion, therefore you must embrace open immigration, or you must not insist on the enforcement of the immigration laws."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"That is very, very manipulative. No one would say that because you love people or care for people, you should leave the doors of your house unlocked, or you should open up the jail cells in your own community," he said.
Anders Hagstrom is a reporter with Fox News Digital covering national politics and major breaking news events.

title: How an Uzbek truck driver’s fatal crash exposed troubling fraud trend in Middle America: ‘Chameleon carriers’
summary: Uzbek-linked trucking companies in southwest Ohio face scrutiny over CDL fraud, English proficiency violations and fatal semi-truck crashes on U.S. roads.
story: Fox News Digital spoke to Victor Louis, a trucking industry veteran in southwest Ohio, about the rise in trucking fraud and influx of potentially illegal immigrant drivers causing danger on the roads.

CINCINNATI, OH - A young man killed by an Uzbek truck driver earlier this year in Ohio, along with several instances of illegal immigrant truck drivers involved in fatal crashes, has sparked a larger conversation in southwest Ohio about fraud, crime, immigration and how gaps in trucking industry oversight are putting Americans at risk.

Tobias "Toby" Forsythe, a 21-year-old goalkeeper from Ohio on the University of Massachusetts Lowell men’s soccer team, was killed July 5 when authorities say a semi-truck driven by 42-year-old Uzbek national Bekhzod Asrarov, who entered the country under the Biden administration's diversity visa lottery program, rear-ended Forsythe’s Honda Accord on Interstate 71 in Madison County, Ohio.

It was later determined, according to court documents, that Asrarov could not speak or understand English well enough to communicate with responding state troopers without the use of Google Translate, despite holding an Ohio commercial driver’s license, and that he allegedly removed a dashboard camera from his truck after the fatal crash in an effort to conceal or destroy evidence.

"We cannot let truckers like Asrarov, who can’t read our road signs or speak to law enforcement, drive 80,000-pound rigs on America’s highways," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy posted on X after the crash.
IMMIGRANT TRUCK DRIVER ADMITTED TO US UNDER BIDEN ALLEGEDLY KILLS UMASS SOCCER STAR, SPOKE NO ENGLISH

The death of college soccer player Tobias "Toby" Forsythe, who was allegedly struck and killed by truck driver Bekhzod Asrarov (pictured) in Ohio, has fueled debate over commercial trucking safety. (Madison County Sheriff's Office ; Kevin Carter/Getty Images)

In southwest Ohio, a researcher known as Nodawolf has been sounding the alarm to his growing follower count about a vast network of trucking companies, many of them owned or operated by Uzbek nationals, that have popped up in communities like Loveland, Middletown, and Maineville, where Asrarov resides, in recent years and could be contributing to the unsafe practices that took the life of Forsythe, and many others across the country.

Nodawolf, who Fox News Digital granted anonymity due to the death threats he’s received from his online reporting, said his research has focused on what he describes as an interconnected network of Uzbek-linked trucking companies in southwest Ohio, including companies that have donated money toward construction of a local Islamic center, according to the center's own website.

"All of them have English violations and have manipulated ELDs," Nodawolf said, referring to electronic logging devices that track a trucker’s driving hours and are intended to enforce federal limits on how long drivers can stay behind the wheel.

The Islamic Center, located in Maineville, told Fox News Digital that a "charitable contribution or participation in a community fundraising activity, by itself, should not be interpreted as evidence of an ownership, employment, contractual, commercial, or other business relationship with the Islamic Center or its leadership."

A Fox News Digital review identified hundreds of trucking companies and other trucking entities registered in Maineville and surrounding southwest Ohio communities, including dozens that were registered in recent years. A separate review of companies identified as connected to the local Uzbek community found serious FMCSA safety violations, including drivers cited for failing English-proficiency requirements and other federal trucking violations.
TRUMP ADMIN TRUCKING CRACKDOWN LANDS 51 IMMIGRATION DETENTIONS, 36 ENGLISH LANGUAGE PROFICIENCY VIOLATIONS
Emergency crews responded to a multi-vehicle crash involving semi-trucks on the I-10 Freeway in San Bernardino County, Calif., on Oct. 21, 2025. (@BillMelugin via X)

"This really concerns me, you know, as a father," Nodawolf told Fox News Digital. "I mean, it's clearly obvious that they either don't understand our laws, they don't care about our laws, or they know our laws and they're taking advantage of it."

Nodawolf has reported on Uzbek trucking networks communicating on the social media platform Telegram. One of those Telegram channels, named "UzbegimAmerica," has routinely mentioned the Uzbek community in Maineville. Court documents show the owner of that channel, Farkhod Faiziev, is a suspected illegal immigrant from Uzbekistan.

The Trump administration has made significant progress on the issue of removing foreign truck drivers who pose a danger being removed from the road – including a recent multi-agency operation in Arizona’s Yuma Sector, which led to the arrest of 95 illegal alien truck drivers earlier this month – striking at the heart of human and drug smuggling operations at the U.S. southern border.

The Departments of Homeland Security, Transportation and Justice recently announced a coordinated crackdown on trucking and CDL fraud targeting fraudulent licensing, unauthorized employment, identity-document fraud, shell companies and other criminal activity. The effort includes inspections at more than 200 driving schools across 23 states, investigations based on more than 1,000 leads, enforcement operations targeting illegal immigrants with commercial licenses and a new multi-state DOJ task force focused on trucking-related fraud and roadway safety.

A trucking-industry veteran with decades of experience who spoke to Fox News Digital under the condition of anonymity for his safety described a developing fraud scheme popular with immigrant communities known as "chameleon carriers", a network of trucking companies that appear separate on paper but, he said, share the same drivers, trucks and operations. The arrangement starts when operators establish one company that is "quote-unquote legitimate," he said, then create additional carriers and authorities while using the same underlying assets across them.
ILLEGAL TRUCKER CASES FUEL GOP PUSH TO CRACK DOWN ON CDL MILLS AS DEMS LARGELY SILENT

The point, the industry expert said, is to "spread out their safety liability across multiple companies." Rather than allowing inspections and violations to pile up under one carrier, he said, the operation can distribute them among multiple motor-carrier authorities.

"If they have 10 inspections and 10 violations across 10 different companies, that doesn’t hurt the safety rating as much," he said. "But if it was one company that had 10 inspections and 10 violations, that one company is going to get hammered."

The separate companies can also serve as a contingency plan, he said. If one carrier is shut down, loses insurance or becomes too damaged by safety problems, "they’re able to immediately move all of the equipment and drivers and everything under one of the different companies," the industry veteran said. "Their operation never stops. There’s no way to shut them down."

He further alleged the structure can facilitate cargo theft, with a company disappearing after obtaining a high-value shipment while the broader network continues operating through its remaining entities. "They lost one of their shell companies, basically, but they just got $5 million in iPads," he said.

The industry expert said the model can be particularly dangerous, in his view, because it allows companies to keep operating despite safety problems while allegedly using drivers who may not be legally authorized to work in the United States. He said operators can make that harder to detect by classifying drivers as independent contractors rather than employees, potentially avoiding the ordinary employee I-9 verification process.

"If you’re using a bunch of people from a third-world country that just showed up in the United States as drivers, whether they’re here legally or not, how well do you think they’re going to maintain their equipment and be able to follow the laws?" he said.
Seven of the trucking schools targeted by the Department of Transportation last month are located in Ohio, DOT told Fox News last month.

A Notice of Proposed Removal was recently issued by the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration for Turan CDL School, a Middletown-based company that has advertised CDL training to Uzbek speakers, including advertisements suggesting students could obtain a CDL without first learning English, as well as Google reviews from customers claiming they earned their licenses in as little as one week.
ILLEGAL ALIEN'S ‘INEXCUSABLE’ CRIME SPARKS INTERSTATE CLASH BETWEEN GOP SEN, DEM GOV: ‘YOU SHOULD BE ASHAMED’

"There's 'what do the rules say' and then 'what's happening on the ground," Andrew Poliakoff, vice president of the Commercial Vehicle Training Association, told Fox 28 Columbus shortly after the crash that killed Forsythe. "We're seeing now is that there are a lot of people committing fraud, and engaging in a variety of bad actions issuing commercial driver's licenses."

Victor Louis, whose Cincinnati based company Load Secure verifies the identities of drivers entering its network, told Fox News Digital that he has seen local advertisements promising prospective truckers a CDL in as little as a week immediately raise red flags.

"Trucking is such an inherently dangerous activity. Essentially, you're driving a 40-ton missile down the road," Louis said. "To think that someone is going to be certified to do that within a week, that may or may not speak English, like that doesn't make any sense."

Louis said his company is also seeing a significant number of non-domiciled drivers, foreign drivers who hold commercial licenses issued by a U.S. state despite not having their permanent residence in that state. He said roughly 15% to 20% of drivers entering Load Secure's network fall into that category and estimated the figure could be around 20% among long-haul truckers nationwide.

"Whether they're here legally or not, I don't know, but they are essentially foreign nationals," Louis said. He argued that long-haul trucking can be particularly attractive to migrants because drivers can spend weeks at a time living on the road rather than maintaining a permanent home near their workplace.
Louis said cargo theft and the security of the broader supply chain are among his biggest concerns.

"What we see with that market of non-domiciled drivers is a high propensity of cargo theft, an extremely high propensity," he said. "It’s wreaking havoc on our supply chain. Number one, it's extremely dangerous and number two, it is very unsecure. We don't know if things are being tampered with. This exposes our supply chains."

The Ohio Bureau of Motor Vehicles told Fox News Digital that it is reviewing the state’s nondomiciled commercial driver’s license holders in coordination with the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration. Of the roughly 5,000 nondomiciled credentials originally issued, about 3,500 remain active, meaning approximately 1,500 are no longer active as the review continues.
On Sept. 16, Fox News reported that ICE arrested two Uzbek illegal alien truck drivers in New Jersey as part of nationwide crackdown on fraudulent CDLs.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"We are starting to go into those thousand leads of fraud, waste and abuse into our trucking industry," DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a press conference last month. "We're going to prioritize going after employees that are suspected of accepting payments to help illegals bypass driver's license and CDL requirements."

In Brown County, Ohio, on Sept. 2, an Indian national with a CDL out of California crashed his semi-truck head-on into the car of 50-year-old Brenda Watson, who died at the scene. The driver, Manjit Singh , was later determined to be an illegal immigrant and ICE announced in a press release that a detainer was placed along with a charge of aggravated vehicular homicide.

"One state’s regulatory failure becomes every state’s highway threat," Ohio attorney Mehek Cooke told News Digital. "Republican governors cannot assume their states were insulated from Biden’s border crisis simply because they opposed his policies."
Fox News Digital reached out to Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine's office for comment.
Last month, ICE launched a tip-line for reporting fraudulent CDL licenses.

"Too many American lives have been lost or permanently changed because illegal aliens who have no business being on our roads have been granted CDLs," Mullin said in a press release. "ICE and our federal partners, including the Department of Transportation, will be cracking down on CDL fraud so that not one more American life is lost to a reckless illegal alien behind the wheel of a semi-truck."
Andrew Mark Miller is a reporter at Fox News. Find him on Twitter @andymarkmiller and email tips to AndrewMark.Miller@Fox.com.

title: Trump touts ‘golden age’ at Ohio rally, urges voters to deliver GOP midterm wins
summary: President Donald Trump urged Ohio rally-goers to "pretend I'm on the ballot" as he stumped for Jon Husted and Vivek Ramaswamy in the midterms.
story: President Donald Trump urged his audience in Ohio to "pretend that I'm running" ahead of November's midterm elections in the Buckeye State, during Saturday's speech in Vandalia, Ohio.

President Donald Trump swept into Ohio Saturday night promoting what he calls a new "golden age" for America, pointing to billions of dollars in investment and new jobs in the Buckeye State as he urged voters to help keep Republicans in power in November.

For the third time in as many nights, Trump rallied supporters outside Dayton for Republicans Sen. Jon Husted and gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, casting the midterms as a chance to extend the economic and political gains he said the GOP has delivered since his return to the White House.
And with his own name absent from the ballot, Trump gave voters gathered a simple instruction.
TRUMP CAMPAIGN INSIDER REVEALS STRATEGY BEHIND MIDTERM BLITZ THAT WHITE HOUSE HOPES PAYS OFF BIG

President Donald Trump takes the stage at the Butler-Vandalia Student Activity Center during a campaign rally on Saturday, in Vandalia, Ohio. Trump is traveling across the U.S. in the final weeks before the midterm elections to campaign for Republican candidates. (Getty Images)
"Just pretend that I’m running," Trump said. "When I run, we win."

Trump, who carried Ohio in all three of his presidential campaigns, later echoed the same message as he sought to rally his political coalition behind Republicans fighting to maintain control of Congress.
"If you don’t mind, please pretend that I’m on the ballot," Trump said. "And you need to turn out for a midterm victory."
The president used much of the rally to make an economic case for the Republican ticket, declaring Ohio is "booming" as he hailed investments he credited to both his trade and tariff policies.
Trump pointed to a $400 million Stellantis investment in Toledo and an $850 million Electra aerospace investment near Springfield.

Weaving in an anecdote about his daily aspirin habit, the president also featured Bayer’s plans for a $2.2 billion pharmaceutical manufacturing campus near Columbus, which the company says will support approximately 600 permanent jobs and 1,500 construction jobs.
"Your state is booming," Trump told the gathered crowd. "Every state is booming."
FIRST DATA CENTER BILL CLEARS HOUSE AS BOTH PARTIES SCRAMBLE FOR ANSWERS ON AFFORDABILITY
A supporter holds a "Trump Country" flag as President Donald Trump speaks during a campaign rally in Vandalia, Ohio, Saturday. (AFP via Getty Images)

Trump credited the investments to his tariff agenda, arguing the U.S. is finally leveling the playing field after years of other countries using tariffs against American products while giving companies a powerful incentive to build at home.
The president also threw his support behind Husted’s Ratepayer Protection Act, legislation aimed at shielding consumers from additional electricity costs associated with data centers.
"We want them," Trump said of data centers. "There’s so much money to be made for Ohio. You can’t just turn them off. They’ll go to China."
Husted brought the legislation to the Senate floor days before the rally, where it failed to advance. President Trump pledged to sign it if Congress can send it to his desk.
TRUMP DEFENDS $5,000 DIVIDEND PROPOSAL, PRAISES 'BEAUTIFUL' TARIFFS ON 'INGRAHAM ANGLE'

Vivek Ramaswamy, Sen. Jon Husted and former NFL coach Jon Gruden listen as President Donald Trump speaks at the Butler-Vandalia Student Activity Center during a campaign rally in Vandalia, Ohio. (Getty Images)
"I will sign this Ratepayer Protection Act into law immediately," Trump said.

Trump broadened his victory lap from Ohio to the country as a whole, hailing stock market records, manufacturing growth, investment and employment while contrasting his own administration’s economic record with former President Joe Biden's.
"Our nation is doing better now than ever before," Trump said.

He also praised GOP-backed tax provisions, including no tax on tips and overtime, and reiterated his previously announced proposal for $5,000 payments to adult Americans if Republicans retain the House and Senate.

Trump then shifted to immigration and Springfield, Ohio, dedicating his recitation of the poem "The Snake" to the city that became a national flashpoint during the 2024 presidential campaign over an influx of Haitian nationals into the community.
President Donald Trump smiles during a campaign rally in Ohio. (AFP via Getty Images)
"I dedicate this to Springfield, Ohio," Trump said. "They went through hell."

After finishing the poem, which the president has long admired as an immigration allegory, he told the crowd, "That’s what happened at our border," before hailing his administration’s immigration crackdown.

The president also briefly touched on Venezuela, claiming the U.S. had more than recouped the costs of its military operation against former Venezuelan dictator Nicolas Maduro through the country's vast oil resources.
"We paid for the cost of the war many, many times over," Trump said. "We’re making a fortune with it."
President Donald Trump takes the stage at the Butler-Vandalia Student Activity Center during a campaign rally in Vandalia, Ohio. (Getty Images)
Trump repeatedly weaved the election 31 days away into his remarks, urging Ohioans to support Husted, Ramaswamy and Republican congressional candidates.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
He also pitched Ohio as a potential home for the U.S. National Space Academy, citing both the state's aviation history and the Wright brothers.
"If we win the midterms, Ohio will be very, very strongly considered for this," Trump said. "I really want you to go out and vote again for Jon Husted and for Vivek."
Jasmine Baehr is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital, where she covers politics, the military, legal debates surrounding life and family policy, as well as faith and culture.

title: Trump drops Republican Senator's phone number in social post over fury on stalled bill
summary: President Donald Trump posted Tom Cotton's alleged cell phone number on Truth Social, urging Arkansas voters to pressure him on daylight saving time.
story: President Donald Trump spoke candidly on efforts to pass a bill ending daylight savings time that has stalled in the U.S. Senate before boarding Marine One en route to Ohio Saturday.
President Donald Trump appeared to share the personal cell phone number of Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., on Truth Social amid his push to pass a bill which would end daylight savings time.
Trump called out Cotton, who he describes as "a friend," for stopping the "Sunshine Protection Act" from going to a vote last October.

"For some reason, Tom is stopping the Bill and, in the Senate, it’s very easy to do, it only takes one! It should pass overwhelmingly, in a Bipartisan fashion," Trump posted on Truth Social. "So, everyone in Arkansas, a State I love, and won 3 times, the last by 34 points, tell Tom to, GET IT DONE!"
TRUMP URGES SENATE TO PASS BILL MAKING DAYLIGHT SAVING TIME PERMANENT AFTER OVERWHELMING HOUSE VOTE

President Donald Trump wants to make daylight saving permanent, but a geographic coalition of northern and southern states are in a heated debate over the merits of the change, which spells doom for the bill. (Evan Vucci-Pool/Getty Images; Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Trump doubled down on his pressure campaign Saturday while speaking with reporters at the White House before boarding Marine One for a trip to Ohio, arguing that Americans are fed up with changing their clocks twice a year.

"We want to get away from this ridiculous way and custom of, every twice a year, turning your clocks back, turning your clocks forward, being late for dinner, being late for very important meetings," Trump said. "It's ridiculous."
Trump said Americans want more daylight in the evening and argued the twice-yearly time change is costly and disruptive.
"People want to have light in the evening," Trump said. "But really, what they want more than that, more than that by a lot, they don't want to have to go around changing clocks."
HOUSE PASSES DAYLIGHT SAVING TIME REFORM AS TRUMP SIGNALS SUPPORT FOR ENDING CLOCK CHANGE
Trump says Americans want more daylight in the evening. (Kyle Mazza/Anadolu via Getty Images, File)

At the end of his post, Trump prompted Arkansas voters to call Cotton's number, which he included. Fox News Digital called the phone number associated with the Dardanelle, Arkansas, area code but did not reach Cotton.

The Truth Social post from Trump comes as the Senate is out of session until Nov. 3 and unable to vote on the bill until after the midterm elections. The House passed its version of the bill in July by 308–117, garnering bipartisan support. The House bill was referred to a Senate committee, but it hasn't been touched.

Trump has been a leading advocate of ending the twice-yearly clock change, arguing that it would help "decrease Robbery and Murder Rates, Reduce Car Accidents (especially those involving Pedestrians!), Lower Risk for Cardiac Issues, Stroke, and Seasonal Depression," among a laundry list of other benefits of having an extra hour of daylight in the evening.
But the bill’s failure to pass despite bipartisan support marks another setback for Trump, who has made the SAVE America Act a priority but has been unable to get it signed into law.
TRUMP FACES REPUBLICAN REBELLION OVER DAYLIGHT SAVING TIME AS SENATE BILL NEARS DEAD END
Trump says Americans want more daylight in the evening and argued the twice-yearly time change is costly and disruptive. (iStock)

After Trump called out Cotton for rejecting a bipartisan unanimous consent made by Sens. Rick Scott, R-Fla., Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I. and Tommy Tuberville, R-Ala., to move the Senate bill last Fall, the Arkansas senator doubled down on his support for daylight savings time.

"No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Savings Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter," Cotton psoted on X. "Arkansans don’t want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I’ll always put Arkansas first."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

This isn’t the first time Trump has publicly disclosed a lawmaker’s cellphone number. In 2015, while campaigning for president, Trump shared the number of then-Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., at a rally in South Carolina. The move came after Graham called Trump a "jackass" on CBS that morning.
Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment.
Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

title: Tennessee prison chief resigns after failed execution as former US attorney tapped to lead independent review
summary: Frank Strada resigned as Tennessee's corrections commissioner after Christa Pike's botched lethal injection left her hospitalized on a ventilator.
story: Fox News host Jon Scott discusses Tennessee officials announcing the resignation of the state's prison chief following the failed execution of Christa Pike on 'Fox Report.'
The head of Tennessee's prison system is resigning after the state's failed lethal injection of convicted murderer Christa Pike left her hospitalized and on a ventilator.
Tennessee Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada will step down this month, Gov. Bill Lee said Saturday.

In a statement distributed by the governor's office, Strada said stepping aside was "in the best interest of Tennesseans" while an independent review examines what went wrong during the botched execution.
"I believe this review is entirely appropriate and necessary, and I look forward to doing everything I can to help determine exactly what occurred," Strada said.
FILE - Strada said stepping aside was "in the best interest of Tennesseans" amid an independent review of the failed execution. (AP Photo/George Walker IV)
DEATH ROW INMATE UNCONSCIOUS ON VENTILATOR AFTER BOTCHED EXECUTION FOR TEEN’S KILLING: ATTORNEYS

At Lee's request, the Tennessee Attorney General's Office has retained former U.S. Attorney Ed Stanton to conduct an independent review of the correction department's actions in carrying out Pike's court-ordered sentence, the state announced Saturday.

The review will examine the state Department of Correction's actions in carrying out Pike's court-ordered sentence, including whether the state's execution protocol was followed and whether additional recommendations are needed.
Lee also called off the remaining execution scheduled in Tennessee this year pending completion of the review.

Stanton previously conducted an independent review of Tennessee's lethal injection protocol in 2022. His work prompted the state and Attorney General's Office to substantially rewrite the protocol before executions resumed.
"The Governor has appropriately called for an investigation. We need to know what happened," a spokesperson for the Tennessee Attorney General’s Office told Fox News on Sunday.
Dorinda Carter, communications director for the Tennessee Department of Correction, said, "We have no additional information to provide at this time."
Lee said Strada served with integrity, adding that he appreciates his "willingness to put the interests of Tennesseans first during this difficult moment."
"I have accepted his decision to step down and am grateful for his commitment to ensuring a smooth leadership transition," Lee said.
Christa Gail Pike would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee since 1819 for the brutal 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer. (Tennessee Department of Correction via AP)
CHRISTA PIKE’S BOTCHED LETHAL INJECTION TAKES FOCUS OFF VICTIM, JEOPARDIZES EXECUTION: FORMER POLICE CHIEF
Pike, 50, was injected with two doses of pentobarbital on Wednesday night, and prison officials used at least seven needles while trying to find a vein.
Pike was heard crying, whimpering, and breathing loudly during the execution, according to a Friday court filing from her lawyers.
She was taken to the hospital, where she had to be intubated and put on a ventilator, her lawyers said.
In a statement obtained by The Associated Press, Pike's four-person legal team celebrated the departure of Strada but said it wasn't enough.

"What happened to her Wednesday reflects a systemic failure that goes far beyond any one person," they said. "We hope the governor’s call for a full, independent review will expose the profound problems within Tennessee’s entire death penalty system."

Her lawyers said in the court filing that the prison staff did not correctly place the IV lines. They also claimed staff failed to realize that one of Pike's veins burst, leading to at least some of the pentobarbital entering her body.
Christa Gail Pike is seen during her trial for the murder of Colleen A. Slemmer March 18, 1996, in Knox County Criminal Court. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)
DEATH ROW INMATE TONY CARRUTHERS WON'T FACE EXECUTION FOR AT LEAST A YEAR AFTER IV LINE FAILURE IN TENNESSEE

Strada became commissioner of Tennessee's correction department in January 2023 after serving as deputy director of the Arizona Department of Corrections. In late 2024, he announced that Tennessee would solely use pentobarbital as its execution drug.
Four people have been executed in Tennessee since last year, according to the department.
On the evening of Jan. 12, 1995, Christa Pike, then 18, lured 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer into a wooded area near the University of Tennessee's agricultural campus.
Pike and her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, then spent 30 minutes torturing Slemmer, while 18-year-old Shadolla Peterson served as a lookout.
According to her confession to authorities, Pike killed Slemmer because she believed she was interested in her boyfriend romantically.
Christa Gail Pike appears remotely from Deborah K. Johnson Rehabilitation for her hearing in Knox County Criminal Court in Knoxville, Tenn., on Aug. 11, 2026. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Even though Shipp directly participated in the murder, he was ineligible for the death penalty because he was 17 at the time. He was sentenced to life in prison with parole, which he has not yet received.
Peterson, who cooperated with investigators and testified against Pike and Shipp, was given 460 days in jail after pleading guilty to being an accessory.

Pike was the only one in the case sentenced to death and became one of the youngest women to be sent to death row. She would have been the first woman to be executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.

title: Firebrand GOP rep: Democrats side with Iran 'simply because they hate' Trump
summary: Rep. Randy Fine discusses the rationale for backing the conflict in Iran, explains the meaning of an America First foreign policy, and denounces Rep. Ilhan Omar on immigration fraud
story: Florida congressman warns America is losing the battle against radical Islam and accuses Democrats of siding with Tehran
MAGA firebrand Congressman Randy Fine, R-Fla., warned the U.S. must stop Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons as he cautioned America is losing the battle against radical Islam.

In a wide-ranging interview with Fox News Digital, he weighed in on the debate over whether Rep. Ilhan Omar D-Minn., should be deported after the recent announcement by Tom Homan that the Department of Homeland Security was investigating the congresswoman."If she engaged in immigration fraud, she should be deported. And by the way, as should anyone who engaged in immigration fraud. And look, the woman is enmeshed. She's bathed in fraud. I think the best example that we know is fraud is when she said she made 30 million dollars, which she either did and then lied about it and said she didn't make it, or she made it up in the first place," he claimed.
FROM CAMPUS RADICALS TO BEIJING'S AI SABOTAGE: REP. RANDY FINE SAYS 'US FIGHTING TO SAVE WESTERN CIVILIZATION'
Rep. Randy Fine, R-Fla., leaves the U.S. Capitol after the last votes of the week on Thursday, September 4, 2025 (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

"I mean, this is someone whose community that she comes from engages in wholesale welfare fraud. Some of her relatives had been involved in that as well, and if she engaged in immigration fraud she should be denaturalized. She should be deported back to her home country of Somalia."
A request sent to Omar's office for reaction to Fine's accusations was not returned by time of publication.
Fine said that the battle against political correctness is directly tied to mainstream Islam.

"Well, I don't know that we're winning. I think we're losing. And you can see it in the unbelievable fear that people have about talking about mainstream Islam. I saw a video today about a mosque in Texas that [is] literally showing the erasing of a church and the building of a mosque. They are openly fundraising on the premise that they will eliminate Christianity in this country.

"And people are absolutely petrified to speak the truth about it. That is a battle we are losing. And if we're not willing to tell the truth about mainstream Islam, we're done. You can see what has happened in the United Islamic Kingdom. That will happen to America if we are unwilling to deal with this problem," he said.

"I'm not surprised because when they stood up, the Iranians killed an estimated 100,000 of them. People are afraid. They don't have weapons. They don't have access to the internet to learn about what is going on."
Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., speaks during a press conference on Wednesday, in which she blamed President Donald Trump for death threats and attacks against her.  (AP Photo/Adam Gray)
MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD-LINKED NETWORKS EMBEDDED ACROSS CANADIAN INSTITUTIONS, NEW REPORT ALLEGES

He continued, "And I think they're hoping that the American pressure, both military and economic, will cause the regime to either restructure or collapse. I certainly would like to see them stand up for themselves and overthrow the mainstream Muslim religious leaders that are in charge there."
Following the IRGC's recent call to the American electorate to oppose Donald Trump in the midterm elections, Fine said that the move has the potential to impact the ballot box.
"Well, I hope it does. Look, it's been clear to me, based on my time in Congress, that the Democrats are on the side of Iran, and it's simply because they hate Donald Trump.

He added, "I think we need to make sure people understand that Muslim terrorists in Iran have endorsed the Democratic Party. That's who you're voting for. You're voting it for the people supported by Muslim terrorists if you vote Democrat."
Despite strong support for Trump's military engagement in Iran, Fine does not believe that regime overthrow is an imperative.

TURKEY’S NATO ROLE UNDER SCRUTINY AMID NEW REPORT ON HAMAS, MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD TIES

title: Springsteen, other stars share stage with hardcore leftist groups at music fest
summary: Bruce Springsteen and Dave Matthews headlined a Power To The People festival featuring anti-Trump nonprofits mobilizing ahead of midterms.
story: Comedian Mick Thomas joins "Fox News Saturday Night With Jimmy Failla" to discuss Bruce Springsteen saying that his new tour is going to be political.

As rapper Macklemore draws controversy for his activism against Israel, rock stars Bruce Springsteen and Dave Matthews headline a Power To The People music festival today that features a partisan network of nonprofits and activists mobilizing against President Donald Trump ahead of the midterms.

Performers from a hip-hop band, The Neighborhood Kids, launched the festival with Macklemore's anthem of protest, chanting, "Free, free Palestine!" and continued with a declaration about protesting from "the belly of the beast" against the "funding of genocide" and the "terrorist organization" Immigration and Customs Enforcement."
It dedicated its performance to "the martyrs" and railed against "Western imperialism."
The marketing language on the Power To The People festival's official website speaks to activating "the power everyday human beings have" to "shape" the world "on, and beyond, Election Day."
PARTY POOPERS' FIGHT CARD: JANE FONDA, 'NO KINGS,' COMMUNISTS ROLL OUT RIVAL SPECTACLE TO TRUMP'S 250TH

The festival bears clear signs of alignment with the Democratic Party and spotlights the intersection of pop culture, nonprofit fundraising and partisan politics, revealing how celebrity drawing power translates into money, visibility and voters for organizations advancing a political agenda.

In the chat, awaiting a livestream broadcast on the Democratic-aligned MS NOW, a user wrote, "BLUE WAVE," symbolizing a anticipated Democratic Party victories in upcoming elections. Others peppered their comments with blue wave and blue heart emojis.

By combining performances with voter registration, activist organizing and charitable donations, Power To The People offers participating groups a platform to turn fans’ enthusiasm for music into political engagement — and votes — ahead of the midterms. Festival organizers didn't respond to a request for comment.
Singer Bruce Springsteen performs at a Harris-Walz campaign rally in Philadelphia, Pa., Oct. 28, 2024.  (Nathan Morris/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

With musical artists passionately urging festival goers to vote Democratic, the event raises questions about whether participating nonprofits cross the line from permissible voter engagement into partisan campaign intervention, which federal tax law prohibits for 501(c)(3) organizations.
Jane Fonda and Rep. Ilhan Omar appear onstage during the No Kings Rallies in St. Paul, Minn., March 28, 2026. (Adam Bettcher/Getty Images)

A Freedom Village, set up on the festival grounds of the Merriweather Post Pavilion in Columbia, Maryland, outside the nation’s capital, features a roster of nonprofit organizations, including Indivisible, which is funded by billionaire George Soros; Third Act; the ACLU; and other groups that have been at the heart of coordinating "No Kings," "Tesla Takedown" and "Hands Off" protests against Trump over almost two years.

Last year, Springsteen performed at a "No Kings" protest at the state capitol in St. Paul, Minnesota, organized by Indivisible and featuring anti-Trump activist Jane Fonda. He also headlined a "No Kings" event at the Target Center in Minneapolis.
FIRST ON FOX: ‘NO KINGS’ PROTEST NETWORK BEHIND FIGHT AGAINST AI DATA CENTERS AND FLOCK CAMERAS
Bruce Springsteen & The E Street Band perform during the Land of Hope & Dreams American Tour at Target Center March 31, 2026, Minneapolis. (Kevin Mazur/Getty Images)

Many of the festival's performers and organizers bring a documented history of campaigning for Democrats and far-left activism. Festival organizer Tom Morello, guitarist of the band Rage Against the Machine, has called socialism a "necessity."

Opening the concert after the hip-hop group The Neighborhood Kids, Morello blasted the "fascists and the would-be dictators" and the "oligarchs," symbolic references that protesters have used for almost two years of protests against Trump.

According to an online fundraising form, the Power To The People Festival Fund is identified as a fiscally sponsored project of Catalyst Philanthropy Fund, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit established in 2024 in Nashville with $6.5 million in annual revenue, according to its latest tax filing.
Tom Morello performed with Bruce Springsteen at Madison Square Garden Monday. (Taylor Hill/WireImage)
Springsteen endorsed the Democratic presidential ticket in 2024, declaring, "I’m supporting Kamala Harris for president and Tim Walz for vice president."
He also called Trump "the most dangerous candidate for president in my lifetime."

Artist Dave Matthews participated in the 2020 I Will Vote concert, which his official website promoted as supporting Biden, Harris and Democrats down the ballot. Earlier, Matthews backed socialist presidential candidate Bernie Sanders, writing, "When it comes down to it, Bernie Sanders represents what I want from my government."
Artist and festival DJ Shepard Fairey created the iconic Obama "Hope" poster and the "Forward" image supporting Harris in 2024.

"I believe VP Kamala Harris and her VP pick Tim Walz are our best chance to move forward," Fairey wrote on his website. He offered the image for grassroots activism and linked readers to Head Count Inc., a nonprofit receiving proceeds from the festival, to "help fans register to vote and learn more about how to participate in upcoming elections."
Based in New York City, Head Count Inc. has about $14 million in revenues, according to its latest IRS tax filing.
The other nonprofit receiving proceeds from the festival is VoteRiders, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit based in Washington, D.C., with $7.8 million in revenues, based on its last tax filing.

The festival's "community partners" include Ben & Jerry's, the ice cream company whose co-founder Ben Cohen, a far-left activist, was a guest at the wedding of communist tech tycoon Neville Roy Singham and Jodie Evans, co-founder of CodePink, a fierce anti-Trump nonprofit that has received $1.33 million from Singham.

Another community partner is Red Emma's, a bookstore in Baltimore with a "Marxism, Socialism & Communism" tab on its website, selling "Teachings of Karl Marx" by communist philosopher Vladimir Lenin, "Black Marxism" and "Flowers for Marx."

The political leanings extend to younger performers. Musician Grandson, whose real name is Jordan Benjamin, has described using his platform to advance climate advocacy, voter registration and youth empowerment through his XX Resistance Fund. In a September 2020 interview, he praised Biden’s policy platform and made his electoral preference explicit: "We should elect that dude."

At the festival, he blasted "the AI apocalypse" and sang from a trademark song celebrating the self-immolation of a U.S. service member, Aaron Bushnell, in 2024 at the Embassy of Israel in Washington, D.C., protesting Israel's military response to the Oct. 7, 2023, attack by Hamas.
"Martyrdom is meditation, self-immolation," the musician sang, bouncing on stage.
Bruce Springsteen performs during the opening of the Obama Presidential Center in the Jackson Park neighborhood of Chicago June 18, 2026.  (Talia Sprague/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

At Power to the People, the concept of "solidarity" comes with a VIP upgrade. The festival pairs its message of collective action with a familiar concert-business model: tiered admission, exclusive viewing areas and premium hospitality. Fans can choose between People’s Park lawn admission, People’s Pavilion access and the Solidarity Circle VIP package, which offers reserved seating, expedited entry and an "exclusive VIP deck with premium bar and food available for purchase."

The top-tier "Robinhood Package," branded a "VIP SUPER SUITE," adds an exclusive suite, a dedicated viewing area at the second stage and an elevated balcony advertised as offering "the very best view of the stage and the festival." Buyers also receive a commemorative poster and laminate, a phone-charging station and a "VIP host with concierge service for bar/food available for purchase." Even at the highest tier, the advertised refreshments cost extra.

Organizers say the premium packages serve a charitable purpose, but the website uses differing descriptions of the donation pledge. Its overview promises a portion of all ticket proceeds and "100% of the net proceeds from VIP tickets" to VoteRiders and Head Count.
The package descriptions instead promise "all proceeds from VIP sales" to nonprofits supporting human rights and social justice.

The commercial offerings extend beyond the venue. The festival’s website promotes a paid membership with its livestream partner, MS NOW, advertising access to "daily live interactions and Q&As" with personalities including Democratic-aligned hosts Rachel Maddow, Jen Psaki, Al Sharpton and Joe Scarborough and Jen Psaki, a former Biden spokeswoman.
Alongside calls for "grassroots organizing" and "mutual aid," the event offers a marketplace of upgraded access, media subscriptions and "hospitality."
Back on stage with the Neighborhood Kids, the hip-hop artists continued their blast of ICE and pumped their fists in the air to inspire the concertgoers. "Power to the people!" they shouted.
"Rest in peace to all the martyrs," one member of the group yelled. "Free the world! Free Palestine! Free Congo! Free Armenia! Free Sudan! And free everywhere in the world from Western imperialism."
"And we got merch in that tent!" the member of the group continued, pointing toward the "Freedom Village," as another yelled "¡Viva la revolución!"

title: Newsom slaps 25% tax on private detention centers in sweeping pushback against key Trump policy
summary: Gavin Newsom signed a 25% tax on private detention centers in California, targeting every ICE facility in the state and their profits directly.
story: Hans von Spakovsky, senior fellow with Advancing American Freedom, believes the policy will bottleneck available space for ICE detentions.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a bill earlier this week that would impose a 25% tax on private detention centers, a policy that would apply to all the facilities that partner with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in the Golden State.
"If we can’t kick out private facilities, we’ll go after their profits," Newsom said in a press release.

The move, which Newsom hailed as a way to push back against President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown and what he sees as the practice of privatizing federal enforcement, is raising concerns among immigration experts who believe the increased tax could force the government to explore alternative sites less suited to housing detainees.
It also poses questions about what would happen if all eight of ICE's detention centers chose to suspend operations in California.
CITIZENS BANK CUTS TIES WITH ICE PRISON CONTRACTORS AFTER MONTHS OF ACTIVIST PRESSURE
Gov. Gavin Newsom speaks March 26, 2025, in Los Angeles. (Frazer Harrison/WireImage)
That’s the view of Hans von Spakovsky, senior legal fellow and an immigration expert with Advancing American Freedom, a conservative-leaning think tank.

"It's very clear that there's only one purpose to this California gigantic tax increase, and that is to make sure that the federal government cannot find any private property owners, any private contractors in California that are willing to lease space to the federal government," Spakovsky said in an interview with Fox News Digital.

"The alternative for the federal government is to look at all the different federal properties that the government actually owns out there, over which neither Newsom nor anybody else in California can impose any kind of tax, and see if any of those federal facilities can be converted to being a detention facility."
Spakovsky explained that could mean repurposing warehouses or office space.

The newly minted law, AB 1633, is among 20 bills that Newsom signed Tuesday. In its current form, the 25% tax applies to the gross income of any private detention center and applies to federal, state and local contract recipients.

Revenue from the bill will go to a Due Process for All Fund, designated for immigration-related services, according to the bill’s language. Now that AB 1633 has been signed into law, it will go into effect July 1, 2028.
Newsom also signed a handful of other restrictions.
ICE EYES $20M PURCHASE OF ELECTRIC SHOCK GLOVES AS HOCHUL WARNS OF LEGAL CONSEQUENCES

Gov. Gavin Newsom speaks during a news conference about new funding for homelessness and mental health efforts and criticized President Trump in San Francisco Jan. 16, 2026. (Tayfun Coskun/Anadolu via Getty Images)
"We’re also banning the Orwellian practice of using shock gloves in enforcement activity as well as further protecting access to our court system," Newsom said.
"We may not be able to dictate federal immigration policy, but we can make clear that activities taking place in California will be subject to California law."
Despite Newsom’s framing, Spakovsky believes the governor will affect federal immigration law enforcement by limiting the overall space it has to operate.

He pointed to reporting from Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) that details its detention needs. He explained that the government relies on private contractors, at least partially, to avoid the costs of building their own facilities.
"If you look at that report, currently ICE has about enough detention space for about 66,000 aliens. OK, that's the full size of the federal government's detention capacity," Spakovsky said.
If an entire state’s private detention contractors decided the tax is too high, ICE’s overall capacity could shrink.
California is home to eight ICE detention centers, according to reporting from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). All of them are privately operated.

The GEO Group, a corrections company, owns five facilities. Imperial Valley Gateway Center LLC, a local detention company, owns one more. Two more were purchased by DHS in July but are run by CoreCivic, a prison company, and have contracts through 2027 and 2029.

Although the bill won’t go into effect until 2028, in Trump’s last year of his second term, Spakovsky believes the government might begin evaluating where else it can find partnerships to meet its detention needs sooner rather than later.
ICE MAKES NATIONWIDE ARRESTS OF ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS, MURDERERS, PEDOPHILES IN HOLIDAY BLITZ

California Gov. Gavin Newsom listens during a news conference about fentanyl seizures and border security at Montgomery-Gibbs Executive Airport Feb. 2, 2026, in San Diego. (K.C. Alfred/The San Diego Union-Tribune via Getty Images)

"Look, if I was the federal government and I couldn't find enough federal properties in California to do this, I would then go into neighboring friendlier states that I could quickly transport aliens I've detained, and I would lease and rent facilities there.

"I'd go to Arizona. I'd potentially go to Nevada. I'd go to other states where they might be eager for federal government money and the increased employment from private contractors hiring people to work on these facilities."

title: Mac malware can hide commands in your iCloud calendar
summary: MacSync malware hides malicious commands inside iCloud calendar events to download additional payloads onto infected Macs without raising suspicion.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

You probably use your calendar to keep track of appointments, birthdays and the occasional reminder you immediately snooze. Hackers apparently see another possibility. Security researchers have uncovered a new version of MacSync malware that can use a public iCloud calendar event as part of its infection chain. Hidden inside the calendar data are commands that help download more malware onto a Mac.

The calendar itself does not suddenly infect your computer because someone sent you an invitation. The attack starts earlier, usually after someone downloads and runs a malicious app. Still, the iCloud trick shows how attackers can hide parts of an attack behind familiar services many of us trust. Once MacSync gets inside, it can go after a lot more than your calendar. Here's how MacSync works, what it can steal and the steps you can take to protect your Mac.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways AI can help you get better healthcare.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class Get Better Healthcare with AI has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways AI can help you prepare for appointments, remember important details, understand complicated medical information, research prescription questions and organize your next steps. No technical experience is needed.
Plus, recordings of all our past classes are available, including How to Stop Spam, Phone Security and Financial Protection, each with a free downloadable checklist.
Watch the free replays and get your checklists at CyberGuyLive.com
THOUSANDS OF HACKED SITES TRICK YOU INTO INSTALLING MALWARE
Researchers found that one MacSync infection chain used commands hidden inside a public iCloud calendar event to help download additional malware. (Apple)
What is MacSync malware?

MacSync is an information-stealing malware family targeting macOS. Earlier versions shared similarities with the Atomic macOS Stealer, better known as AMOS. Researchers say MacSync has since developed additional capabilities of its own. Kaspersky says the malware first appeared on the dark web in 2025 under the name Mac.c. Its creators later renamed it MacSync. Researchers first spotted this newest version in the wild in September 2026.

MacSync operates under a malware-as-a-service model. That means different criminals can use the malware while choosing their own methods for getting it onto someone's Mac. Attackers have previously spread MacSync through social engineering and ClickFix-style attacks, where a bogus message tells someone to copy and run a command. Criminals have also disguised it as free software, cracked applications and unfamiliar new apps. We've seen similar tricks before. In one Mac campaign, fake CAPTCHA instructions convinced users to paste commands into Terminal, which then installed information-stealing malware.
How hackers can abuse iCloud calendars

Here's where this latest version gets particularly sneaky. Kaspersky found one MacSync infection chain where a downloader connected to a public iCloud calendar. Instead of using the calendar to schedule anything, the attackers placed malicious commands inside the event description. The malware then feeds that calendar information into the Mac's Zsh command-line shell.
FAKE CHROME UPDATE SCAM COULD INFECT YOUR COMPUTER
The new MacSync backdoor disguises itself as Finder while using persistence techniques designed to keep it running after a Mac restarts. (Apple)

Most of the calendar text produces errors because the Mac does not recognize normal calendar information as commands. However, when it reaches the malicious instructions placed after the event's description field, those commands can run. They ultimately download a compressed archive from iCloud containing another malicious app. That app then starts another stage of the infection.

Think of the calendar as a hiding place for instructions. The attacker still needs to get malicious software running on the Mac first. However, using Apple's infrastructure during the infection chain can make the activity look less suspicious. Importantly, Kaspersky says at least one sample pointed to a public iCloud calendar. Other samples used attacker-controlled servers instead.
A fake crypto wallet helped spread MacSync

Researchers also found attackers disguising MacSync as a fake cryptocurrency wallet called Toria. The criminals went beyond creating a download page. Kaspersky says they built a dedicated website for the nonexistent wallet and promoted it on X and Telegram.

That is a good reminder that a polished website or active social media account tells you very little about whether software deserves your trust. Crypto owners appear to be an especially attractive target because stealing wallet data or browser extension information can quickly lead to stolen funds. However, you do not need to own cryptocurrency to have something MacSync wants.
What MacSync can steal from your Mac

Once installed, the information-stealing portion of MacSync searches through a wide range of sensitive data. Researchers say it can target browser history, cookies, saved logins and passwords. It also searches for crypto wallet extension data, cryptocurrency wallet applications and Telegram information.

MacSync can collect the Mac user's login information and Keychain file. It also gathers system details including installed apps, running processes, hardware information and the device model. Developers and more advanced users face additional exposure because the malware searches configuration files for SSH, ZSH, AWS, Kubernetes and Git. It can also collect Zsh and Bash command histories. For the average Mac owner, the takeaway is simpler. If malware gets access to saved passwords or browser data, an attacker may gain another route into your online accounts.
The new MacSync backdoor raises the stakes

Kaspersky also discovered a separate backdoor component written in Objective-C. It disguises itself as Finder, the file-management app built into macOS. The malware tries several methods to stay on the Mac after a restart. These include a LaunchAgent, changes to the .zshrc configuration file and modifications to global Git hooks. It can also terminate several macOS notification processes. Kaspersky says this prevents the system from notifying the user about the new LaunchAgent. From there, attackers can send instructions to the infected machine.

Researchers found commands designed to deploy a browser extension, replace an installed Ledger wallet app and collect additional system information or files. Most of those commands ultimately execute AppleScript supplied by the attacker's command-and-control server. Kaspersky inferred what the individual commands do from their names and the status messages they send because researchers did not have the AppleScript payloads themselves. That limitation is important. Researchers can see what the backdoor appears designed to accomplish, but they did not observe every possible server-delivered script.
One MacSync command remains a mystery

Researchers also found a command called live_browser. That command downloads and executes a component called sn_relay. Kaspersky says its exact contents and purpose remain unknown. Based on the command's name and messages sent back to the server, researchers suspect attackers may use it for some form of man-in-the-middle attack against browser traffic. Kaspersky has not confirmed exactly how that function works. That unanswered question shows why malware research often changes as investigators obtain more samples.
Why Mac users keep getting tricked

Macs include built-in security protections, but many recent attacks focus on persuading the person sitting in front of the screen to bypass those protections. ClickFix attacks are a perfect example. A website may tell you something went wrong and provide a command that supposedly fixes the problem. In reality, you may end up launching malware yourself. We've previously reported on Shamos malware, another Mac threat that used bogus troubleshooting instructions to trick people into running commands in Terminal. The same basic lesson applies here. Be suspicious whenever a website asks you to open Terminal, paste a command or enter your Mac administrator password to install an unfamiliar program.
Mac malware increasingly targets familiar tools

MacSync fits a pattern we've been tracking for a while. Attackers often disguise malicious software as something useful or familiar, whether that means a fake app, a bogus utility or software promoted through social media. In this case, researchers found one infection chain that used Apple's iCloud infrastructure to help deliver additional malware. That does not mean opening iCloud Calendar puts your Mac at risk. The bigger warning comes earlier in the attack. Be cautious when an unfamiliar app asks for your administrator password or a website tells you to open Terminal and run a command.
MacSync can imitate legitimate-looking macOS prompts to trick users into entering an administrator password or continuing with a malicious app. (Kaspersky)
Apple says macOS has built-in protections against these attacks

According to Apple, macOS includes several layers designed to help prevent malicious software from running, including Gatekeeper, XProtect and Apple's notarization system for software downloaded outside the Mac App Store. Apple recommends the Mac App Store as the safest place to get Mac software. For apps downloaded elsewhere, Apple says macOS uses protections such as notarization and XProtect to detect known malware and block it from running.

On macOS 26.4 and later, Apple added protections aimed more directly at attacks that try to trick people into pasting commands into Terminal. Terminal paste protection can show a warning when text is pasted into Terminal from common attack sources such as web browsers, messaging apps and other communication software. Apple says XProtect can also inspect activity that starts from pasted commands, including in third-party terminal apps. It can check related network activity against Apple's Safe Browsing Service and block behavior associated with known malware techniques.

Apple also says macOS 26.4 and later can scan AppleScript and JavaScript for Automation scripts using XProtect. If a script matches a known malicious signature, macOS can block it and alert the user. Safari adds another layer of protection. According to Apple, Fraudulent Website Warning can alert users when a website is suspected of phishing or distributing malware, while Apple Safe Browsing is designed to block malicious domains associated with attacks.

Apple also stresses that social engineering remains a major part of attacks like these. Scammers may try to persuade people to download software or paste malicious commands themselves. Apple recommends downloading software only from sources you trust and keeping your Mac updated with the latest available software and security fixes.
8 ways to protect your Mac from MacSync malware
MacSync relies heavily on getting someone to run a malicious app at the beginning of the attack. That gives you several opportunities to stop it.

A legitimate website rarely needs you to copy an unfamiliar command into Terminal to prove you're human, repair a browser problem or complete a download. Apple says macOS 26.4 and later can warn some users when commands copied from places such as websites, messages or email are pasted into Terminal. XProtect can also block activity associated with known malicious commands and techniques.

Whenever possible, get software through the Mac App Store or directly from a developer's official website. Apple recommends the Mac App Store as the safest place to get Mac software. For apps downloaded elsewhere, macOS uses protections including Gatekeeper, notarization and XProtect to help identify and block malicious software. Be especially cautious with cracked software, free copies of paid apps and unfamiliar programs promoted through social media.

MacSync's infostealer asks the user for an administrator password and adapts its prompt to match the app it is impersonating. If an unfamiliar app unexpectedly asks for your password, stop and verify why before entering anything.

Strong antivirus software can help detect malicious downloads and known malware before they compromise your Mac. It can also give you another layer of protection when a convincing scam gets past your first line of defense.
