title: Is your personal data changing what you pay online?
summary: The FTC proposed a new enforcement policy on personalized pricing, warning companies that hide how personal data shapes the prices shoppers see.
story: Jessica Lachs, DoorDash's chief analytics officer, says the company's latest Cheeseburger Index highlights just how dramatically restaurant prices can vary from one local economy to another.

Retailers and the companies working behind the scenes can collect information about where you are, what you search for, what you buy and how you behave online. The FTC says pricing systems can use personal data to estimate how much an individual consumer may be willing to spend. That concern is now getting serious attention in Washington. On Aug. 19, 2026, the Federal Trade Commission published a proposed enforcement policy statement aimed at personalized pricing.

The FTC says it cannot ban the practice in every situation, but companies that fail to clearly tell consumers how personal data affects the prices they see could violate federal consumer protection law. So, could the information companies collect about you actually change the price, discount or product you see? Here's what the research shows and what you can do before your next online purchase.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways AI can help you get better healthcare.
MARYLAND MOVES TO BAN SURVEILLANCE PRICING IN GROCERY STORES

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Get Better Healthcare With AI, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com
Data brokers can collect personal information from multiple sources and build profiles that companies may use to better understand consumers. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Dynamic pricing and personalized pricing work differently

You've probably encountered dynamic pricing already. Dynamic pricing adjusts prices based on broader conditions such as supply, demand, available inventory, time or location. Rideshare fares may rise when lots of people need cars at once. Airline tickets and hotel rooms can also change as availability and demand shift. That does not mean every shopper will always see the exact same dynamic price.

Timing, location and other market conditions can change quickly. Personalized pricing is different because information about a particular consumer helps determine the price or offer that person receives. That means two people looking for the same product could potentially receive different offers because of information connected to them.

There's also price steering. A retailer may leave the actual prices alone while changing the order of the products shown to you. FTC research found that pricing tools can use consumer data to give certain products more prominent placement, including potentially showing higher-priced products first. The FTC says consumers generally expect prices to change because of supply and demand. What can come as a surprise is a price influenced by someone's browsing habits, buying history or other personal information.
What companies can potentially learn about you
FTC research into surveillance pricing found that third-party pricing companies can use surprisingly detailed information when helping retailers tailor prices, promotions or product rankings.
That information can include:

Your approximate or precise locationBrowsing patterns and historyShopping and purchase historyProducts left in an online cartDemographic informationThe time, location or channel used to make a purchaseYour behavior and preferences on a websiteEven your mouse movements on a webpage
Your approximate or precise location
Browsing patterns and history
Shopping and purchase history
Products left in an online cart
Demographic information
The time, location or channel used to make a purchase
Your behavior and preferences on a website
Even your mouse movements on a webpage

The FTC found that the pricing intermediaries it examined worked with at least 250 clients selling goods and services ranging from groceries to clothing. The FTC's research also found that companies can combine first-party information with data from outside sources. Those sources can include loyalty programs, reservation systems, e-commerce platforms and data brokers. That does not show that every one of those clients charges individualized prices. It does show that technology exists to combine detailed consumer information and use it to influence prices, discounts and which products shoppers see.
A 2026 rideshare test found big price differences

A newer investigation brings the Uber example much closer to today. In June 2026, Consumer Reports published results from a months-long study of Uber and Lyft pricing. The investigation used 174 volunteers who checked more than 40 routes across the U.S. For the 30 virtual routes in its analysis, Consumer Reports found a median gap of 42.4% between the lowest and highest price groups.

On some routes, people checking the same trip within minutes of one another received several different prices. Consumer Reports designed the study to reduce the effects of time-based pricing by having volunteers check routes at roughly the same time. However, the investigation could not control for every factor inside Uber's and Lyft's pricing systems, including driver supply, estimated arrival times, traffic, routing differences and network delays.

Uber and Lyft disputed Consumer Reports' conclusions. Both companies said they do not use personal data to personalize base fares and do not engage in behavioral or surveillance pricing. So, the study shows that riders can receive significantly different prices for similar trips checked around the same time. It does not prove those price differences were caused by personal data.
WHAT YOUR INTERNET PROVIDER, WEBSITES AND ADVERTISERS SEE
Comparing the same item across apps, websites and retailers can help you spot price differences before you buy. (Anna Barclay/Getty Images)
Shoppers have also seen different grocery prices online

Online groceries have produced another eye-opening example. In December 2025, Consumer Reports, Groundwork Collaborative and More Perfect Union reported that nearly three-quarters of the grocery items they tested on Instacart were offered at different prices to different shoppers. The investigation involved 437 shoppers across four U.S. cities.

Some items showed differences of as much as 23% between the lowest and highest prices. Researchers also found that totals for identical baskets varied by an average of about 7%. Using an Instacart figure for how much a household of four spends on groceries, the researchers estimated that a similar difference over a year could amount to roughly $1,200.

Instacart strongly disputed that annual extrapolation and said the limited tests should not be treated as though a household would continually pay higher prices throughout an entire year. The company also said the pricing tests were randomized and did not use personal information, demographics, shopping history or individual behavior to decide who received each price.

Instacart ended the item price tests in December 2025. The company now says customers shopping for the same item at the same store location at the same time will see the same item price. So, the investigation showed that Instacart shoppers could receive different prices during those tests. It did not prove that Instacart used personal profiles to select those prices.
Online price personalization goes back years

Researchers were finding customized shopping experiences long before today's AI-powered pricing systems. In 2014, Northeastern University researchers studied 16 major retail and travel websites and found evidence of price discrimination or personalized search results on nine of them. CheapTickets and Orbitz offered reduced hotel prices to members. Expedia and Hotels.com steered some users toward more expensive hotels. Home Depot and Travelocity personalized search results for mobile users.

Priceline personalized the order of hotel search results based on a user's history of clicks and purchases. However, the researchers said those different result orders did not correlate with price, so they did not classify that Priceline example as price steering. The researchers also emphasized that most of their experiments on the 16 sites did not uncover price steering or price discrimination.

Then, in 2015, ProPublica found that The Princeton Review charged different prices for an online SAT tutoring package depending on a customer's ZIP Code. Prices for its Premier package ranged from $6,600 to $8,400. ProPublica found that people living in ZIP Codes with larger Asian populations were 1.8 times as likely to be offered a higher price, regardless of income.

The Princeton Review said its pricing was based on the costs of running its business and competitive conditions in each market. It said its prices were set by geographic region rather than a customer's race. That example was geographic pricing rather than a retailer setting a unique price for each individual shopper. It still shows how data connected to where someone lives can lead different groups of consumers to receive different prices.
13 ways to reduce personalized tracking when you shop

There is no guaranteed trick for getting the lowest online price. However, you can reduce some of the information retailers, data brokers and tracking companies can connect to you while giving yourself more ways to compare offers.

Look at a product while signed out before logging into a retailer or loyalty account. Then compare the price or promotion after signing in. A difference does not automatically mean personalized pricing. Membership discounts and other promotions can also explain a change. Still, comparing both views gives you more information before you buy.

If you do not need a retailer account, consider checking out as a guest. That keeps the purchase from automatically becoming another entry in a logged-in shopping history. Guest checkout does not make you anonymous. A retailer may still receive information such as your email address, payment details, shipping address, browser data or device information.

When a website gives you the choice, reject optional advertising and tracking cookies. The site may still need essential cookies for things such as your shopping cart, security and payment. Rejecting optional cookies mainly reduces some tracking and advertising activity.

Retailers are only one source of personal information. Data brokers and people ssearch companies collect information from numerous sources and combine it into profiles. FTC research found that pricing systems can incorporate third-party data, including information from data brokers. Reducing what's available through those companies may shrink one part of your broader data footprint. It does not guarantee a lower price or prevent a retailer from using information it collects directly from you. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.
HOW SCAMMERS BUILD A PROFILE ON YOU USING DATA BROKERS
Online retailers can collect information about how you browse and shop, which may help shape the prices, promotions and products you see. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

A private browsing window generally creates a separate browsing session that does not use the normal session history and most existing cookies from your regular browsing window. It does not make you anonymous. Websites may still see information such as your IP address and information you provide directly. The FTC specifically points to private browsing as one step consumers might use when trying to avoid higher personalized prices.

Look for choices such as Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information, Your Privacy Choices or controls for targeted advertising. The options available depend on the retailer and the privacy laws that apply where you live.

Review which shopping apps can access your precise location. If an app does not need your exact location, consider switching to approximate location or turning location access off. Keep in mind that websites and apps may still estimate your general location from other information, including your IP address.

Your phone may let you limit how apps track activity across other apps and websites. Turning off unnecessary tracking can reduce some third-party data collection. It will not stop a retailer from using information you provide directly through its own app, website or account. For step-by-step instructions on iPhone and Android, see our guide to improving your digital privacy.

Cookies can help websites recognize the same browser when you return. Clearing them can remove some of those stored identifiers. However, other tracking methods may still recognize your device, and signing back into an account reconnects your activity to that account.

Before making an expensive purchase, check the retailer's website and app. Then compare the same product with other sellers. Any difference you find may have a simple explanation, but comparison shopping gives you a better picture of the available prices.

For products supported by price-history services, check whether today's deal really is lower than recent prices. A retailer's sale banner only tells you what it wants to advertise. Historical pricing can give you additional context before you buy.
A lower price may require a loyalty membership, subscription, automatic renewal or another commitment. Make sure the offer actually saves you money after those conditions are included.

A VPN can hide the public IP address assigned by your internet provider and replace it with the address of the VPN server. That can make your IP-based location appear different. The FTC specifically lists VPN use as something consumers might try when they are concerned about personalized prices. A VPN cannot erase your retailer account, purchase history, cookies or location information that an app already has permission to access. Websites may also use other signals to recognize you. For the best VPN software, see my expert review of the best VPNs for browsing the web privately on your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.
Kurt's key takeaways

What gets my attention here is how much information can now go into deciding what we see when we shop online. We do not have evidence that every retailer is quietly setting a different price for each person, and seeing two different prices does not automatically prove personal data caused the change. What we do know is that companies have technology capable of using location, browsing behavior, shopping history and other information to shape prices, discounts and product rankings.

My advice is to compare prices before you buy, limit tracking you do not need and avoid assuming the first offer on your screen is the best one available. The less unnecessary information you hand over, the less there is to feed into a detailed profile about how you shop.
Would you change where you shop if you learned a retailer was using your personal data to decide what price or offer you see? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Apple's $250M Siri settlement: How to claim up to $95
summary: The $250 million Apple Siri AI settlement is now accepting claims, with eligible iPhone owners potentially receiving up to $95 per device.
story: Bernstein managing editor and senior analyst Mark Newman speaks on the future of Apple intelligence after the release of their new Siri AI on 'The Claman Countdown.'

If you bought one of Apple's AI-ready iPhones because you expected the smarter Siri Apple had been talking about, check when you purchased it. You could have some money coming your way. A proposed $250 million Apple Siri settlement now has an open claims process for qualifying iPhone owners.

The case centers on allegations that consumers bought certain iPhones expecting Siri features powered by Apple Intelligence that they did not receive during the period covered by the lawsuit. Apple denies the allegations and says it did nothing improper or unlawful.

The amount may sound small next to the price of a new iPhone, but filing a claim could put as much as $95 per eligible device back in your pocket. There are a few important catches, though, including exactly which iPhone you bought and when you bought it.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways AI can help you get better healthcare.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Get Better Healthcare With AI, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com
8 BIGGEST THINGS WE LEARNED FROM APPLE'S 2026 EVENT
Apple’s proposed Siri settlement covers eligible purchases of the iPhone 15 Pro and iPhone 15 Pro Max made during the settlement period. (Anna Barclay/Getty Images)
Why Apple agreed to a $250 million Siri settlement

The lawsuit is called Landsheft, et al. v. Apple Inc. and is pending in federal court in Northern California. The plaintiffs alleged that Apple promoted certain Siri features powered by Apple Intelligence, leading buyers to expect capabilities that were not delivered during the class period. Apple denies those allegations. The company agreed to put $250 million into a settlement fund rather than continue litigating the case. The agreement received preliminary court approval on July 17, 2026. The court has scheduled a final approval hearing for Feb. 24, 2027. That timing is especially interesting because Apple finally began rolling out its long-awaited Siri AI beta with iOS 27 in September 2026.

The updated Siri can use personal context from information on your device, handle follow-up questions and take more actions inside supported apps. We recently took a closer look at iOS 27 and the new Siri AI features.
Which iPhones qualify for the Apple Siri settlement?

The settlement covers seven models: iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max, iPhone 16, iPhone 16e, iPhone 16 Plus, iPhone 16 Pro and iPhone 16 Pro Max. The regular iPhone 15 and iPhone 15 Plus are excluded. Owning one of those eligible models alone does not qualify you. You must be the original purchaser and live in the United States. You also must have purchased the phone in the United States between June 10, 2024, and March 29, 2025. The purchase had to be for personal or business use rather than resale. There is another important requirement. When you submit the claim, you must confirm that you expected to receive certain Siri Apple Intelligence features when you bought the device and did not receive those features as expected. Businesses can qualify, too. The official settlement site has separate filing options for individuals and organizations that purchased eligible devices for business use.
How much could you receive from the Apple settlement?

The settlement sets the payment at $25 per eligible device, but the final amount can change. If fewer valid claims come in, the payment may increase to as much as $95 per eligible device. If more claims come in, the payment can fall below $25. Administrative costs, approved attorneys' fees and other court-approved expenses also come out of the $250 million fund. You can submit a claim for each eligible device you purchased. That could make the payout more meaningful for someone who bought multiple qualifying iPhones during the class period. However, nobody knows the final payment yet. The settlement administrator has to count and validate the claims before that figure can be determined.
12 BIGGEST APPLE WWDC 2026 TAKEAWAYS YOU NEED TO KNOW
Eligible iPhone owners could receive $25 per device, with payments potentially reaching up to $95 depending on the number of valid claims. (iStock)
How to file your Apple Siri settlement claim

The claims period officially opened on Sept. 21, 2026. You can file through the official Smartphone AI Settlement website at smartphoneaisettlement.com. The deadline is Dec. 21, 2026. The claim form asks for your contact information and information that can confirm your eligible purchase or ownership. You also need to certify that you expected the covered Siri Apple Intelligence features when you purchased your iPhone and did not receive them as expected. I would have your iPhone's serial number handy before you start. On your iPhone, open Settings, tap General, then tap About. Your serial number appears near the top of that screen. You can press and hold it to copy it. The settlement site also says you may find the serial number on the phone's original packaging or purchase documentation.
Do you need to have received a settlement notice?

The official site says people who received an email or postcard can file a claim. It also says people who believe they belong to the settlement class can submit a valid claim even if they did not receive a notice. So, I would not automatically write this off because nothing showed up in your mailbox or inbox. Instead, compare your purchase with the eligibility requirements and use the official settlement site. Be careful with links arriving through unexpected texts or emails. Large settlements often attract phishing attempts because scammers know people are looking for claim information. I recommend going directly to the official settlement website rather than clicking a claim link in an unsolicited message.
When will iPhone owners actually get paid?

Do not expect a payment right after submitting your claim. The court has scheduled its final approval hearing for Feb. 24, 2027. The judge will decide whether to give the settlement final approval. Appeals could delay the process further. The official settlement administrator says payments will be processed after the settlement becomes effective, assuming the court approves it and any appeals are resolved. In other words, filing now secures your claim before the deadline. The check or digital payment could come much later.
YOU COULD GET PAID FROM GOOGLE’S ANDROID DATA LAWSUIT
Claims for Apple’s $250 million Siri settlement must be submitted by Dec. 21, 2026. (Amazon)
What if you do nothing?

If you qualify but do nothing, you will not receive a settlement payment. You will also remain bound by the settlement if the court gives it final approval, which affects your ability to pursue your own case against Apple over the claims covered by this lawsuit. The deadline to request exclusion from the settlement or formally object is also Dec. 21, 2026. Anyone considering those options should read the official settlement notice carefully because the legal consequences differ from simply submitting a claim. CyberGuy reached out to Apple for additional comment but did not hear back before our deadline.
Kurt's key takeaways

Apple spent a lot of time building excitement around what Apple Intelligence would bring to Siri. If you bought one of these iPhones expecting those promised features, you may have been left waiting much longer than expected. Apple has now agreed to put $250 million into a settlement fund while continuing to deny the allegations. If your iPhone and purchase date qualify, I would take a few minutes to check your eligibility and file a claim. You could receive as much as $95 per device, depending on how many valid claims come in. This is also a good reminder to pay close attention when a company promotes upcoming software features as part of the reason to buy new hardware. What you are promised at launch and what you can actually use on day one may be very different.

title: The next connected device could be the shirt you're wearing
summary: ShareAScan turns T-shirts into scannable digital business cards with QR codes that link to profiles the owner can update anytime they choose.
story: Smart refrigerators, cars and computers can show ads after updates, raising privacy and ownership concerns, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson explains.

A T-shirt has always been able to tell you something about the person wearing it. Maybe it shows a favorite band, sports team or funny message. Now, it can potentially open an entire digital profile. That is the idea behind ShareAScan, a startup using QR code clothing to connect apparel and other physical products with digital content that can change over time.

Scan a code with your smartphone, and you can see whatever experience the owner has chosen to share. That might include text, photos, video, music, a portfolio, social content or information about a business. The shirt itself does not contain a battery, Bluetooth connection or hidden computer. The technology starts with a printed QR code and the web platform behind it. So, could the next connected device actually be something you wear?
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways AI can help you get better healthcare.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Get Better Healthcare With AI, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
EMPTY ENVELOPES IN YOUR MAILBOX? DO NOT SCAN THAT CODE
ShareAScan co-founders Kailey and Shara Zuckerman show off QR-enabled shirts designed to turn a quick scan into a digital connection. (ShareAScan)
How QR code clothing works

The basic idea is simple. ShareAScan prints a unique QR code on products such as T-shirts, hoodies, hats, mugs and other merchandise. A person scans the code using the camera already built into a smartphone. No special scanning app is required.

However, the interesting part happens behind that code. Instead of permanently tying the printed QR code to one piece of content, ShareAScan lets the owner change what appears later. The physical code stays the same while the digital experience behind it changes. For example, someone could use a shirt to share a portfolio at a conference and later update the content to promote a project or event.

The company describes its technology as a patent-pending platform connecting physical products with dynamic, user-controlled digital identities. Its September announcement says a single product can become a changing introduction, portfolio, personal message or business card. That makes the concept more interesting than simply printing a website address across your chest.
The idea recently made its way to the Emmys

ShareAScan was founded by sisters Shara and Kailey Zuckerman. Shara is a college student studying business, finance and artificial intelligence, while Kailey is still in high school. The company got a major dose of exposure this month when its QR merchandise was included in gift bags distributed around the 78th Emmy Awards. ShareAScan merchandise went into gift bags for nominees, presenters and performers. Still, the bigger story goes beyond an awards-show gift bag. It is another example of physical products gaining a digital layer that can change long after you buy them.
Your shirt could become a changing digital business card

There are plenty of ways people could use this. A business owner could wear a shirt that introduces a company. A creator could share recent work. Someone at a conference could use it as a digital introduction. Meanwhile, a musician could share new content or an organization could promote an event. Because the material behind the QR code can change, the same physical product can serve different purposes over time.

ShareAScan says purchases start at $19 and current customers do not pay an ongoing subscription fee. The company also tells CyberGuy that customers who buy under the current model will not later face a subscription charge even if its terms change for future customers. That gives the physical product something most ordinary clothing never had before: content that can keep changing after you take it home.
What happens when someone scans your shirt?

ShareAScan tells CyberGuy that scans are anonymous. The company says it collects no information about the scanner unless an owner's access restrictions require it to check whether that scanner is allowed to view the content.

If someone does not have permission, the company says that person simply does not receive access. ShareAScan also says it does not currently give the wearer scan analytics. In other words, wearing one of these products does not give you a dashboard showing who walked by and scanned your code. The company says owners can choose who gets access to their content and can completely delete their account and associated data.

However, there is still another side to privacy: what you decide to reveal. If you make your full name, workplace, photos, social accounts or other personal information publicly available, someone who scans you may learn quite a bit. That is why anyone using connected clothing should look at the experience from a stranger's point of view before wearing it in public.
QR CODE EMAIL SCAM TARGETS EMPLOYEE REVIEWS
A QR-enabled ShareAScan hoodie shows how clothing can become a gateway to digital content that changes over time. (ShareAScan)
Can a ShareAScan QR code send you to a malicious website?

This required an important clarification from the company. ShareAScan tells CyberGuy that its QR codes cannot point directly to an outside website. Instead, scanning the code first opens the experience hosted through its platform. However, content within that experience can include links. The company says it scans uploads for malicious links, phishing links, pornography and other inappropriate material. It also says people review flagged material.

ShareAScan acknowledges that its screening cannot catch everything. That makes its setup different from a random QR sticker that directly sends your browser to an unknown website. Even so, you should never treat every QR code as automatically safe simply because scanning has become second nature.

The FTC continues to warn about criminals using QR codes to send people to fake websites designed to steal passwords, financial information and other personal data. In a fresh warning published Sept. 3, the agency again advised people to inspect the destination before opening a QR link. So, the familiar security advice still applies whenever you pick up your phone to scan something.
ShareAScan requires users to be 18 or older

Connected clothing could naturally catch the attention of younger users, especially when it links fashion with social content. ShareAScan tells CyberGuy that account holders must be at least 18 years old.

At the same time, the company acknowledges that an age requirement cannot completely stop someone younger from trying to create an account. That makes conversations about public sharing especially important for families. A QR code someone wears outside can potentially expose information to people they have never met.
What happens after you wash the shirt?

A scannable shirt also has to hold up to everyday wear. ShareAScan says its QR codes have been tested through repeated washing and continue to scan after normal use. Of course, a QR code still needs to remain physically readable. Heavy damage, fading or distortion could eventually interfere with any printed code.

There is another longevity issue too. Unlike a normal graphic on a shirt, this feature depends on the online platform behind it. ShareAScan says it plans to keep the platform operating and has purchased insurance intended to help support continued operation. That is worth keeping in mind with any connected product that depends on a company's servers long after the initial purchase.
QR codes are becoming part of the physical world

QR codes are already everywhere, from tickets and restaurant tables to payment screens and packages. Now, they are starting to show up on the things we wear. ShareAScan takes that familiar technology and gives it a more personal use. Instead of linking to one fixed piece of information, the code can connect to content that the owner changes over time.

That means a sweatshirt could introduce your business at a conference, while a T-shirt could share your latest project, interests or something you simply want people to know about you. A quick scan could even become an easy way to start a conversation. But once your clothing can share information about you, it is worth thinking about exactly what you are putting out there. Anything you make public could potentially be seen by someone you have never met.
AI CHATBOT PRIVACY: WHAT YOUR AI MAY KNOW ABOUT YOU
A ShareAScan T-shirt puts the QR code front and center, letting someone open the digital experience linked to the clothing. (ShareAScan)
6 ways to use QR code clothing more safely
If clothing is going to become scannable, a few simple precautions can help you share without giving away too much.
Start with your public profile. Look at exactly what appears to someone who does not know you. Avoid exposing your home address, private phone number, personal email or other sensitive information.
Review who can access your content. ShareAScan says owners can limit access, so use those controls when you want to share something with a smaller group.
Create content specifically for public sharing. That can help you avoid giving strangers access to personal accounts filled with years of photos, posts or identifying information.

Treat QR codes like links. ShareAScan says it screens content on its platform, but QR codes in general can still lead to trouble. If anything asks for a password, payment information or other sensitive data unexpectedly, stop.
Look at the address your phone shows before opening a QR link. The FTC recommends checking for misspellings and switched letters that can signal an impersonation site.

Install and keep strong antivirus software active on your devices. It can help detect malicious links, phishing pages, dangerous downloads and other threats you may encounter after scanning a QR code. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com. Also, keep your phone's built-in security protections and software updates turned on too. No security tool can make every QR code safe, so always check where a code is taking you before entering passwords, payment information or other sensitive data.
Kurt's key takeaways

What I like about this idea is how simple it is. There is no battery, Bluetooth or complicated hardware inside the shirt. The QR code does the work, and the person wearing it can keep changing what people see after they scan. ShareAScan also says it has built in some useful controls. Scans are anonymous, owners can limit who sees their content and the code itself does not send you straight to an outside website. The company also says it checks uploaded content for malicious material. The bigger question is how much of yourself you want to make scannable. If your shirt becomes part of your digital identity, take a minute to look at exactly what a stranger could learn about you before you wear it out the door.
Would you wear a shirt that could turn a quick QR scan into a new connection? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com.

title: Malicious browser extensions can hijack AI assistants
summary: BragJack research reveals how a single malicious browser extension could hijack Gemini, Perplexity Comet and Edge AI agents with zero clicks.
story: CSIS cybersecurity expert Jim Lewis explains how AI is accelerating cyberattacks while cautioning that worst-case predictions about the technology may never materialize.

AI assistants are moving deeper into the browsers we use every day. They can summarize a webpage, explain what you are looking at and, in some cases, take action on websites for you. That convenience also gives these tools access that a normal webpage would never have. Now, security researcher Gal Weizman of Forever Security has shown how a malicious browser extension could potentially turn those powerful AI capabilities against you. His research, called BragJack, targeted Gemini Live in Chrome, Perplexity Comet, Microsoft Edge Actions, Opera Neon and Anthropic's Claude in Chrome. The findings resulted in more than $20,000 in bug bounties and two CVEs.

There is one important detail before you panic. The attack still required the malicious extension to be installed first. After that, Weizman demonstrated attacks that needed zero additional clicks from the victim. So how could one extension get that far inside the browser? It comes down to how these AI assistants are built.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways AI can help you get better healthcare.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Get Better Healthcare With AI, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
AI MALWARE CAN REWRITE ITSELF TO EVADE DETECTION
Gemini in Chrome can work across webpages, but researchers showed how a malicious extension could potentially abuse those deeper browser privileges. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How a malicious extension can reach your browser's AI

Weizman describes these AI systems as having a "brain" and a "body." The AI model works out what should happen. A privileged component inside the browser then carries out the request. Depending on the product, that privileged component might read webpage content, capture a screenshot or interact with a website. That setup becomes risky if something else inside the browser can manipulate the connection between those pieces. The proof-of-concept attacks relied heavily on Chromium's declarativeNetRequest, or DNR, system. Browser extensions can use DNR to modify how network requests work. That can include changing response headers or redirecting resources. Forever Security showed how those capabilities could let an extension interfere with web content trusted by a browser's AI features.
Chrome's Gemini flaw exposed files and screenshots

Chrome was one of the more striking examples. Google's Gemini side panel essentially has two pieces. Gemini handles the intelligence behind the request while Chrome provides the browser-level abilities needed to carry it out. Researchers found that Chrome already prevented extensions from directly injecting scripts into the Gemini page. However, the researchers discovered that an extension could still manipulate certain network requests used inside the Gemini experience. That gap allowed Weizman to demonstrate access to browser capabilities that the extension itself should never have received. According to the research, he could access local files, capture screenshots and obtain browser profile information. The researcher says the flaw also let him turn on the camera and microphone with zero clicks from the user. Google awarded the researchers a $7,000 bounty for reporting the vulnerability, which received the identifier CVE-2026-0628.

Google has since confirmed to CyberGuy that it has closed this specific attack path. A Google spokesperson told us, "Confirming we've released a patch in Chrome so this method no longer works on the Gemini side panel." That means the technique demonstrated by the researchers should no longer work against the Gemini side panel in an updated version of Chrome.
Perplexity Comet could take the attack further

Perplexity Comet raised a different concern because its AI agent can take actions inside websites. Weizman found that Comet's built-in agent trusted several Perplexity domains. One testing domain lacked the same extension protections used on the main Perplexity site. Normally, that testing address redirected elsewhere. The proof-of-concept used DNR to remove the redirect and load the page instead. That gave the extension a path to communicate with Comet's built-in agent. The demonstrated access included browsing history, screenshots and local files. Then things became more personal. Weizman demonstrated sending an instruction that told the agent to access Perplexity, summarize the victim's recent emails and send the information to another email address. The AI agent performed the browser actions using capabilities it already had.
Microsoft Edge had safeguards that researchers bypassed

Microsoft built safeguards into Edge to keep outside prompts from easily controlling what its AI agent could do. Researchers still found a way around them. Weizman discovered a timing flaw known as a race condition. In simple terms, his test extension could feed the AI a prompt and then quickly switch on its ability to take action before Edge finished checking whether the request should be allowed. That opened the door for the AI agent to carry out a command it should not have accepted. Microsoft tracked the flaw as CVE-2026-55945 and rated it medium severity. The company says Edge versions before 150.0.4078.48 were affected. Updating Edge closes this particular security hole.
Opera Neon and Claude in Chrome were vulnerable too

Forever Security also demonstrated related attacks against Opera Neon and Claude in Chrome. There is an important difference with Claude. Claude in Chrome is itself a browser extension, rather than a complete browser. The researcher found that a page on Claude's domain could send prompts to the extension's side panel. Another extension could manipulate that trusted page and force prompts into Claude. Forever Security says Anthropic awarded a bounty for the finding and classified it as medium severity. Opera Neon also allowed the proof-of-concept extension to reach its AI agent. According to the researcher, that access could force the agent to carry out instructions on websites. All five demonstrations were Chromium-based, which helped the researcher reuse the same basic attack approach.

We reached out to Google, Microsoft, Perplexity, Opera and Anthropic for comment on the research. Google responded with the update included above. Microsoft pointed us to its CVE-2026-55945 security advisory and said it had nothing further to share. We did not hear back from Perplexity, Opera or Anthropic before our deadline.
LOCK DOWN YOUR CHATGPT ACCOUNT BEFORE THE NEXT AI ATTACK
Perplexity Comet’s AI agent can take actions on websites, which is why the demonstrated attack could go beyond simply reading browser data. (Donato Fasano/Getty Images)
Prompt Forcing gives attackers another way to abuse AI

You may already have heard about prompt injection. That usually involves hiding malicious instructions in something an AI reads. Weizman calls this new approach Prompt Forcing. Here, the attacker does not need to hide instructions inside a webpage and hope the AI follows them. The attacker can force a complete prompt into the agent through a channel that the browser or assistant trusts. The AI can then turn that plain-English instruction into legitimate browser actions. That creates an interesting problem for security software. A suspicious program stealing an email may be easier to spot. An approved AI agent opening a website and clicking a button can look like normal browser activity. The published BragJack research describes proof-of-concept attacks and does not report that these techniques have been exploited in the wild. Still, the research shows how the security equation changes as AI agents receive deeper access to browsers and computers.
Why you should take another look at your browser extensions

The attack starts with something many of us barely think about anymore: a browser extension. CyberGuy has covered malicious extensions that pretended to be AI assistants, hijacked online accounts and even turned trusted extensions into data-stealing spyware. That makes extension cleanup one of the easiest steps you can take right now. Maybe you installed a coupon extension two years ago and forgot about it. Perhaps you tested an AI sidebar once and never opened it again. If you no longer need an extension, there is little reason to keep giving it access to your browser.
8 ways to protect yourself from malicious browser extensions

Browsers receive security fixes regularly, so install updates as soon as they become available. Google's response makes that especially relevant here. The company says it has already released the Chrome patch that blocks the Gemini side-panel method demonstrated by the researchers. Restart Chrome after an update if prompted so the newest version can finish installing.
Open your browser's extension manager and remove anything you do not recognize or no longer use. Here is the quickest way to check:
Chrome and Claude in Chrome: Click the three-dot menu → Extensions → Manage extensions → find the extension → Remove. Google confirms this path in its current Chrome instructions.
Microsoft Edge: Click the Extensions puzzle-piece icon → Manage extensions → find the extension → Remove.

Opera Neon: Open the Extensions area from the browser sidebar or menu → review your installed extensions → remove anything you no longer trust or use. Opera documents its extensions manager through the Extensions icon and menu.
Perplexity Comet: Open the browser's extensions manager and review imported or installed Chrome extensions. Comet supports Chrome extensions and can import them from Chrome.
Pro tip: If you are unsure about an extension, disable it first and research the developer before removing it.
THOUSANDS OF HACKED SITES TRICK YOU INTO INSTALLING MALWARE

Microsoft Edge includes AI tools that can act inside the browser, and researchers found a race condition that could force the agent to follow an attacker-controlled prompt. (Serene Lee/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)
Look carefully when an extension asks for broad access to websites or browser activity. The permission should make sense for what the extension actually does.
Some browsers let you decide whether an extension can run on every website or only certain sites. Give an extension the narrowest access it needs to work.
An extension that uses a familiar AI name may have no connection to the company behind that AI service. Check the publisher before installing it.

If your browser gives you the option to disable an AI assistant or agent you never use, consider turning it off. That reduces the number of powerful browser features available if another component gets compromised.

Strong antivirus software can help flag malicious downloads and suspicious activity connected to bad extensions. It adds another layer of protection if something slips past you. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com.
Do not install one because it sounds useful for five minutes. Every extension adds code and permissions to the browser you use for email, banking, shopping and other private activity.
Kurt's key takeaways

What gets my attention here is how much more powerful a bad browser extension can become when an AI agent enters the picture. We already knew extensions could spy on browsing or steal account data. This research shows a possible path to something with much broader privileges. There is also a practical takeaway. These demonstrations still required the attacker-controlled extension to get inside the browser first. Once it was there, however, the researcher showed that the attack could continue without another click from the victim. I would take five minutes and look through your extensions today. If you cannot remember why you installed one, find out what it does. If you stopped using it months ago, remove it. As browser AI grows more capable, the companies building these tools also need strong barriers between ordinary extensions and the privileged systems that let AI act for us.
Would you still let an AI assistant control parts of your browser if a malicious extension could potentially turn that access against you? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com.

title: Portland teen faces terrorism, attempted murder charges after school cafeteria chemical scare
summary: A 15-year-old Benson Polytechnic High School student faces 19 counts including domestic terrorism after allegedly mixing toxic chemicals in the cafeteria.
story: Multnomah County DA Nathan Vasquez demands school safety as he seeks an adult trial for a 15-year-old charged with attempted murder and domestic terrorism after a Portland school chemical incident. (Credit: Portland Police)

An Oregon high school cafeteria chemical scare that left a student in critical condition has escalated into a domestic terrorism and attempted murder case against the same teenager school staff rushed to save.

The 15-year-old Benson Polytechnic High School student faces 19 criminal counts after authorities said he brought chemicals from home and mixed them inside the Portland school Sept. 8, releasing toxic gases that endangered students and staff.
"Safety in our schools is not something that can be negotiated," Multnomah County District Attorney Nathan Vasquez said during an Oct. 2 news conference.
"That violence or the threat of violence in a school… it doesn't just stay in that building. It follows families home. It sits at the dinner table with them."
THREE SCHOOL SAFETY STEPS EVERY PARENT SHOULD KNOW BEFORE CLASSES BEGIN
Benson Polytechnic High School in Portland, Oregon, where authorities said a student mixed hazardous chemicals in the cafeteria Sept. 8, 2026. (Google Maps)

Investigators uncovered "concerning behaviors and statements" before the incident, including an interest in hazardous chemicals, explosives and violence, Portland Police Bureau Public Information Manager Mike Benner said.
MIDDLE SCHOOL STUDENT ARRESTED AFTER ALLEGEDLY STASHING HOMEMADE GUNS FOR ROBBERY PLOT: SHERIFF
Portland authorities discuss attempted murder and domestic terrorism charges against a 15-year-old Benson Polytechnic High School student during an Oct. 2, 2026, news conference. (Portland Police)

The teenager, whose name has not been released because of his age, faces 10 counts of attempted aggravated murder, one count of attempted first-degree murder, one count of attempted second-degree murder, one count of first-degree domestic terrorism and one count of second-degree domestic terrorism.
Additional charges include unlawfully manufacturing and possessing a destructive device, possessing a weapon in a public building, unlawfully using a weapon and recklessly endangering another person.
15-YEAR-OLD ACCUSED OF FIRING INTO CROWD DURING DEADLY SEATTLE MASS SHOOTING CLAIMS SELF-DEFENSE
The teen’s lawyers denied the allegations and said he is receiving treatment at an inpatient mental health facility, The New York Times reported.
Vasquez said his office would seek to move the case from juvenile court to adult court, emphasizing the safety of the students and staff.
"And I want to be clear, they're teenagers, but these are children, and they deserve a safe environment," he said.
But the prosecutor sharply criticized what he called a broader failing of Oregon’s juvenile system, which ends its oversight at age 25 even if the person still poses a danger to the public.
A Portland teenager faces attempted murder and domestic terrorism charges following a chemical incident at Benson Polytechnic High School. (Multnomah County District Attorney's Office)
"I think that that is wrong," Vasquez said, arguing that the cutoff fails to account for the danger someone convicted of multiple killings or domestic terrorism could still present.
"I'm looking at conduct and how dangerous that is and what I consider to be safe for the community going forward," he said.
INJURED LOUISIANA BOY HAILED A 'SUPERHERO' FOR SEEKING HELP DURING DEADLY STABBING RAMPAGE
The chemical incident unfolded shortly before 8:30 a.m. while numerous students and staff were near the teenager, Assistant Chief of Investigations Franz Schoening said.
Teachers and administrators moved students away as the school nurse began treating the teen before first responders arrived. He was taken to a hospital in critical condition but survived.
SUBSTITUTE TEACHER ARRESTED AFTER ALLEGEDLY TRIGGERING FALSE ACTIVE SHOOTER ALERTS AT 5 SCHOOLS: SHERIFF
"Those first few moments were critical in preventing further harm and lives being lost," Schoening said.
More than 100 students and staff were assessed after evacuating, and at least seven required medical care following the incident, he said.
DETROIT-AREA COUPLE ACCUSED OF THROWING EXPLOSIVE DEVICE WITH ALARMING 2-WORD MESSAGE INTO NEIGHBOR'S YARD

An empty cafeteria is pictured in this illustrative image. A chemical incident at Benson Polytechnic High School in Portland led to attempted murder and domestic terrorism charges against a student. (Craig F. Walker/The Denver Post via Getty Images)
Sgt. Jim DeFrain, who supervises the investigation and the Metropolitan Explosive Disposal Unit, said initial testing indicated the presence of hydrogen sulfide, a toxic gas.
An Oregon National Guard team agreed with that assessment. Samples were sent to an FBI laboratory for further testing, with results still pending at the time of the briefing, DeFrain said.
The FBI was also examining electronic equipment seized during searches.
Vasquez said the investigation remained open and that anyone else found to have criminal involvement could face charges.

"If we determine or find any links, if there are people that can be charged, this office will charge them," he said.

title: Florida TikTok creator lands in jail after allegedly turning women’s private data into posts
summary: Florida TikTok creator Mark Stephen Asea allegedly exposed women's private data in over 100 videos after gaining unauthorized access to their devices.
story: Cybersecurity and privacy attorney Leeza Garber discusses how hackers used Meta's A.I. chatbot to breach prominent social media accounts on ‘Fox Report.’

A Florida TikTok creator who calls himself a "demonologist" and "Grey Hat Hacker" is back behind bars after allegedly exposing women’s private information online and boasting that he could track their movements through their phones.

Mark Stephen Asea, 36, of Port St. Lucie, was booked into the St. Lucie County Jail Sept. 30 on a felony charge of offense against computer users. His bond was set at $35,000, according to sheriff’s office records.

The arrest revived a criminal case that had been closed months earlier. Asea was first arrested in April on stalking and computer-related allegations, but prosecutors dropped those charges in May before bringing a computer-access charge in September, court records show.
TIKTOK COUPLE CHARGED WITH ARSON AFTER HOUSE FIRE CAUSES $10K IN DAMAGE

Mark Stephen Asea, 36, was booked into the St. Lucie County Jail Sept. 30, 2026, on a charge of offense against computer users after prosecutors reopened his criminal case. (St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office)
The police affidavit describes two women who said their private information surfaced in Asea’s TikTok posts, including one who had trusted him to help with a computer problem.
In a video reviewed by a detective, Asea allegedly rattled off details about one woman’s devices and claimed to know her recent spending.
"Let’s talk about your actual password," he said, according to a transcript in the affidavit.
"How about we talk about the last 10 purchases you made online?"
The woman told investigators the password had been shared only in a closed TikTok group chat. Asea was not a member, she said, although she suspected he might have joined through a fake account.
Nobody in the chat had permission to share it outside the group, she told police. She also said she did not know how he would have obtained her phone identification number or banking information.
FBI INVESTIGATES AFTER SHINYHUNTERS HACKERS CLAIM THEFT OF AGENTS' PERSONAL DATA
Security experts warn exposed email addresses and phone numbers can fuel phishing and impersonation scams. (Annette Riedl/picture alliance via Getty Images)
For the second woman, the concerns began after what she described as a routine request for tech help.

She told police she allowed Asea to remotely access her computer in October 2025 to troubleshoot an application. Months later, she said, he claimed he had essentially placed a virus on the computer while she was in the bathroom, allowing him to view information without her knowledge.
She said she never authorized that access.
Then a photograph from a private Telegram message on her phone allegedly appeared in one of his TikTok posts.
Asea claimed in a comment that the image came from a WhatsApp exchange, according to the affidavit. But the woman provided investigators a screenshot showing the photograph in the Telegram message.

title: Terror cells inside foreign airlines 'certainly a possibility,' retired pilot warns
summary: Retired Air Force and Delta Air Lines pilot Buzz Patterson said terror cells could infiltrate foreign airlines after a FlyDubai copilot attacked a captain.
story: Retired Air Force Lt. Col. Buzz Patterson warned that terrorist cells could be lurking in international airlines, highlighting the need for vetting pilots, cabin crew and airport staff beyond current "self-reporting."

The man who once carried the nuclear football for former President Bill Clinton is sounding an alarm on potential terror cells inside foreign airlines after a FlyDubai copilot allegedly attacked the captain of an Israel-bound flight and sent the plane into a death-defying, aeronautics-defying dive.

"It’s possible that terror cells can exist inside airline companies – overseas, probably a lot easier than here, but it's certainly a possibility," retired Air Force Lt. Col. Buzz Patterson, a former Delta Air Lines pilot of 16 years, told Fox News Digital on Thursday. "And I think it is something that DOJ needs to take a... really good look at."

The warning came after a FlyDubai flight from the United Arab Emirates to Tel Aviv was forced to make an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, after the copilot attacked the captain mid-flight, reportedly with the crash ax. The flight was carrying 174 passengers and eight crew, and investigators are still probing the motive, including possible terrorism or mental health factors – both of which leave Patterson concerned for public safety, if not national security.
FORMER ISRAELI PM HAILS ‘HEROISM’ AFTER PASSENGERS HELP THWART ALLEGED COCKPIT ATTACK

Capt. Smit Machchhar, the Indian pilot who allegedly was attacked on a FlyDubai plane heading to Israel on Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026, was hailed by retired Lt. Col. Buzz Patterson as a "hero" for hitting the button to unlock the cockpit door during a stabbing attack. (Israel Foreign Ministry)

"If you’ve got somebody that’s, you know, radicalized and if he doesn’t tell his company or his buddies, you’re never gonna know," Patterson said, noting most protocols rely on "self-reporting your activities." "So that's part of the problem, I think, that we're going to start seeing pop up in airline profiles and pilot profiles is we have a lot of people out there that probably shouldn't be flying airplanes."
The warning comes amid the revelations that a crash ax found behind the copilot chair in the Boeing 737 was used to bludgeon the pilot in an effort to commandeer the aircraft.

"Every 737, and that's what I flew my entire life of all the different models, has a crash ax in the cockpit right behind the copilot so that we can, if we have to, either crack into the door or crack into the windows in the event of an emergency, we can do it," Patterson said. "If the copilot used the crash ax, that is savage because that thing will hurt you."
FLYDUBAI PILOT SHOWED WORLD 'THE HIGHEST FORM OF COURAGE,' INDIA'S PM SAYS

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told "FOX & Friends" on Thursday morning that the copilot appeared to have undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination," but said officials would need days to determine whether he had ties to Iran. President Donald Trump since expressed the belief there were ties to Iran.
WATCH: PATTERSON CALLS COCKPIT AX ATTACK 'SAVAGE':

"International carriers and a few domestic carriers cast a very wide net looking for applicants to be aircrew members and pilots," Patterson said, noting he has emailed Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy of his concerns. "And sometimes that net is a little too wide for who they attract to their airlines."

Patterson said U.S. and foreign airlines typically focus heavily on background checks, medical history and aviation violations, but warned that personality changes or radicalization can be difficult to detect once a pilot is hired.
Patterson also warned that pilots often fly with colleagues they barely know – much less a deep understanding of their mental health.

"You never know what you're gonna bring to the table, what you gonna find in the cockpit next to you when you first get to the cockpit, because we don't fly with the same guys multiple times – we fly with different people almost every single time," he continued. "So every single time we get in a cockpit, we're meeting somebody for the first time, nine times out of 10.

"So we never know who we're getting either. And that's why the initial conversation in the cockpit's important. What's your background? What's mine? How's your family life? What's going on in your world? That kind of stuff will flesh out some of that stuff, but you can't flesh it all out. There's just no way. And you don't know."

There remains a potential security loophole that needs to be closed with that 737 crash ax in the cockpit, regardless of whether U.S. commercial crews are only randomly screened at airports, according to Patterson.

"It's right there," Patterson said Thursday before official reports noted the crash ax as the weapon used by the suspected terrorist. "You know, I can easily see the copilot saying he needed to stretch. He pulls out of the seat because we do this in the 737. It's a very tight cockpit.

"Occasionally one pilot will get up, stand in the back of the cockpit and just stretch, you know, get the blood pumping. And it would be very easy for the copilot just to reach down while standing up and grab that ax. I mean, I can see it happening, and God forbid if it did because that's brutal."
AMERICA BUILT A FORTRESS AFTER 9/11. THEN THE THREAT STARTED HIDING IN PLAIN SIGHT
Israeli tourists leave a FlyDubai plane which departed from Ben-Gurion International Airport in Tel Aviv and landed in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, Nov. 8, 2020. (AP Photo/Malak Harb)
The terrorist scheme emphasizes that the U.S. should scrutinize not only domestic airline hiring, but also foreign crews entering American airspace, he warned.

"I think the United States needs to take a close look at not only who we are allowing to operate heavy machinery in this country, and by heavy machinery, I mean aviation, airplanes," Patterson said. "Who we are hiring and putting into those positions of authority, and then more importantly, who are we allowing from the other carriers to fly into our airspace?"

Netanyahu noted to Fox News that the FlyDubai copilot attack was an Omani national who made it through a "loophole" of an Israeli restriction against pilots from countries that do not have diplomatic relations with Israel.
While "9/11 changed everything in terms of aviation for everybody," clearly there is far more work to be done to ensure airline safety, he concluded.

"You never know what you're carrying on the back of the airplane," he said. "Sometimes the guy you're flying with is a wild card and sometimes the guys in the back of the airplane are a wild card. And I think that just some companies do the job, the security job, and they do the vetting screening better than other companies do."

title: South Carolina birthday girls’ trip allegedly turns deadly at the hands of bartender, friend says
summary: Ruth Peterson said she watched her best friend get shoved down stairs at Coot's Bar & Grill on Edisto Island, South Carolina, during a birthday getaway.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A long-awaited getaway for two best friends celebrating birthdays together ended in tragedy when a bartender allegedly shoved a woman down stairs, leaving her fatally injured outside a South Carolina beachside bar.
Mary Lopez Hunt, 68, has been charged with voluntary manslaughter and assault and battery of a high and aggravated nature, according to Colleton County court records.
Ruth Peterson recalled the painful memory to Fox News Digital on Oct. 1, 2026, just two days before the one-year mark of her friend’s death.

Peterson had just left to get their car, as her friend, 62-year-old Minnesota resident Joyce Tomlinson, went to settle their tab at Coot’s Bar & Grill on Edisto Island at about 11 p.m. on Oct. 3, 2025.
Best friends since childhood, Joyce Tomlinson, left, and Ruth Peterson, right, enjoyed raising their families together, Peterson told Fox News Digital. (Courtesy of Ruth Peterson)
SEND US A TIP
Hearing her friend’s voice, Peterson turned at the bottom of the stairs and looked up, she said.
At the top of the stairs, she saw Tomlinson — a woman she described as meek and friendly — exchange words briefly with another woman behind her. She couldn’t hear what was said.
"Next thing I know, Joyce had turned around to head back down [the stairs], and this woman runs at her, and with both hands just pushes her, and she just sailed," Peterson said, stifling tears.
"She didn't fall down the steps. She didn't roll down the steps… She didn't touch the steps."
"She went head first and landed on this concrete slab."
Peterson rushed to her friend and couldn’t find a pulse, she said. Tomlinson began bleeding from her mouth and ears, she said.
"I knew it was bad."
Hunt told authorities that Tomlinson was belligerent and yelled at bartenders before she was asked to leave, records show. She alleges that Tomlinson fell down the stairs.

Mary Lopez Hunt has been charged with voluntary manslaughter after allegedly pushing Joyce Tomlinson down the stairs outside Coot's Bar & Grill in Edisto Beach, S.C., on Oct. 3, 2025. (Colleton County Sheriff's Office)
Authorities arrived at the bar and found Tomlinson lying on the pavement at the bottom of the stairs, according to a heavily redacted report.
GOT A TIP?
Tomlinson was flown to a hospital by helicopter and she died a little more than three weeks later.
‘Itty-bitty, tiny woman’
Tomlinson was an "itty-bitty, tiny" woman with a "meek and mild" personality, Peterson said. She can’t believe the legal aide who helped people resolve financial issues would start a fight, she said.
Tomlinson and Peterson had been friends for 50 years, Peterson said.

As young girls in Minnesota, they loved to roller skate together. And as they grew older and started families of their own, their children grew up playing together, too. Eventually, they moved away from each other but remained close friends.
For years, they’d discussed meeting to celebrate their 60th birthdays together. But "life got in the way," Peterson said.
Then in 2025, Tomlinson called and said she was coming to visit in October so they could celebrate their birthdays together, Peterson remembered.
When they checked into their rented condo in Edisto Beach, South Carolina, an employee recommended Coot’s Bar & Grill, she said.
Edisto Island (seen here) is one of South Carolina's several Sea Islands. (Getty Images)
They sat at the bar and each had two drinks, Peterson said. When a solo performer began playing music, the two women stood up and danced.
Then the bar became crowded, so they decided to leave and catch up at the condo, Peterson said.

Tomlinson went to pay the bill. Peterson went for the car.
"I left the bar and walked down the steps, the same steps that we came up [to go] in. I turned around to see how far behind me she was… and that's when I saw her standing at the top of the steps."
Moments later, her friend was unconscious. They never spoke again.
Joyce Tomlinson, left, and Ruth Peterson, right, enjoyed raising their families together, Peterson told Fox News Digital. (Courtesy of Ruth Peterson)
‘Loving mom,’ ’trustworthy friend’
Tomlinson’s friends and family still are trying to piece together how the fight could turned violent so quickly, Peterson said.
At her funeral, friends and family remembered Tomlinson as "a loving mom" and "a trustworthy friend," Peterson wrote in a eulogy read at the funeral. She wasn’t married but did leave behind a son.
"It's just been very surreal," Peterson said. "It's very hard to believe that she's gone and that somebody would do that to another person."

Hunt was released on $100,000 bond for each of her charges. Later, bond was revoked and she was taken back into custody in the Colleton County Jail in Walterboro, South Carolina. It was not immediately clear why her bond was revoked.

A 12-year-old girl was killed and three adults were wounded after two gunmen allegedly opened fire during a dispute near a youth football game in Baltimore, Maryland, authorities said Saturday.

The preteen girl was apparently caught in the crossfire at Leon Day Park, where a youth football league was holding its homecoming event, Baltimore Police Commissioner Richard Worley said during a news conference.
The two men are believed to have been in a dispute that started over a parking space, according to Worley.
"What we know is that there was some type of argument between two cowards, and of course, they both opened fire on each other," Worley said.

As of Saturday evening, police said they were searching for at least two suspects, whom authorities described as adult men. No arrests had been announced as of late Saturday night.
Baltimore police told Fox News Digital that officers responded to the 1200 block of North Franklintown Road at approximately 6:15 p.m. after receiving multiple reports of gunfire.
Officers found a 25-year-old woman suffering from an apparent gunshot wound and the 12-year-old girl, who was transported to a hospital but later pronounced dead.

title: Cornell president says university 'must do better' on handling of sexual assault allegations

story: Cornell University President Michael Kotlikoff delivers remarks following an alleged gang rape involving students. (Cornell University)

Cornell University President Michael Kotlikoff said Saturday that the institution "must do better" as it faces questions over its response to sexual assault allegations involving seven former fraternity brothers.

"What happened to Jane Doe in 2024 is deeply disturbing and will weigh heavily on our community for years to come. My heart aches when I think of what she experienced," Kotlikoff said in a video statement to the Cornell community.

Kotlikoff said the case raises questions about sexual assault, campus party culture, alcohol and drug abuse on the Ithaca, New York, campus, as well as the investigation conducted after the allegations were reported.

"I want to acknowledge something that can be difficult for an institution to say we don't have all the answers, but we are committed to investigating and finding the answers our community deserves. I believe we as an administration, and we as a community must do better," Kotlikoff said.
INSIDE EXPLOSIVE CORNELL RAPE ALLEGATIONS: 7 MEN ACCUSED, CONFLICTING ACCOUNTS AND A POLITICAL FIRESTORM

Kotlikoff welcomed an independent review by an outside law firm into Cornell's handling of the case and said the university supports Gov. Kathy Hochul's decision to turn the criminal investigation over to New York Attorney General Letitia James.
He said Cornell would not wait for those reviews to conclude before making changes to prevention and education, student support, mental health and substance use resources and investigative processes.

"We will act," Kotlikoff said.Jane Doe alleges in a lawsuit that seven former Chi Phi fraternity brothers drugged and sexually assaulted her during an October 2024 night at the fraternity house. Doe was a 20-year-old Cornell undergraduate at the time.

The men have denied wrongdoing, with some maintaining the sexual activity was consensual and others denying they participated. No criminal charges have been filed against the seven men.
Doe filed a 101-page lawsuit last month accusing the former fraternity members of sexual assault and rape and naming Cornell and other entities.

The case came under renewed scrutiny after Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said his office had not received the full transcript of Doe's November 2024 interview with Cornell University Police before prosecutors initially declined to pursue charges.

Van Houten reopened the investigation before Hochul appointed the Office of the Attorney General as special prosecutor. James said Friday that her office was conducting an "active criminal investigation."

The Chi Phi fraternity house at Cornell University, left, and New York Gov. Kathy Hochul with Attorney General Letitia James, right. Kotlikoff also addressed frustration over Cornell's communication about its response to the allegations and said the university would make a greater effort to be transparent.

"There are real legal and privacy limits on what we can say, but we will make a greater effort to explain what we can to provide context about the actions Cornell has taken and to be more transparent," Kotlikoff said.

"Hello … Hello red …Hello red … Hdudhdbdbbd … 7888ejdj … Yolo … Ddodjjf … 890 … Hdjd … Djdj … red … Yup red … Hello … Jhhhuuh … Hhdj … Jjjjjjjjjjjj … Hello red … Red red," Crooks' messages said.

title: Coast Guard finds debris field off Nantucket after Boston-bound medevac plane vanishes with 6 on board
summary: A Gulfstream G100 with 6 people on board vanished en route to Boston from Bermuda on Saturday as search crews deploy off Nantucket to conduct a search. Officials said a debris field has been found.
story: Fox News correspondent CB Cotton discusses the Coast Guard’s assistance in the search for a jet missing off the coast of Nantucket on ‘Fox Report.’

U.S. Coast Guard search crews located a debris field off the Nantucket coast that has been confirmed to be associated with a medevac flight with six people on board that disappeared Saturday morning while en route to Boston from Bermuda.

Crews are continuing to search for potential survivors, and the Coast Guard cutter William Sparling will continue search efforts throughout the night. The Coast Guard said it would hold a news conference Sunday morning.

Authorities are searching for the Gulfstream G100, a twin-engine, midsize jet, off Nantucket. Both air and surface crews have been deployed to the area, according to the Coast Guard Northeast District.
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) reported losing contact with the aircraft early Saturday, the Coast Guard said.
FRANTIC SEARCH UNDERWAY FOR CREW AFTER BOEING 737 WRECKAGE FOUND BY OFFICIALS
U.S. Coast Guard crews search off the Nantucket coast for a medevac plane believed to have crashed en route to Boston from Bermuda, Saturday. (U.S. Coast Guard)
Earlier Saturday, the FAA issued a statement that said it is "coordinating with the Rescue Coordination Center and the U.S. Coast Guard to locate the aircraft."
Canada’s foreign affairs department said it was "deeply concerned" by the aircraft’s disappearance and confirmed Canadians were among those on board.
Two Canadian pilots, two medical workers, one patient and a patient's companion were on board.
Consular officials are in contact with relevant authorities as search and rescue efforts continue, the department said in posts on X.
"Our thoughts are with everyone on board and their loved ones," the department said, thanking the U.S. Coast Guard and others involved in the search.
According to data from FlightAware, the plane took off from Bermuda L. F. Wade International Airport at 11:41 p.m. ET.
The FAA told Fox News Digital it issued a Search and Rescue Alert Notice at about 1:20 a.m. ET.
The Massachusetts Port Authority (Massport), which operates the state's three major airports, confirmed that the aircraft did not arrive at Boston Logan International Airport as scheduled.
"Our thoughts are with those on board and their loved ones as the search continues," the agency said.

Nantucket harbormaster and police search the south shore of the island Saturday, after a Boston-bound plane reportedly vanished off the island. (Nantucket Current)
The Canadian-registered aircraft is owned by Latitude Air Ambulance, the company confirmed to Fox News Digital, adding that it was a medevac flight.
Latitude Air Ambulance is a medical transport company that brings patients home from around the world when they require specialized care.
Latitude Air Ambulance said the flight was supposed to take about two hours.
The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) told Fox News Digital that it is currently gathering information and declined to provide an update on the situation.
A Coast Guard HC-130 Hercules is among the assets searching for the plane. (U.S. Coast Guard, File)

"My thoughts are with the six people aboard the missing air ambulance traveling from Bermuda to Boston, and their families," Bermuda's Premier David Burt said in a statement. "Government has contacted the family and US search and rescue authorities. We are praying that everyone will be found safe."
The plane plummeted from 24,000 feet to 11,000 feet in just three minutes at around 1 a.m., according to data from FlightAware.

Skyport, the company that manages the airport in Bermuda, confirmed that a "Canadian-registered air ambulance departed L. F. Wade International Airport for Boston at approximately 12:41 am on Saturday, October 3, 2026, with six souls on board, including four crew members and two passengers."

"The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration has advised that air traffic controllers lost contact with the aircraft off the coast of Nantucket Island, Massachusetts, and a search is currently underway. Skyport has no further information to provide at this time," the company added.
Waters off the Nantucket coast, where the Coast Guard is searching for a missing plane. (Stan Grossfeld/The Boston Globe via Getty Images, File)

"This aircraft was dealt a dire one-two punch: a critical safety in-flight problem, followed almost immediately by a perilous weather event and an 11,000-foot plunge," former U.S. Department of Transportation Inspector General Mary Schiavo said in analysis shared with Fox News Digital.
