“I thought it was a plane malfunction, but then I started hearing screaming about the stabbings,” Aviatar Alevi, a 17-year-old student, told NBC News. “Then I understood the weight of the actual situation.”
Alevi said he thought he was going to die as he felt the plane rapidly descend, with “screaming, people running, panicking, blood.”
Another passenger, Motti Cohen Or, 70, told NBC News that he heard a woman shouting that “someone is stabbing someone in the cockpit” before the aircraft dived “toward the ground.”
Flight data indicates the Boeing 737, flight number FZ 1073, plunged by 14,125 feet in just 29 seconds, according to Flightradar24.

All Flydubai flights to and from Israel have been temporarily suspended as authorities continue their investigation into what occurred on Flight FZ 1073, a spokesperson for the airline said in a statement.
“This temporary suspension will allow the relevant authorities to continue their work and establish all the facts surrounding the incident,” the spokesperson said in the statement.

The midair incident led to a diversion and an emergency landing at Saudi Arabia’s Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz International Airport, known as Tabuk Airport. A rescue flight later brought passengers to Israel’s Ben Gurion Airport.

At Ben Gurion, Netanyahu personally thanked a passenger still wearing a bloodied T-shirt, who told cameras he was among those to enter the cockpit and subdue the attacking pilot. Netanyahu’s office named the man as Hayun. Netanyahu later said that Hayun is a plumber in an interview on Fox News.
Hayun told Netanyahu that, as he made his way to the cockpit, the plane took a steep nose dive which knocked him sideways, according to the Israeli government press office.
Three other passengers helped in the effort to save the plane and those aboard, Hayun told reporters at Ben Gurion.
The group struggled to open the cockpit door.
“We managed to get it open, but what made it difficult for us was the pilot himself — he had been stabbed and was on the other side of the door,” he said.
Netanyahu said on the CBS program that when Hayun went in the cockpit he saw the pilot who had initiated the attack trying to crash the plane.
“He wasn’t sitting in the pilot seat, trying to stabilize the plane, he was trying to jam the equipment,” Netanyahu said.
Hayun told Netanyahu that he confronted the pilot who had initiated the attack, according to the Israeli government press office.
“I grabbed the attacker, and choked him, pulled him out first,” Hayun said. “I started pulling the controls.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Hayun told Netanyahu that he took actions based on what he had seen on a TV show and helped stabilize the plane, according to the Israeli government press office.
“Thank God, we pulled it off. We really put our heads together and worked as a team,” Hayun said.
“It was between fear and a sense of a do-or-die situation,” Hayun added. “We had to win. We had to pull through and come out on top.”

Israeli officials also praised the stabbed pilot, identified as Indian national Captain Smit Machchhar, for his actions in opening the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to rush in, secure the cockpit and prevent the plane from crashing.
“He saved the lives of 174 people, including Israeli citizens and other nationals,” Netanyahu said on X. “I wish Captain Machchhar a speedy and full recovery. He is a true hero.”
In the interview on Fox News, Netanyahu said that there were 30 children on the plane.
Video from on board appeared to show two people lying on the floor, visibly bloodied as others crowd around them.
Machchhar is in stable condition in a hospital in Saudi Arabia, according to the Indian Embassy in Riyadh.
Four U.S. citizens, who are dual nationals, were on the flight, per two U.S. officials.
Prime minister’s spokesperson Doron Spielman said that “there is a strong opinion” that the incident was a terror attack, “but we can’t be sure until we debrief everybody.”
No country or terror organization has claimed the incident.
Two senior U.S. law enforcement officials briefed on the investigation also told NBC News that investigators say the pilot who began stabbing the co-pilot is from Oman.
The officials did not name that pilot.
The Omani Embassy in the U.S. did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
An investigation by Saudi authorities is ongoing, David Mencer, a spokesperson for the Israeli Prime Minister’s Office, said.

The stabbing increasingly looks like an act of terrorism based on the early results from the investigation, according to a senior U.S. official briefed on the Israeli investigation and a Saudi official briefed on the investigation.

The spokesperson for the Saudi Embassy in the U.S., Hessa Alyahya, said authorities were waiting to determine whether the attack was a dispute between the pilots or whether it was an act sponsored by Iran or the Houthis. She said it was expected that more would be known within 24 hours.

Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan, deputy prime minister and foreign affairs minister of the United Arab Emirates, and Israel’s foreign affairs minister, Gideon Saar, spoke on the phone Wednesday afternoon.

According to the UAE Foreign Affairs Ministry, Al Nahyan asked about the safety of passengers on the Flydubai flight, which had “experienced a security incident that was successfully brought under control” and wished “good health and well-being” for the passengers.
There are no indications that Iran directed or was involved in today’s attack, a senior U.S. official briefed on the Israeli investigation told NBC News.
The preliminary Israeli investigation strongly suggests that the incident was an attempted terrorist attack by the Omani pilot who stabbed his co-pilot, the official said.
Netanyahu said on CBS that it was too early to tell if there was any Iranian involvement.

“We’ve had signs that Iran, in particular through its proxies, was intending to heighten terrorist attacks against Israel and Israeli nationals abroad,” Netanyahu said. “But I think it’s too early to say whether there was Iranian collusion here. I think we’ll find out. It won’t take a long time.”
The aircraft was “successfully secured” and landed by on-duty crew traveling on board, Flydubai said.

“At this early stage, the underlying reasons and motives behind this event are unknown and remain subject to a formal investigation,” the airline said, adding: “We urge all parties to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts.”
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz meanwhile told Israeli media the incident “was a jihadist terrorist attack attempt,” without saying how he reached that conclusion.

After hours on the ground in Saudi Arabia, the diverted passengers were brought back to Ben Gurion Airport, where they were greeted by well-wishers waving Israeli flags and reunited with family members.
Some of those returning waved to the cameras and discussed their experiences, while exhausted parents carried their young children through the terminal.
Peleg Itali, 17, said there was a family with small children near him on the flight.
“The mother doesn’t even know what to tell them,” he said. “No one knows everything, because no one knew what was going on.”

At least one person, a passenger in his 50s, was taken to a hospital with a “chest injury,” said Aryeh Myers, a paramedic with Magen David Adom, Israel’s national emergency agency. Myers described the person’s health condition as “mild.”
Earlier, U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee expressed relief on X that the incident didn’t turn out to be “more serious.”
“This had everyone in the Middle East (esp Israel) on FULL ALERT this morning,” he said. “Having pilots inflight detouring to ‘fist city’ not your ordinary experience.”

Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters that domestically, the TSA will continue to be “at high alert,” adding: “We have no credible threats to us right now that would coordinate what took place over there.”

The incident comes at a time of high tensions in Israel ahead of next month’s parliamentary election, a key test for Netanyahu as he faces discontent over Gaza and Iran. The leader has made national security a core part of his platform ahead of the vote on Oct. 27, while also facing pressure from hardliners who favor a more aggressive stance in the West Bank.
Matt Bradley and Yarden Segev reported from Tel Aviv, Chantal Da Silva and Raf Sanchez from London and Nicole Acevedo from New York.

title: British police find no explosives in vehicles of men detained near base used by U.S.
summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the incident near RAF Fairford, which facilitates strikes on Iran, “clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor,” an allegation British officials haven’t confirmed.
story: No explosives were found in vehicles searched after five men were arrested in connection with a huge security operation near an air base the U.S. Air Force uses to facilitate strikes on Iran, British counterterrorism police confirmed Tuesday.

In an update explaining Monday’s decision to release all five suspects who were arrested on terrorism and explosives charges on bail, Laurence Taylor, Britain’s head of counterterrorism policing, said “a quantity” of gasoline was recovered from three vans near RAF Fairford.

“Those vehicles have been subject to extensive examination, with the support of military assets and forensic experts, and we can confirm that no improvised explosive devices were found,” he said, adding that investigators had searched properties in London.
Taylor said it was an “investigative decision” to release the men on bail, “grounded in experience and careful considerations of policing powers.”
No charges have been filed against the men.
President Donald Trump told reporters Tuesday that he was disappointed about that decision.
“I’m just disappointed that they caught terrorists — they did a good job, and then they sort of let them go,” he said, adding, “How do you give bail to a terrorist?”
Asked if it was a long-standing investigation, Trump replied, “A long standing. Yeah, we were involved in it.”
“They put them out on bail. I assume they have, they have them watched closely. But these were serious people, seriously bad people, and they should not have done that,” he added.

Trump also said he was surprised about the decision to release the men on bail on Monday. “I would have said, ‘Don’t let them have bail,’” Trump said in the Oval Office. “I’m surprised that they released them. I wouldn’t have done that.”

title: Settlers clash with Israeli forces to block Palestinian family’s return home
summary: It is the second time the Tubassi family has suffered at the hands of Jewish settlers in just over a month. On Aug. 28, masked settlers attacked and injured them and an NBC News crew that was interviewing them.
story: TEL AVIV — Dozens of Jewish settlers repulsed an attempt by Israeli security forces to return a Palestinian family to its home in the occupied West Bank before setting fire to its property and car.

The Tubassi family was forced to leave its home in July following a weekslong siege by violent settlers in the West Bank town of Jalud. But after security forces tried to enforce an order by Israel’s High Court of Justice to facilitate the family’s return Monday night, an extended and violent confrontation ensued, Mahmoud Tubassi, 60, said.

“I went through a terrifying experience that I could never have imagined,” he said in a telephone interview Tuesday. “We saw death with our own eyes. Death came very close to us at the hands of the settlers.”

It is the second time that Tubassi and his wife, Aida Ahmed Abdullah, 51, have suffered at the hands of Jewish settlers in just over a month. On Aug. 28, masked settlers attacked and injured them and an NBC News crew that was interviewing them. The crew were injured and Abdullah was beaten unconscious but has since recovered.
Add to Google
Add to Google

Tubassi said their latest ordeal began just before midnight Monday when Abdel Azim Wadi, the mayor of the nearby village of Qusra, which has also faced serious settler violence, told him that Israeli officials would accompany him, his wife and their son Wael Tubassi, 33, to their home in Jalud.
After they were picked up by four Israeli vehicles, they were driven the short distance to their home — two structures that sit in a small walled compound atop a hill, he said.
As the family arrived, settlers started throwing stones at the armed police and military, who responded with tear gas and stun grenades, he said.

“They could shoot rubber bullets, they could fire live bullets in air,” Tubassi said of the Israeli security forces’ response. “They could use force, but they didn’t do anything, unfortunately,” he added.

title: A search for their loved ones’ remains, three months after Venezuela earthquakes
summary: Sleeping in tents in front of collapsed buildings and removing rubble with bare hands, family members and volunteers search the ruins with at least 1,500 people missing.
story: LA GUAIRA, Venezuela — Upon entering the ruins of the Jurel building, one hears two things: the murmur of a few curious passersby gazing at the tomb of memories left by the June 24 earthquakes and the creaking of the rubble.

Three months have passed since two earthquakes in quick succession shook this area of ​​the Venezuelan coast. But the devastation continues to resonate for those who haven’t been able to properly say goodbye to loved ones.

Cristian Verdú, 23, lost his brother, his cousin and his mother that day. The bodies of the latter two remain buried in the building’s rubble. A drone search confirmed their location, along with the bodies of other victims.
The building’s collapse is so severe that his search has become — to say the least — nearly impossible after months of searching.

“I never left her alone while she was alive. Anyone who knew my family knew my mother and knew that no matter what happened, I was always there for my mother,” said Verdú, who survived on June 24 because he was in Naiguatá, a town about 45 minutes from Playa Grande, where the Jurel is located.

The search for Verdú’s family went viral following a video posted by journalist Maryorin Méndez in which Verdú pleaded for help recovering his loved ones’ bodies. Others had been able to retrieve their family members’ remains. Finding himself alone, Verdú set up a tent near the Jurel to oversee the search for his mom.

A Mexican rescue team tried to get her out, but the danger of the building collapsing was too great. The Jurel building had 12 floors. Verdú’s mother was on the eighth floor and ended up on the sixth: Its collapse wasn’t like others in that the lower floors partially withstood the earthquake, but the upper floors collapsed one after another.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
What was revealed were the exposed rooms, bathrooms and halls. A swimming pool sloping toward a precipice warns passersby that a tragedy occurred in the building.
‘Still had a conversation to finish’
Verdú recounted that the Jurel was his family’s vacation home; they lived in Caracas, in the 23 de Enero neighborhood, a popular area in the western part of the city.

On the day of the earthquakes, Verdú went for the first time to the San Juan drumming festival, a coastal tradition honoring St. John the Baptist that is celebrated every June 24. Going to the festival is the reason he’s alive, he explained.

The day before, he was with his family and had spent a lot of time with his mother. “My little brother was in the pool, and I spent the day with her. We talked, and she took some secrets with her because I told her things that day, and we still had a conversation to finish,” he told Noticias Telemundo.

When the earthquake struck and he saw that practically nothing remained of his vacation home, he said he experienced a mental breakdown. “I ran out, screaming, not finding my family alive and then having to report that my cousin and a friend of my brother had also died,” Verdú said, adding that it was a difficult situation because other family members thought he had also died.
He immediately began searching for his family, especially his mother.

On the eve of his birthday, almost two months after the earthquake, Verdú announced on social media that he was ending his search for his mom and cousin. Without resources, there was no other option but to leave.
“I wasn’t feeling well anymore. I was exhausted,” Verdú said, adding that the situation was getting more complicated every day.
Even so, Verdú continues to wait and hope. “The case was closed on social media, but the search hasn’t stopped because there are still people who want to get her out and want to help me,” he said.
If they demolish the building with his mother’s and cousin’s remains still inside, Verdú is prepared to continue searching for her, even if it’s among what remains of the rubble.
“It won’t be easy, but believe me, after they demolish the building, I will go back for my mother,” he said, hoping perhaps he can find some peace.
Verdú said that every night he dreams that his mother wants to tell him something, but she always stops or gets scared.

“Many things were left unfinished. My mother’s birthday was coming up, and we had a trip planned, but life had other plans. Perhaps my mother and my little brother had to take a trip that I couldn’t go on,” he said.
Living in a camp, and waiting
Stories like Verdú’s are repeated throughout La Guaira. At Residencias Caribe, family members and volunteer rescuers continue the search for people.
Residencias Caribe was part of a residential development and consisted of three towers. Two of them remained standing; the other collapsed completely.

At the pool area, which overlooks the towers, residents wait for loved ones’ bodies to be recovered. Rescuers don’t have a precise number, but they estimate that more than 70 people’s remains are still in the complex, even though fewer than that number have been declared missing there. Residents have two theories for the discrepancy: Either some people’s relatives didn’t know they were there or entire families perished, with no one left to claim them.

Lying in a tent, next to a fan that cools the air and keeps the mosquitoes away, is Angie Sojo. She has lived in Residencias Caribe for over 20 years and for the past three months has been searching for her husband, Gustavo Adolfo Riascos Gómez, 51.

Her life collapsed along with her home in a single night, and now she awaits news from the rescuers. Sojo’s husband was on the second floor of Tower B of the residences. After the collapse, his body ended up in the parking lot, and for three months they have been trying to recover it without success. Sojo currently lives in the encampment with other neighbors and rescuers who stay overnight.
“At first we all slept on a mattress, and then they started bringing us tents,” she said.

The story of Residencias Caribe is not so different from that of other buildings in the area: There was no help, no rescuers, no supplies. Little by little, some help arrived, and even then, it wasn’t enough.
At Residencias Caribe, the problem isn’t just the collapse, but also the flooding. The first floors are full of water, and pumps have been needed to lower the water level.

On June 24, Sojo was working in Caracas, about 40 minutes from La Guaira. She said that when she got to the building, she was so disoriented that she just started shouting her husband’s name. She and her 20-year-old daughter have been waiting for news for three months and are happy every time a neighbor’s remains are rescued, but she said her heart breaks thinking about when her turn will come.

“It causes anxiety and joy at the same time because it’s another neighbor who’s leaving. I cling to our love,” Sojo said about her husband, “and if it had been the other way around, he’d be here looking for me, too.”
‘Something I owe her’

Valeria Alcalá has been searching for her mother since the earthquakes struck. Alcalá is 18 years old and will soon start university. But for now, she waits every day for news about the search for her mother.
“I’ve been here since it all happened. This has been a constant struggle because I feel like it’s something I owe her,” she said.
Alcalá lost track of her mother and stepfather on June 24. The last time she saw them was the day before, at the San Juan drumming festival. Alcalá remembers them telling her to behave.
They both died in the collapsed buildings; they were downstairs, having arrived five minutes before the earthquakes. Alcalá’s relatives helped her, but they didn’t know where to begin the search.

Her stepfather’s body was found a month ago. It was one of the hardest moments, she said. “Knowing they’re there is not the same as having the body pulled out and having to say, ‘Yes, it’s him.’ Recognizing the body is difficult,” Alcalá said.
She relied on neighbors who had become rescuers. One of them is named Chelo. He also lost his family in the earthquakes and stayed to continue helping fellow former residents.

Nayibe Geromes is searching for her mother, Leída Josefina Mata Cupido, 64. On June 24, she didn’t know if her mother had managed to escape, so she went to shelters hoping for an answer. There was none. Since then, she has been staying at the residences where her mother lived, waiting for her body to be found.
“I’m certain she’s here because they came in and took things that indicate she was here, like her ID, which I still have, her wallet with all her cards, and her cellphone. She’s here,” Geromes said.

The Residencias Caribe residents have become like family after spending three months searching for their loved ones in the rubble. Their only remaining support comes from volunteer rescuers and family members.
“I want to give her eternal rest and get her back so that we too can move on because life goes on. We have cried a lot,” Geromes said.
The neighbors explained that they no longer feel sadness when they find a body and are happy the person’s remains will get the rest they deserve.

“My mom deserves rest. Angie (Sojo)’s husband, all of us who are here I think deserve to be at peace and go home, because this is a tireless fight,” Geromes said, “but I assure you that we will be here until the very end.”
These rescuers aren’t leaving

Marcel Hernández is one of the volunteer rescuers at Residencias Caribe. He has been pulling bodies from the structures for three months. He was a construction worker by trade, but since June 24, he has done nothing but recover corpses. He recounted that the first bodies he recovered at Residencias Caribe were those of his family: his cousin, his cousin’s wife and their four children.
“We started with a pickax — breaking slab after slab. To this day, I haven’t stopped searching,” Hernández said. He got his family out 17 days later.
Hernández promised fellow resident Chelo that they wouldn’t leave until they found his family, and Chelo promised him the same. They insist they won’t leave until they’ve rescued everyone.

Yessamin Medina, known as “La Topito” (“Little Mole”), is another volunteer rescuer at Residencias Caribe. Medina explained that before the earthquakes, she was afraid of the dark and was claustrophobic, but she overcame that fear there.

“I became a ‘mole’ out of love and empathy, without receiving anything in return, simply out of love for my fellow man. I can’t be at home when they still need help here. I’m here out of love for them,” she said.

Medina is 20 years old and became a “mole” thanks to the foundation she created, Puente de Esperanza (Bridge of Hope), after the earthquakes. The volunteer rescuers have left family, homes and jobs to continue helping.

“We have practically been working here with our hands, but with our hands we have achieved many things,” she said, explaining that the lack of machinery and the disastrous nature of the collapse have made the work extremely difficult.
The anguish of the families is the hardest thing, according to Medina. “At home, I’m talking to myself and trying to figure out how I can get them out faster,” she said.
An earlier version of this article was first published by Noticias Telemundo.

title: Terrorism suspects arrested near British air base used by U.S. are released on bail
summary: The five British nationals were detained after a massive security operation near a base the U.S. uses to facilitate strikes on Iran.
story: LONDON — Police have arrested five British nationals in connection with a massive security operation near a base used by the U.S. Air Force to facilitate strikes on Iran, the counterterrorism officials running the operation said Monday.

The five men, all from London and in their early to mid-20s, were arrested Sunday on suspicion of terrorism and explosives offenses after three suspicious vehicles were seen moving toward RAF Fairford, a Royal Air Force station about 90 minutes west of London.
Dozens of homes were evacuated in the early morning, and a large emergency presence was seen around the installation, shaking the normally quiet area in rural Cotswolds.

But after “extensive interviews and inquiries,” the head of Counter Terrorism Policing, Laurence Taylor, said Monday that they had been released on bail, adding that “does not mean that the investigation is over.”
“They are subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others,” he added.
